title: short lyric poem|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
Parking Lot Snow

The sodium lamps bleed amber
over rows of empty cars.
One flake, then another, lands
on the windshield's scar.

No footprints yet, no tire track—
the world holds its breath
while inside, someone's monitor
beats back the dark, steady as death.

Snow settles on the wheelchair ramp,
on the curb's chipped edge,
hiding every oil stain,
hiding the ledge.

I stand here in my thin coat
and let the quiet grow—
the first clean thing all winter,
falling slow, falling slow.

title: ballad in quatrains|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
First Snow, IU Health Parking Garage, Level 3

The sodium lights bleed tangerine
where slush cakes the wheel of a transport chair
left propped by the pay station, chipped paint sheened
with flakes that stick like ash from a prayer.

A kid in a cancer center hoodie
presses his palm to the passenger glass,
traces a snowflake that melts before he
can pin down the shape it meant to pass.

I’m here for the scan that won’t give answers,
boots crunching salt crumbs sharp as broken pills,
when a flake lands light on the lanyard tassel
strung with my mom’s old key to the house we sold.

The plow driver blares old Taylor Swift,
scraping the lane where the hearse idles slow,
snow sticking thick to the magnetic gift
shop ribbon tied round its side mirror’s bow.

No hush. No soft blanket. No clean slate.
Just static, a cough, a car alarm’s blare,
flakes sticking fast to the cold steel plate
bolted to the leg of the vet who stands there
holding a takeout cup of burnt decaf,
watching the snow stick first to the grime—
the oil slicks, the gum smudges, the crumpled half
of a get-well card someone tossed before time.
One flake lands square on the barcode sticker
stuck to the envelope holding my bill,
white as the blank space where the doctor’ll write her
best guess at how much of me’s left to kill.

It doesn’t care if we’re well or we’re breaking,
doesn’t save itself for the pines, for the yards.
It settles first on the spaces where waiting
has worn all the shine off the world’s hard parts.
I brush it off my coat when the crosswalk sign blinks,
taste one when I breathe, sharp as a new scar—
the first snow don’t fix a single goddamned thing.
It just shows up, same as we are.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
The Moon Over a Refugee Camp

When silver moon doth climb the tent-fringed hill,
Her soft light spills on beds of straw and dust,
Where hollow eyes, which woe and coldness chill,
Gaze at her glow with unfulfilled trust.

She looks no more on courts or gardens fair,
But tattered canvas stretched on barren sand;
The wail of babes, the voiceless, worn despair,
Steal through her beams across the war-torn land.

Yet doth she lay same light on far-off home,
On ruined orchards and the broken door;
She tells the lost, though they in exile roam,
One gentle heaven still doth them deplore.

So let her shine, till dawn shall break the chain,
And night give place to peaceful homes again.

title: blank verse meditation|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
First Snow, Hospital Parking Lot, 6:17 a.m.

The salt crunches thin under my scuffed clog—
left sole split where I caught it on the curb
last Tuesday, when I ran in for the code
that didn’t land. The snow sticks first to the rust
crust on the pickup three spots over, the one
with the sticker that says MY KID CAN BEAT UP YOUR HONOR STUDENT,
faded to the color of old bruise. It doesn’t stick
to the asphalt yet, just melts into dark splotches
like the coffee I spilled on my scrub top at 3 a.m.,
the one the new CNA tried to dab off with a chlorhexidine wipe
so now it smells like hospital and burnt roast, sharp.

I lean against the lamppost, the cold seeping through
the thin polyester of my coat, the one I stole
from my ex when I moved out, the pocket torn
where his old work knife used to sit. A sparrow
huddles on the stop sign arm, fluffed so fat
it looks like a crumpled tissue someone tossed,
and for a second I can’t tell if the white fleck
on its wing is snow or the dried betadine
I can never scrub out from under my nails, no matter
how many times I wash them. The plow guy idles
by the entrance, radio blaring that old country song
about drunk girls and Christmas, his exhaust curling
up to meet the snow, same wisp as the breath
that fogged the window of room 412 last night,
when the daughter held her mom’s hand and said
I’m here, I’m here, even when the monitor flatlined
and the breath didn’t come back.

A snowflake lands right on my eyelash, blurs
the glow of the ER sign so it bleeds pink into the gray,
and for half a breath I think I could stand here forever,
not going back in to chart the death, not going home
to the empty apartment with the milk gone sour
in the fridge, just watching the snow stick slow
to the wheelchair ramp rail, to the cracked plastic
of the abandoned patient water bottle by the trash can,
to the hood of the car where the dad is sitting
head in his hands, keys dangling from his finger,
snow piling thin on the crown of his baseball cap
like he doesn’t even feel it. No one’s out here but me,
the sparrow, the plow guy, him. The snow doesn’t care
what we’re here for. It doesn’t fall softer for the grieving,
doesn’t melt faster on the cars of people who get good news.
It just sticks where it lands, for as long as it can.
My pager buzzes against my hip, sharp as a needle stick.
I brush the snow off my sleeve, and my hand is shaking
a little, I don’t know why. I don’t look up again
when I walk toward the doors. The sparrow flies off
somewhere I can’t see. The snow keeps coming down.

title: villanelle|a beekeeper in winter
text:
The Beekeeper in Winter

The hives stand white beneath the frozen thatch,
where wind writes thin and cold across the snow.
He leans to listen, fearing what they lack.

His gloves are stiff; his breath goes blue and black.
The cedar smoke has long forgotten how to glow.
The hives stand white beneath the frozen thatch.

Around each entrance, ice has sealed the track;
no golden drummers rise, no hum runs low.
He leans to listen, fearing what they lack.

Summer is stored in amber, stacked on stack,
a sun he tasted once, then watched go.
The hives stand white beneath the frozen thatch.

He breathes for them through weather’s narrow crack,
a quiet man beside a quiet row,
and leans to listen, fearing what they lack.

April is only a rumor coming back,
a clover moon beneath the crust of snow.
The hives stand white beneath the frozen thatch;
he leans to listen, fearing what they lack.

title: free verse poem|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
First Light Through the French Press
The dark holds the grit of last night’s dreams
still settled at the bottom of the glass carafe.
Boiling water kisses the grounds slow—
no clock ticks loud enough to rush this,
no floorboard creaks yet to steal the hush.
Steam curls first toward the window,
where the sky is still the color of unwashed denim,
not yet blushed pink where the sun will pry over the roofline.
The first gurgle is the day’s first secret,
spoken only to me.

---

 Steam Thawing the Windowpane
I press my palm to the cold glass,
mug warm enough to seep through my thin sleep-shirt sleeve,
and trace a half-moon in the fog my breath and the coffee weave.
The world outside is still soft-edged, unsharpened:
the neighbor’s cat curled on the fence post,
the maple’s last fall leaves stuck to the sidewalk,
no car engines grumbling to break the spell.
The first sip burns just right,
bitter as the quiet, sweet as the knowledge
that for ten more minutes, no one needs anything from me—
no lists, no voices, no questions,
only this heat spreading from my tongue to my toes,
only the slow bleed of gold over the horizon.

---

 The First Floorboard Creak
The last of the coffee sits dark and rich in the mug,
when I hear it: the soft thud of small feet on the hallway carpet,
the mumble of a half-asleep greeting still thick with pillow lint.
The sky has turned fully honeyed now,
the cat stretching on the fence,
a distant garbage truck rumbling three streets over.
I pour a second mug, add an extra splash of cream,
and don’t wipe the half-moon I drew on the fogged glass.
The quiet doesn’t break, really—
it just softens, makes room,
carries the scent of coffee out to meet the first person
who comes looking for the light, and for me.

title: ode|grief after a dog dies
text:
I bend for the leash
hooked on the kitchen chair,
its nylon frayed where you shook
rain over the radiator.

The house still keeps
your map of warm spots:
a pale coin on the rug,
a dent beside the couch,
the threshold you watched
like a small, furry border guard.

Tonight, two nails click
in the hallway. I turn
to nothing. Not a ghost—
just my own hard heels
learning to be louder
than the silence.

I find your gray hair
caught in a sweater,
bright as piano wire,
and understand how grief
keeps a person by scent:
old straw, peanut butter,
the damp coin of your breath.

Outside, the maple drops
its keys without sound.
No one herds the wind.
No one circles three times
before lying down in the dark.

The vet handed me your collar
like a bell removed from winter.
I set it by the door.
It does not ring.
The whole world passes now
without permission.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
Sonnet to Insomnia and the Refrigerator Hum
When heavy sleep doth seal all mortal eyes,
And drowsy curtains draw on day’s last hum,
I lie alone, where unspent thought still flies,
Chasing faint ghosts that will not let me come
To that soft rest where all my cares should cease;
No poppy’s breath, no hush of midnight deep
Can lull my brain, nor bid my pulses peace—
Till low, steady, through the wall doth creep
Thy drone, thou cold steel heart of kitchen gloom!
No bird’s first note, no lover’s tender sigh
Hath power to soothe my fretting, fevered room
Like thy slow throb, that tells me time drifts by
On even wings: thou hum’st my wakefulness
To drowse, as thou dost guard the cream and cress.

title: elegy|the stars seen from a desert
text:
I camped alone where the saltbush thinned,
my sock still stiff with a hole I’d meant to mend,
and the dark came down not gently,
but like a dropped gate.

First one star, then another,
then the whole sky loosening
over mesas the color of old bones.

I thought of my mother’s hands,
how she counted change on the kitchen table,
breath smelling of lemon drops,
and how she said the dead were only far away.

Tonight I did not believe her.
Tonight the dead were nearer than my pulse—
scorpion under the canvas,
cold can of pork and beans,
the rental car’s cracked headlight
pointed toward nothing.

The stars were not lamps.
They were not promises.
They were holes in a black roof,
and behind them
more roof, more black.

I lay back on sand still warm
from a day I had wasted arguing with a man in town
about fuel, about water,
about whether the road went through.

A meteor fell,
small and sharp as a pin,
and I made no wish,
only watched it go out
over the place where the road should have been.

Coyotes, far off,
laughing at something.
My lips cracking.
The Milky Way smeared above me
like milk spilled on black cloth
that no one will clean.

I stayed until my neck ached,
until the fire was a gray breath,
until the stars began to seem not beautiful
but patient,
the way a judge is patient,
or a mirror
in a house no one returns to.

Then I crawled into the tent,
zipped the dark shut,
and left them up there—
not watching,
not caring,
still burning anyway,
each one
a small hard fact
I could not answer.

title: poem in tercets|the night shift at a diner
text:
Night Shift at the Lincoln Diner
*(tercets, unrhymed, slant cadence for late-hour breath)*

The Formica sweats old coffee rings
under the neon that stutters *EAT*—
the third letter died when the frost bit in last fall.

I stack the mugs lip to cold lip,
count the cracks that hold the ghost of cream,
while the radio bleeds a 1987 country ballad.

The trucker in booth three stirs his hash
like he’s sifting for something he lost on I-80:
a daughter’s graduation photo, a wife’s last goodnight.

A kid in a prom dress, tulle torn at the hem,
slides in alone, orders a chocolate shake,
doesn’t wipe the mascara track that cuts her cheek.

The snow sticks to the window like static,
blurs the streetlamp to a smudge of honey,
erases the edge between the road and the dark.

I slide the shake across the counter, extra whipped cream,
don’t ask why her corsage is crushed in her palm.
Some hurts don’t need words, just a spoon that’s not bent.

The cook flips a burger, the grease spitting soft,
tells me his kid made the honor roll again,
says he’s saving up for a bike with a neon frame.

At 3:17 the cop pulls in, uniform stiff with cold,
nods like we share a secret we don’t speak of:
the quiet that holds the town when all the lights go out.

He drinks his black coffee in two sips,
leaves a five that’s crumpled like a used tissue,
pulls back out into the snow, siren off, lights low.

The prom kid falls asleep with her head on the counter,
the shake half-melted, the whipped cream curdling sweet.
I turn the radio down, don’t wake her.

The neon *E* flickers, *A* flickers, *T* stays dead.
The Formica stops sweating. The snow slows.
I wipe the ring from where the trucker sat.

We are all just passing through the linoleum dark:
the lost, the tired, the ones who don’t know where to go
when the rest of the world has locked its doors.

The sun bleeds pale pink over the water tower,
the day shift girl unlocks the door, smells like lavender,
says *how was the night?* like she already knows.

I hang my apron on the hook by the grill,
taste the last of the coffee, bitter and warm,
step out into the snow that’s already starting to melt.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
I. Spring’s First Vow
The orchard stirs from winter’s frost-bound sleep,
Pink buds unclasp along the bough’s brown line;
A soft wind breathes where cold once used to creep,
And bees first seek the bloom’s faint sweet design.
The gardener leans to test the swelling shoot,
While dew hangs pearls on every newborn leaf;
No trace remains of storm or frozen root,
All quiet hope, untested yet by grief.
The robin carols from the topmost bough,
As earth renews the vow she made before:
That frost shall loose its grip and warmth allow
Bright fruit to swell where blossom hovered o’er.
Then spring steps light, her floral task begun,
And all the orchard leans toward the sun.

 II. Summer’s Gold, Autumn’s Hoard
When summer climbs to noon’s broad burning height,
Green boughs bow low beneath their hidden weight;
Warm winds drift slow through dappled leaves till light
Turns amber on the fruit that swells elate.
Then autumn slips her russet mantle on,
And paints each leaf in crimson, bronze, and gold;
The harvest bins stand ready, one by one,
As crisp airs bear the orchard’s wealth unfold.
The picker’s call rings through the thinning trees,
Sweet cider scents wreathe upward from the press;
Late wasps drone low where fallen apples ease,
And dusk draws in with soft, faint smokiness.
Two seasons turn, one ripening, one reaping—
Warm glow then gold, all stored for winter’s keeping.

 III. Winter’s Silent Verse
Now bare boughs etch their dark lines on the gray,
And frost has sealed the last faint autumn sound;
Soft snow lays smooth where fallen fruit once lay,
And hushed the paths where late the harvest wound.
No leaf remains, no bloom, no clustered prize,
Yet boughs hold fast the promise of the root;
Beneath the crust, the dormant orchard lies
And dreams of bud, though all the world is mute.
The moon rides high above the drifted row,
Each branch bears crystal in the cold’s sharp art;
The gardener rests, and waits the longer glow,
While sleep knits strength through every quiet heart.
So springs, then summers, autumns, winters meet—
The orchard’s year, full circled, complete.

title: ghazal|the ocean during a storm
text:
Tempest-Ghazal of the Shore-Swallowing Sea
The waves rear tall as minarets when the storm stokes the sea—
each crest wears foam as a shroud, sharp as old oaths, the sea.

Wind rips the sails off fishing craft snared mid the squall,
salt stings the eyes of the men who beg repose from the sea.

It has swallowed anchor, sextant, lockets strung with lovers’ hair,
it holds ten thousand drowned stories no one knows from the sea.

Thunder booms its old refrain, a drumbeat for the drowned,
lightning gilds the jagged edge of every blow from the sea.

I pressed my palm to wet rock, felt the tide’s raw, thundering pulse—
it does not rage for sport, it only shows its bones, the sea.

At dawn the gulls will cry again, the waves will lull soft as lullabies,
but you would be a fool to think it atones, the sea.

title: elegy|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
Elegy for a City Bus at 2 A.M.

The last lamp bleeds along the empty aisle,
where seats hold shadows like a fading breath;
no passenger remains to stay a while,
but dust keeps vigil over ghostly death.

The driver’s hands dissolve in dashboard glow,
each stop a name unspoken, unanswered;
the farebox hums a requiem, soft and low,
for footsteps that the midnight pavement blurred.

It turns through streets where neon starts to rust,
its windows framing stars the smog has drained;
a metal heart now cooling into dust,
with all its daytime voices lost and chained.

At terminus it bows beneath the dark—
one final sigh of brakes, one fading spark.

title: sequence of haiku|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
Backpack strap snagged tight
on the stranger’s puffer zipper
we don’t make eye contact

Last winter’s gum smudge
crusts the pole my palm sticks to
someone’s tamale steam

Train lurches—my boot
comes down hard on a scuffed white Air Force 1
he just scrolls TikTok

Some kid’s backpack leaks
goldfish crumbs down my coat cuff
I don’t brush them off

We all tip forward
when the brakes screech too sharp
a stranger’s breath on my neck

Doors sigh open at my stop
I spill out with the crowd
left sock slid down my ankle

title: poem in tercets|the first heartbreak
text:
First Heartbreak
The porch light bleeds through rain-streaked glass tonight,
Your coffee mug still holds the dreg’s cold bite,
The swing we carved our names in creaks in white.

I trace the crack where oak and nail split tight,
Your laugh still hangs where jasmine vines take flight,
But silence weighs more heavy than the night.

The lighthouse sent our wishes out to sea,
You said the tides would always bring you me—
Now waves just drag your footprints off the lea.

I fold your hoodie, still with pine’s soft trace,
The zipper sticks where once our hands would race,
The clock ticks slow, as if it knows this space.

Tomorrow’s sun will gild the weathered pier,
But I will stand where I first called you dear,
And let the salt wash off the ghost we were.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the first heartbreak
text:
I. The Unopened Note
We passed the oak where we had carved our vow
At golden hour, when clover breathed sweet dew,
Your knuckles white around the note I knew
Held words that would unspool the summer’s brow.
I laughed too loud, to still the trembling howl
Beneath my ribs, where once your name beat true;
You stared at scuffed white sneakers, never drew
A breath to speak, just let the thin paper bow.
The crickets hushed. The west wind dropped its hum.
I felt the world tilt slow, then crack in two—
No crash, no roar, no sharp and sudden blow,
Just cold that seeped where once your warmth had come,
The note unopened in my pocket, new,
The first sharp edge of what I did not know.

 II. The Ghost in the Throat
I set two mugs out when the kettle sang,
Reached for your hand mid-joke at the café,
Turned at the sound of boots that matched your stride,
Forgot you would not come when the school bell rang.
Your ghost lingered in every small, sharp pang:
The citrus soap you used, the worn folk play
We’d reenact on rainy Saturdays,
The scar on my left palm where your bike had sprang
A fall that left us scraped and laughing, young
Enough to think all scrapes would heal up clean.
I drank both mugs of tea until it burned,
Bit back your name when it rose on my tongue,
Counted the cracks where our old names had been,
And learned how much of me you had not returned.

 III. The Clover Press
I found the note three autumns later, pressed
Between the pages of the Keats you lent,
The ink blurred soft where old, spent tears had went,
Its sharp edge dulled, its ache no longer pressed
Into the hollows of my tender breast.
I traced the carved oak line, now faint and bent,
No longer scoured by the sharp lament
That once made every breath feel like a test.
The heart does not unbreak, does not reset—
It knits the cracks with gold, as old tales tell,
Learns to hold joy and grief in the same breath.
That first sharp cut did not leave me bereft:
It taught me how to love, how to farewell,
How to carry soft what once felt like death.

title: short lyric poem|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
Subway Breath
Doors gulp the tide, we press as one,
shoulder to rib, no room to turn.
A stranger’s coffee steams my sleeve,
earworms through buds in turn.

Lights flicker past the tunnel’s dark,
we sway like grass in wind.
No names, no words, just shared small space—
city’s heartbeat, pinned.

title: villanelle|hope after a long illness
text:
Recovery Villanelle
The IV pole’s shadow unspools from the wall,
I count the cracks where the linoleum splits—
hope doesn’t howl. It learns to crawl.

Last week I couldn’t lift water, let alone call
the sparrow that taps the AC unit fits:
the IV pole’s shadow unspools from the wall.

My nurse left a sour cherry lollipop, all
sticky cellophane, the kind the corner store sells to kids—
hope doesn’t howl. It learns to crawl.

I used to mistake its hum for the beep and the brawl
of monitors counting the beats I almost missed,
the IV pole’s shadow unspools from the wall.

Today I stepped barefoot on the hall
floor’s cold tile, no hand to hold my wrists—
hope doesn’t howl. It learns to crawl.

It doesn’t bloom, doesn’t rise, doesn’t stall
for trumpets: it’s the chipped mug I lift, it fits
the IV pole’s shadow unspools from the wall—
hope doesn’t howl. It learns to crawl.

title: sequence of haiku|the ocean during a storm
text:
The sky bruised purple,
Rain stings my salt-cracked left cheek —
I forgot my gloves.

Waves chew the old pier.
One barnacle-crusted piling
groans, holds, then gone.

Dad's yellow raincoat
zipper stuck halfway down. Cold
slips in, slow, stays.

A gull hangs sideways
wings shaking, refusing
to be anywhere else.

I count thunder, lose
track somewhere around the time
my right sock soaks through.

White foam slings the stairs.
I should probably go in.
The ocean doesn't care.

title: villanelle|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Villanelle for the Cemetery Leaves
The bronze leaves settle where the headstones lean,
They trace the names the rain has worn half-through—
I bring no flowers, only what I mean.

Each gust unspools the gold from oak and green
From ivy tangled where the old yews grew:
The bronze leaves settle where the headstones lean.

They tuck in cracks where chiseled dates have been,
Cushion the footpaths where the mourners go,
I bring no flowers, only what I mean.

A child’s small stone wears a crimson sheen
Of maple, bright as a lollipop’s glow—
The bronze leaves settle where the headstones lean.

They do not grieve as we do, sharp and keen,
No sobs catch in their rustle, soft and slow:
I bring no flowers, only what I mean.

They turn to loam where the long roots drink clean,
Feed the next spring’s bud from the dark below—
The bronze leaves settle where the headstones lean,
I bring no flowers, only what I mean.

---
*(Form note: Strict villanelle structure is observed: five tercets followed by a quatrain, two recurring refrains, consistent iambic tetrameter, and an ABA rhyme scheme across tercets, shifting to ABAA in the closing quatrain per traditional form.)*

title: villanelle|time and memory
text:
Part I: The Fading Room
The clocks fold soft around the things we know,
where sunlight leans across a scuffed oak floor—
I trace the ghost of voices long ago.

A teacup holds the warmth we used to know,
the wallpaper blooms patterns seen before;
the clocks fold soft around the things we know.

I sift through names the years have let go,
each photograph a half-remembered door;
I trace the ghost of voices long ago.

The dust drifts slow where old emotions grow,
and memory keeps what living ignores—
the clocks fold soft around the things we know.

I call your name, but only echoes show
the shape of days that time cannot restore;
I trace the ghost of voices long ago.

The present leans to watch the past burn low,
one fire we keep returning to, and more:
the clocks fold soft around the things we know,
I trace the ghost of voices long ago.

 Part II: The River's Refrain
Time is a river we cannot hold,
it slips through fingers cold and clear;
the past is a story already told.

We walk the banks where our shadows rolled,
and bend to listen, but cannot hear—
time is a river we cannot hold.

The current keeps what the years have sold,
each face a ripple that drifts anear;
the past is a story already told.

We cup the water, bright and cold,
and watch it vanish, and yet revere:
time is a river we cannot hold.

The boats we launched when the world felt old
sail out to dusk and disappear;
the past is a story already told.

But still the river in folds of gold
carries the echo of all we held dear—
time is a river we cannot hold,
the past is a story already told.

 Part III: The Light Remains
Though years unmake what hands have tried to keep,
some light endures when every flame departs;
the hours we loved are buried, not asleep.

For memory sows what time may never reap—
a laugh, a lantern, locked and beating hearts;
though years unmake what hands have tried to keep.

The falling calendar, the darkened steep
of winter, cannot steal the old fire's starts:
the hours we loved are buried, not asleep.

So let the seasons circle, let them leap,
I keep the harvest of my vanished charts;
though years unmake what hands have tried to keep.

The clocks may chime, the tides may run too deep,
but something bright behind the dark still starts—
the hours we loved are buried, not asleep.

And at the end, when all the shadows creep,
time keeps the memory, and memory starts:
though years unmake what hands have tried to keep,
the hours we loved are buried, not asleep.

title: villanelle|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
The Ring at 2 a.m.
The screen glows bright with an unknown area code,
I fumble for the device, half-lost in sleep,
And the voice I thought long buried says *hello*.

The cadence hits first—how he still draws out *go*
The way he did when we were small, knee-deep
In summer creek mud, before the years erode.

He says he found my number scrawled on an old road
Map our dad kept, folded thin where the highways creep
Across state lines, and my throat tightens at *hello*.

I’d rehearsed this a hundred times: the sharp goad
Of anger, the sharp words I’d planned to keep
Locked tight for when the ghost I’d mourned chose to show.

But he says he still has the chipped ceramic toad
We stole from the corner dime store, cheap
And chipped, just like us, before I can say *hello*.

We don’t talk of the fights, the nights he froze
Out on the streets, the silence we thought we’d keep
Forever, until the static cleared, and the call flowed.

I don’t know what comes next—what roads we’ll go
Down, what old wounds we’ll finally let seep
Closed, now that the voice I thought long buried says *hello*.

title: sequence of haiku|the night shift at a diner
text:
I.

Fluorescents hold the night
like a cheap, unblinking god.
The pie case sweats glass.

II.

A trucker stirs his coffee
with the same slow wrist he’d use
to throttle a dream.

III.

Hash browns stick to the grill
in the shape of Iowa.
Nobody mentions it.

IV.

The waitress writes orders
in a shorthand of grief—
ketchup smudge, no onions.

V.

Three a.m. arrives
dressed as a regular: damp coat,
no appetite, no name.

VI.

The jukebox died last Tuesday.
Silence has a beat now—
freezer hum, spoon tap.

VII.

A kid counts out quarters
for pancakes he won’t finish,
his eyes two wet coins.

VIII.

I wipe the same counter
I’ll wipe tomorrow, my rag
a small gray flag of surrender.

IX.

Out on Route 9, headlights
swallow their own pale hunger.
The open sign blinks.

title: ballad in quatrains|grief after a dog dies
text:
The Empty Leash
His leash still hangs where the hook meets the wall,
Frayed where he tugged to chase squirrels at the gate,
I reach for it first when the first dawn birds call,
Then remember he will not come, won’t wait.

I set his chipped bowl down by the old back door,
Scoop kibble slow, like I did every morn,
The floor is too quiet, no scrabble of paw,
No cold wet nose pressed to my palm, warm.

We used to walk the lane when the ferns curled high,
He’d lag to sniff clover, then bolt for the stream,
Now clover blooms thick where the soft reeds sigh,
And I walk the slow path with no shadow to lean.

Last night I woke to a weight on my feet,
Reached down to scratch ears where the soft fur grew,
The dark held nothing but the cold of the sheet,
And the quiet grief only a dog’s person knew.

He left no note, no grand, long last goodbye,
Just fur on the couch, a half-chewed rubber ball,
Love doesn’t vanish when a small heart dies—
It just waits, soft, in every quiet, empty hall.

title: ballad in quatrains|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
The whistle’s throat has gone to rust,
The parking lot is cracked and pale;
A single gate swings in the dust
And strikes a hollow, evening bell.

They pulled the wiring from the wall
And left the windows dark and wide;
The foreman’s shadow leaves the hall,
The timecards yellow where they died.

On Main Street, every second door
Holds one bare bulb, one folded sign;
The diner clock still tells the hour
To cups of cold and turpentine.

At dusk the fathers walk the tracks
Where no late engine ever comes;
Their hands remember weight and cracks,
Their children pack their bags for homes.

Yet from the slag heaps, pale and fine,
The snow comes down like lost paydirt,
And lays a clean and quiet line
Across the mill, across the hurt.

title: sequence of haiku|a beekeeper in winter
text:
Hive Wrap
Burlap tacks tight down
Breath plumes thin where frost bites sharp
Bees hum low, inside

 Winter Check
He lifts the lid slow
Sugar crumbs rest on wood slats
No cold wind slips through

 Thaw Sign
First crocus pushes
He leans on his cedar hive
Hum swells, warm, alive

title: poem in tercets|time and memory
text:
The Hourglass of Remembrance

The clock whispers softly in midnight's deep hush,
Each tick is a thread in the fabric of hush,
Where memories slumber, then softly they rush.

Old photographs fade in the amber-lit dust,
A laugh from the past breaks the quiet and dust,
Time polishes moments it chooses to trust.

We trace the faint footprints our yesterdays keep,
Through gardens of moments we've sown and we keep,
Then wake to find only the present, asleep.

Time carries our memories out like the tide,
Yet leaves the bright shells of the dreams that we bide,
Where love and remembrance forever abide.

title: blank verse meditation|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
The grinder’s burr catches first—low, toothy,
not the scream of a smoke alarm, not the clatter
my roommate’s cast iron makes when he fumbles it
home at 2 a.m.—just a crunch that holds
the dark like a mason jar holds fireflies
before you punch holes in the lid. The kettle
breathes out a thread of steam that fogs the crack
where the window frame won’t seal, where last night’s frost
etched a map of nowhere, all veins and no destination,
across the glass. I measure grounds by the scoop
my sister stole from a diner outside Boise
the summer she dropped out, its handle chipped
where she bit it when the cop pulled her over
for going 92 with a broken taillight.
The pour hits: blooms rise, brown and frothy,
like the rot that pocked the oak we cut down last spring
when it leaned too close to the power line,
sweet, sharp, alive with the smell of turned earth
and something that doesn’t care if the sun comes up.
Outside, the squirrel that chewed through the Christmas lights
skitters along the fence, pauses to stare
like it knows I’m not supposed to be awake,
like it’s got a secret about the way the dark
thins at the edges, not pink, not gold,
the color of an old t-shirt washed so many times
you can’t remember what it said on the front.
I don’t add sugar. Don’t add cream. The mug
is the one the pottery student gave me
after I helped her carry her wheel up three flights,
its wall lopsided, a thumb print pressed deep
into the side right where my index finger rests,
warm as a pulse. Down the hall, my partner’s snore
hitches, holds, starts again. A garbage truck
groans three blocks over, metal on metal,
but here the coffee steams, and for a minute
there is no email, no rent notice taped to the door,
no argument I rehash in the shower,
just the slow creep of light through the frost’s ghost,
the bitter, bright edge of the first sip,
the way the world doesn’t ask anything of me yet—
not even to be awake, just to hold
the warmth, to let the dark drain out slow,
one unmeasured breath at a time.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|teenage summer jobs
text:
Petrarchan Sonnet on Teenage Summer Jobs
When summer spills its gold across the street,
I fold my schoolbag, trade my books for name tags,
Clock in at dawn where neon café signs lag,
Wipe sticky counters, memorize each seat.

I scoop soft cream for toddlers’ sticky feet,
Ring up ripe peaches, haul the heavy rag
To polish shelves until my shoulders sag,
And count small coins where cash drawer edges meet.

At first I chafe at rules, at clock-tied hours,
At scuffed white sneakers, apron strings that bind,
Till laughter hums through busy, sun-warmed bowers—
A regular’s warm thanks, a friend’s close mind:
These small bright coins outshine the summer showers,
And work has etched a gentle, growing kind.

title: blank verse meditation|the first heartbreak
text:
The AC in my mom’s 2008 Civic
died the week you left, so I drove
with all four windows down even when it rained,
the wind slapping so hard it made my ears ring
so I wouldn’t have to hear the country station
we used to scream along to on the way to the lake.

I found your half-eaten bag of sour straws
under the passenger seat last Tuesday,
the sugar crusted hard into the seam
where the vinyl split the night we parked
on the overlook and you said you thought
you might love me forever, the city lights
blurred below us like someone spilled a jar
of crushed glow sticks. I ate three of them
before I remembered you don’t like the blue ones,
that you always picked them out and handed them to me
before you even took one for yourself.

My grandma asked about you at Sunday dinner.
I told her you were busy with soccer practice,
stared at the crack in her Formica table
where I carved our initials when I was sixteen,
the edges smoothed over now from three years
of wiping down spaghetti sauce and spilled Kool-Aid.
She passed me the rolls without saying anything else,
but I saw her tuck the extra jar of your favorite pickles
back into the pantry when she thought I wasn’t looking.

I still sleep in the hoodie you left at my house,
the one with the faded coffee stain on the cuff
from when you spilled your latte on it
the morning we drove three hours to the zoo
just to see the new red panda cub. It smells like laundry detergent now,
not like your pine shampoo, not like the cigarette butts
you stole from your dad’s jacket and smoked
when you thought I wouldn’t notice. Last night
I woke up at 2:47 a.m. reaching for the spot
where you used to curl into my side,
and my hand hit the cold wall instead.

People keep telling me it gets better.
They say time heals all wounds, like my chest
is a scraped knee I got falling off my bike,
like I can just put a Band-Aid on it and go back
to riding around the block like nothing happened.
Last week I walked past the soccer field after school
and saw you kissing her under the bleachers,
her hair the same shade of light brown mine was
the summer before we started senior year.
I didn’t cry. I just kept walking,
the sour straw I’d bought at the gas station
turning sticky on my tongue,
the wind still slapping my face even though
the windows were up, even though the AC
still doesn’t work, even though I don’t know
if I’ll ever be able to listen to that stupid Luke Combs song
again without feeling like I’m going to throw up.

I threw the rest of the sour straws away yesterday.
I didn’t save the blue ones.
I didn’t text you to tell you.

title: free verse poem|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
Static
The number glows unknown,
a name I haven't typed in years.
My thumb hovers,
suddenly too large.

 The Voice
"Hey."
One syllable, older,
weathered around the edges,
and the space between us collapses—
I am fourteen again,
waiting by the porch light.

 Morning After
The phone rests dark.
Outside, the rain begins.
Somewhere a door I thought boarded shut
stands slightly ajar,
breathing.

title: prose poem|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The Keeper’s Last Watch
The beam turns once more, slow as a breath held between tides—
tonight it does not cut the dark, it stitches it,
thread of gold pulled through fog thick as the wool of the sweater
his wife mended three times at the cuffs, the one that still smells
of her lavender sachet and the brine that seeps into every seam of this place.

He runs a palm over the lens first, the way you’d brush the cheek
of a child you’ve watched grow tall: two thousand nights he’s polished
the salt flecks off its curve, talked to it when the gulls fell silent,
when the storm hurled waves high enough to rattle the lantern room glass,
when the radio fizzled out and the only voice in the world was the turn
of the mechanism, steady as the pulse in his wrist.

Down the iron stairs, each step worn thin at the edge by the scuff
of his work boots, he counts them like he’s counting the beats of an old song:
forty-seven, forty-eight, the one that creaks right where he dropped his lantern
in ’98, the night the schooner went down, the night he pulled three men
from the surf, their coats heavy as lead, their lips blue as the mussel shells
that cling to the jetty rocks. He leaves a chipped mug of black coffee
on the third step, still steaming, for the ghost of the keeper before him—
the one who taught him to read the sky like a letter, who said the light
doesn’t belong to the men who tend it, it belongs to the ones who need it.

At the kitchen table, he runs a finger over the carved initials:
his, and his wife’s, and the scratch his daughter made when she was seven,
when she climbed all the way up to the lantern and said the stars looked close enough
to tuck in her pocket. The logbook lies open to the last page, his handwriting
slanted a little with the wind that always hums through the walls:
*Seas calm. Visibility six miles. Light holds.* No grand goodbye,
no fanfare—keep the notes plain, the old keeper always said,
the light doesn’t care for drama. It only cares to be seen.

Outside, the waves hush against the rocks like they know.
A seal bobs in the cove, its dark eyes shiny as polished coal,
the same one that’s come to watch him feed the gulls at dawn for ten years.
He tosses it the last of the herring he kept in the icebox, watches it slip
under the surface, a flash of silver gone before the next swell rolls in.

Midnight comes. The new beam is automated, they told him,
brighter, sharper, no need for hands to wipe the salt away, no need
for a man to sit up through the gales, listening for the faint cry of a ship
lost in the squall. He does not say that the light never needed to be sharper.
He does not say that the hands that tend it are part of its glow,
that the warmth of a human breath on cold glass is what makes it home
to every sailor scanning the dark for something that knows they are there.

He climbs back up for one last look, as the first pale edge of dawn bleeds
over the horizon, turning the waves pink as the conch shell his daughter
left on the windowsill when she moved away. The beam turns, turns,
and for a second it falls across his face, warm as a hand on his shoulder,
and he swears he can hear his wife laughing in the wind, hear the old keeper
humming that sea shanty he used to sing when they oiled the gears,
hear the gulls crying the names of every ship that ever found its way safe
to the harbor because someone stayed up, because someone watched.

He locks the door behind him when he goes, leaves the key under the mat
like he always did when he ran down to the village for supplies.
The path down to the road is soft with sea grass, and when he pauses
to look back, the light is still turning, gold over the water,
and for a minute he cannot tell if the glow he sees is the lantern
or the part of himself he left up there, still turning, still watching,
still holding the dark open for anyone who needs a way home.

title: villanelle|teenage summer jobs
text:
I folded napkins while the hostess chewed a pen.
The walk-in hissed like someone asked to wait.
We clock out smelling someone else’s gin.

A child poured syrup on a laminated wren;
a manager praised Jesus and my plate.
I folded napkins while the hostess chewed a pen.

The dumpster blushed tomatoes. Back again,
the line cook taught me how to separate
the clock-out smell of someone else’s gin

from fear. I dropped a ramekin, and then
the busser laughed, a bright, unbroken grate.
I folded napkins while the hostess chewed a pen.

My mother texted: *home by ten*.
The highway carried trailers filled with freight.
We clocked out smelling someone else’s gin.

I saved each tip in envelopes. A ten
could buy the quiet future I would late-
ly fold like napkins while the hostess chewed a pen.
We clock out smelling someone else’s gin.

title: spoken-word poem|the night shift at a diner
text:
Night Shift at the Lincoln Diner
The linoleum sticks to my work boots at 1:07 a.m.
coffee burn blister on my left thumb,
neon “E” in EATS flickers so hard it paints the rain
pink, then black, then pink again,
like the diner’s breathing, slow,
half-asleep, same as me.

Marty slumps in booth 3, same as every Tuesday,
pie crumbs in the creases of his trucker cap,
black coffee gone lukewarm since he got the call
his daughter’s driving cross-state alone, first time.
He don’t say nothing when I top him off,
just taps the Formica twice—
thank you, kid, don’t need to talk right now.
I don’t push. The night shift don’t do small talk.
We do quiet, the kind that don’t ask you to perform okay.

The cook, Ray, sings old Johnny Cash off-key
through the order window,
flips a pancake so high it sticks to the ceiling tile
we don’t bother scraping, not since ’19.
He slips me a free order of fries when the register’s quiet,
says I look like I ain’t ate since my 3 p.m. lecture,
he don’t know I skipped it ‘cause my rent went up again,
don’t need to. The grease smells like safety,
like the only thing that don’t lie about being hot,
being filling, being there when you don’t got nowhere else to go.

At 2:34 a.m. the door jingles hard,
two kids in prom dresses, tulle smudged with rain,
mascara running, one holding a broken heel,
the other laughing so hard she snorts,
order two chocolate milkshakes, extra whipped cream,
say their dates bailed to go drink beer in a parking lot,
say this is better, anyway. I slide them extra maraschino cherries,
don’t charge ‘em. When you’re 17 and the night feels bigger
than all the stupid plans you made,
cherries don’t cost nothing.

The cop pulls in at 3, lights off,
don’t even need to order—Ray already has his coffee black,
two sugars, a side of hash browns crispy enough to crack.
He sits at the counter, stares out at the empty street,
says there’s a crash out on the highway, bad one,
don’t go into details. We don’t ask.
Night shift don’t trade in gory stories.
We trade in mugs that stay warm,
in seats that don’t kick you out when you sit too long,
in the quiet agreement that some hours
ain’t meant for sleeping, ain’t meant for fixing,
just meant for getting through, together,
not talking, not needing to.

At 4:17 a drunk guy stumbles in,
slurs an order for a cheeseburger,
tries to tip me with a crumpled lottery ticket,
says it’s a winner, I’ll see. I take it, tuck it in my apron pocket,
don’t tell him I got three just like it from last week.
He falls asleep on the counter before his food comes,
Ray wraps the burger up to go, leaves it by his head,
we don’t wake him. The cold don’t care if you’re drunk,
if you’re sad, if you forgot where you parked your car.
The diner cares enough to let you nap 20 minutes,
enough to send you off with something warm in your hands.

The sky bleeds pale gray at 5:48,
neon “E” finally gives out, goes dark all at once.
The baker from down the street drops off a tray of day-old donuts,
the first commuter taps his foot by the register,
waiting for a coffee to go, already checking his work emails.
I count my tips: 17 dollars, the lottery ticket,
a pressed four-leaf clover Marty slipped me when he left,
said he found it on his last run, for good luck on my midterm.
I peel my apron off, hang it on the hook by the kitchen,
my boots still sticking a little to the linoleum,
the blister on my thumb throbbing,
the smell of grease and coffee and rain stuck in my hair.

People ask me why I work the graveyard shift,
say it’s lonely, say it’s dead, say I’m wasting my best years.
They don’t know the dead hours hold the softest people:
the ones running from something,
the ones running to something,
the ones who just don’t know how to be in a house
that’s too quiet, too empty, too full of ghosts when the lights go out.
We don’t need bright lights here.
We got the glow of the coffee pot,
the hum of the fridge,
the quiet thud of a mug set down gentle in front of you
before you even have to ask.
The sun’s coming up now,
and the world’s gonna start rushing again,
loud, sharp, in a hurry to get somewhere that matters.
But for eight hours, we mattered here.
No resumes, no deadlines, no fake smiles,
just sticky floors, burnt coffee,
and a seat at the counter for anyone
who needs a place to wait out the dark.

I lock the door behind me as the day shift girl walks in,
the lottery ticket crumpled in my pocket,
the clover tucked behind my ear.
Tonight, I’ll be back.
The diner will be breathing,
the neon will flicker,
the mugs will be warm.
The dark always needs somebody
to hold the light for the people
who can’t quite find their way home yet.

title: spoken-word poem|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Under the lights where the cornfields end,
the whole town shows up like it’s church, but louder.
My boots stick to last Tuesday’s Coke
on the aluminum bleacher.
Dad’s already arguing with a guy named Ron
about a holding call that hasn’t happened yet.

The announcer’s voice comes through the speakers
thin and cracked as old screen wire:
“Tackle by number fifty-five.”
That’s Tyler Means,
who once cried in study hall
because his beagle got hit by a lawn tractor.
Now parents scream his name
like he invented fire.

The marching band moves in blocks,
boots not quite together,
one trumpet always half a beat late,
one clarinet gleaming like a loose tooth.
They play that song every Southern school plays,
and nobody admits we only know the part
where everybody yells.

Down on the track,
the cheerleaders shake orange pom-poms
that shed in the wind.
Brittany Sellers has on too much blush
and keeps looking at the stands
for her mother, who isn’t here.
I know because Brittany told me
in the lunch line,
holding a fruit cup like it was evidence.

At the concession stand,
Mrs. Pruitt works the hot dog rollers
with the seriousness of surgery.
Her chili smells like cumin and wet pavement.
A kid in a too-big jersey begs for Sour Patch Kids.
Somebody’s grandmother says damn
when the pass bounces off a shoulder pad.
The crowd makes that sound,
half groan, half hymn.

First quarter: mosquitoes.
Second quarter: cold.
By halftime, breath is visible,
and the sky behind the press box
has gone the color of black coffee.
The Junior High Sweethearts run through a paper banner
that tears wrong.
One of them keeps a piece stuck to her shoe
for the whole routine.
No one helps her.
Everyone watches.

My old history teacher, Coach Watkins,
stands by the fence in camouflage pants,
whistling around a toothpick.
He asks where I’ve been,
but before I can answer,
the runner breaks free,
and four hundred people stand up at once,
screaming so hard their faces change.

He gets caught at the twenty.
Someone throws a hat.
Someone laughs too long.
A transistor radio buzzes with the away station,
where a man we cannot see
keeps getting our quarterback’s name wrong.

On the hill behind the end zone,
kids too cool to sit with parents
pass around a Mountain Dew bottle
that is not all Mountain Dew.
A pickup’s headlights sweep across them,
and for one second
they look like animals frozen in a field.

The fourth quarter stretches.
The scoreboard makes its little tin click.
7–6.
Then 13–6.
Then the kind of quiet
where you can hear shoulder pads knocking,
whistles biting,
a chain clank as the markers move.
Our quarterback, Jesse Holcomb,
takes the snap, scrambles, slips,
gets up with mud on his mouthguard,
and throws
the ugliest pass I have ever seen—
ducking, wobbling,
white against the dark—
and somehow,
somehow,
the tight end catches it
right before his knees hit dirt.

The place detonates.
Strangers hug.
Ron screams in my father’s face.
A pom-pom loses half its orange.
The cannon club fires,
and every dog in the county
loses its mind.

We lose, actually.
Two minutes later,
their kicker—
a girl, number 9,
small enough to be a ballgirl—
nails one through the uprights
like she’s mailing a letter.
14–13.
The stands drain slow,
feet grumbling,
cups rolling under benches.

Afterwards, in the parking lot,
tailgates drop.
Someone’s truck plays a song from three summers ago,
the one every girl screamed in someone’s barn.
Players walk out in letter jackets,
hair wet, eyes red,
still wearing eye-black
like war paint that forgot the war.
Jesse stands by a dumpster
drinking Gatorade,
and his girlfriend ties his shoe for him
because his hands are too swollen.

Nobody says the thing that means anything.
We just stand in exhaust and cold,
eating crushed candy,
kicking gravel,
breathing smoke from a barrel
some dad lit in a garbage can.
The lights stay on too long.
Moths batter themselves against them.
Out past the fence,
the dark goes on forever,
full of soybeans and farm roads
and whatever happens after this,
which everyone here
pretends not to think about.

My father finds me in the crowd,
hands me a lukewarm cocoa,
says, “Hell of a game,”
though it wasn’t, really.

Somewhere a gate rattles shut.
The last trumpet case clicks.
A child is carried to a car asleep,
orange pom-pom clutched in one fist.
The scoreboard glows on,
buzzing its one dull note,
then finally,
late,
goes dark.

title: spoken-word poem|a jazz club in the rain
text:
*Jazz Club, 2:17 AM, Rain*
The rain does not knock here.
It unspools slow,
a second bassline
threaded through the crack in the door
where the bouncer leans,
cigarette held cupped in his palm
like a secret he won’t let the weather steal.

First step over the threshold:
the cold sticks to your coat collar,
the smell of burnt bourbon and old velvet
hits first before the sound—
not the brassy blare you expected,
but the piano player’s left hand
working the low keys like he’s pressing bruises
into someone he loved and left.
His right skitters light,
rain on fire escape grates,
and you don’t even take off your coat yet,
just stand there dripping
on the scuffed linoleum where a hundred
other wet coats dripped before you,
each one carrying a rain they couldn’t outrun:
a layoff letter folded tight in a breast pocket,
a text left on read glowing through a jeans seam,
the quiet grief of walking past your old apartment
and seeing a stranger’s light in the window.

The sax player leans into the mic
like he’s whispering to a lover
who’s already halfway out the door,
his notes bending, blue,
the kind of sound that sticks to your wet cuffs
the same way the rain does—
you can’t wipe it off, don’t want to.
A waitress in a sequined dress with a run up the back
slides a rye across the bar without asking,
ice clinking soft as a hi-hat,
says you look like you needed something
that burns going down.
Her nail polish is chipped the color of old brass,
and when she moves between tables
she sways just a little off-beat,
like she’s carrying her own rain
under her sequins.

No one checks their phone here.
The couple in the back booth aren’t talking,
just holding hands across a sticky table,
his thumb brushing the scar on her knuckle
like he’s reading braille of all the hard years
they didn’t spend together.
The college kid in the soaked thrifted trench
is scribbling in a notebook, pen skipping
when the trumpet hits a high note,
and for a second you swear he’s writing you—
the stranger with rain in their hair,
standing in the doorway like you just stumbled
into the only part of the city that hasn’t forgotten
how to breathe slow.

The rain picks up outside,
lashing the neon sign that bleeds *BLUE NOTE*
pink and electric blue across the puddles,
and for a second the club goes quiet—
just the drummer’s brush on the snare,
soft as rain on a car roof when you’re 17
and parked with someone you thought you’d marry,
no place to go, no hurry to get there.
The piano player hits a chord that hangs
thick as cigarette smoke,
and the sax comes in again,
and no one here is trying to be happy.
That’s not the point.
We’re all just here to let the music hold
the parts of us the rain has soaked through:
the apologies we never said,
the dreams that got waterlogged on the commute,
the way it still hurts a little when you hear that one song,
the quiet relief of not having to talk,
not having to be anything
but wet, and warm, and held
by a wall of sound that doesn’t ask you to perform,
doesn’t ask you to be fine.

Last set ends at 3.
The rain slows to a drizzle,
fine as the cymbal’s fade.
The bouncer stubs out his cigarette,
nods at you like he knows
you came in carrying something too heavy,
like he saw it the second you stepped out of the rain.
You button your coat,
the bourbon warm in your bones,
and when you step back outside
the city sounds different—
car horns hum a little lower,
the rain on the awnings keeps time
with the riff still stuck in your head,
and for a second you swear
your own heartbeat has swung,
slow and easy,
into 4/4.

You don’t rush to the train.
The rain doesn’t feel like something to run from anymore.
It’s just the outro,
soft,
unrushed,
playing you home.

title: dramatic monologue|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
The 2 A.M. Route

I hum through streets where streetlights bleed
their amber on the empty grid,
my tires kiss the cracked asphalt
where daytime’s frantic footsteps hid.

The last fare’s crumpled in my till—
a kid with headphones, half-asleep,
a woman clutching paper bags
whose eyes held secrets I won’t keep.

I rattle past the shuttered shops,
the neon signs that flicker weak,
my windows fog with breath of those
who have no other place to speak.

The driver’s radio hums low
a song from years that slipped away;
I bend around the quiet park
where benches hold the ones who stay.

No rush-hour horns, no jostling crowds,
just me and dark and distant stars,
each stop sign like a question mark,
each curb a scar from countless cars.

I carry yawns and lonesome bones,
dreams too thin for walls or beds,
the hum of engines, soft and low,
the things the daylight never reads.

At 2 a.m. the city breathes,
and I’m its heartbeat, slow and known—
one bus, one road, one fading lamp,
no passenger goes truly alone.

title: free verse poem|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
The smell doesn’t live in the cookie jar—
it seeps into the crack where the linoleum curls
by the fridge, the spot where she dropped a jar
of pickled okra in ’98, mopped it up
with a rag that still smells like brine and regret
when she pulls it out from under the sink.
It’s the ghost of burnt toast she scraped
into the chipped ceramic ashtray she swore
she only used for breadcrumbs, the acrid tang
stuck to the edge of the toaster where the cord
frayed, wrapped tight in electrical tape
the color of old bandages.
It’s not cinnamon, not apple pie—
it’s the metallic zing of the pressure valve
hissing on the canner when she put up salsa
every August, the cilantro stems she tossed
in the compost pail that sat on the windowsill,
fermenting slow next to the aloe plant
she slathered on every burn, every scraped knee,
the thick green sap smelling like cut grass
and something that doesn’t heal quite right.
It’s the WD-40 she sprayed on the squeaky
cabinet hinge the week before she moved
to the nursing home, mixing with the vanilla extract
she spilled on the shelf when she reached for it,
the sweet sharp chemical tang clinging
to the box of lemon Jell-O, the jar of peanut butter
with the knife still stuck in it, the crumpled
receipt for my first soccer cleats tucked
in the junk drawer, ink bleeding where a drop
of bacon grease landed on the amount.
Last week I pried that curling linoleum up
when we sold the house, and the smell hit me
before I saw the shard of okra jar,
before I found the rag, stiff as dried bone,
tucked under the floorboard: it was the smell
of her leaning against the counter, smoking
a menthol when she thought no one was looking,
blowing the smoke out the screen door
where the tomato plants grew, their leaves
smelling like green summer and rain,
the smell of her saying I don’t need a recipe
as she dumped too much paprika in the beans,
the smell of the way she laughed so hard
she snort-laughed when I dropped a whole egg
on the floor, the yolk spreading yellow
as a sun that never sets, not even when
the lights go out, not even when the cabinets
are empty, not even when the new owners
tear out the linoleum and paint the walls
that stupid gray everyone likes now.
It lives in the crook of my elbow when I sweat
through my work shirt in July, in the fizz
of a can of pickles I open at 2 a.m.,
in the way my toaster burns the edges of bread
no matter how I set the dial,
a smell that doesn’t taste like nostalgia—
it tastes like brine, like burnt crumbs,
like the sharp, unapologetic rot of something
that stayed, even when she couldn’t.

title: blank verse meditation|the ocean during a storm
text:
The Ocean During a Storm

The wind first speaks in whispers, then in shouts,
It drags the dark clouds low across the swell.
No line divides the water from the sky,
One grey, one heaving mass of cold unrest.

Each wave is born far out where silence once
Held sway through long, unhurried summer tides.
It climbs, it arches, crowned with ragged foam,
Then hurls itself against the waiting rocks.

The sound is not one voice but many: roar,
Thunderous impact, hiss of rushing spray,
The deep, low shudder of the seabed stirred
From ancient sleep beneath the weight of storm.

Rain falls in sheets, sharp needles on the face,
It stitches sky to ocean, wave to cloud.
The gulls have fled; no ship dares test the strain
Of cables screaming in the violent gusts.

Yet there is order in this seeming chaos—
The tide keeps time beneath the frantic surface,
The currents know their paths beneath the churn,
As blood keeps moving underneath the skin.

I stand at edge of stone and let the salt
Sting my wide eyes and settle on my lips.
The storm does not ask pardon, nor does it
Perform for any watcher on the shore.

It is the world unedited, raw truth,
A force that does not flatter or conceal.
And watching waves break, broken, rise again,
I feel some tight knot loosen in my chest.

For I, too, carry storms beneath my ribs,
Dark swells of thought no anchor can hold still.
The ocean teaches what I keep forgetting:
That fury can be holy, calm returns,
That depth is measured not by peaceful days,
But by the strength to weather every surge.

Slowly the thunder drifts toward distant coasts,
The rain thins out, the wind begins to breathe.
The ocean does not apologize; it rests,
Vast, unrepentant, glinting into dark.

title: poem in tercets|drought on a family farm
text:
The well pump gurgles, catches, gurgles again.
Dad kicks the rusted casing with the toe
of the work boot he glued back last Tuesday.

The cornstalks curl like Grandma’s arthritic fingers,
tassels bleached pale as the hair she lost
to chemo, back when we still had rain.

I found a toad yesterday, caked in dust,
huddled under the last damp cinder block
by the foundation where the hose used to leak.

Mom dumps the dishpan on the tomato vines,
says we can skip rinsing the plates for a while—
the suds won’t kill what the sun hasn’t already.

Last night I heard them talking through the wall,
not yelling, just quiet, the way they talk
when the vet comes out to put a cow down.

The county fair prize ribbon from ‘19
is faded on the fridge, next to the bill
for the hay we had to haul in from three states over.

I poured half my soda on the struggling sunflower
I planted by the mailbox back in April.
It hasn’t grown an inch since the first of June.

No rain in the forecast. The wind picks up,
blows topsoil thin across the fence line,
carries the faint smell of someone’s distant grass fire.

Dad stands out in the field at dusk,
hat pulled low, not praying, just staring,
spitting tobacco juice into the cracked dirt.

title: spoken-word poem|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
Still Water
The river arrives before speech does—
slow, unapologetic,
its surface stitching sky to stone.
You do not say good morning.
You tap the gunwale twice,
and I have learned that means *come*.

Our rods bend like questions
we will never ask out loud.
You thread my hook without looking,
fingers calloused as driftwood,
the knot tight enough to hold
a secret, or a small, gasping life.
Silence here is not empty.
It has weight: the weight of moss
on boulders, of herons holding
their breath in the reeds,
of all the words you swallowed
when the world asked too much of you.

I watch the line where it kisses the current.
Sometimes a dragonfly lands there,
a living comma, and you almost smile—
the corner of your mouth twitching
like a bobber before a bite.
You point once at a trout hovering
in the glass-dark pool,
its flank a flash of broken moon.
I nod. We do not need names
for the hush between us,
for the way light spills through pines
in thin, golden threads.

When the sun dips low enough
to bleed into the water,
you reel in my line first,
then yours. No fish today.
You do not say *next time*.
You just lay the rods across the bow,
hand me a thermos of coffee
still steaming, still black,
and the warmth climbs my palm
like something you could never say.

On the drive home, dirt roads
humming beneath the tires,
I count the things you’ve taught me:
that stillness is not absence,
that a river speaks in ripples,
that love can be a knot tied carefully,
a shared silence,
a tap on the gunwale
that always means *come*.

title: spoken-word poem|the sound of a train at night
text:
Rail Hush Before the Whistle
The dark holds its breath first—
screen door slats hum thin,
the maple at the curb tucks its last rustling leaf
into the seam of the porch step.
You don’t hear the train yet.
You feel it in the base of your water glass,
the way it ripples like something remembering
how to move, how to carry a hum
up from the buried rail two blocks over,
before the world remembers to make noise.

 Whistle Split at the Crossing
Then it comes—
sharp, silver, frayed at the edges,
tearing a gash straight through the dark
where the unlit crossbuck hangs its rusted arms.
It doesn’t ask permission.
It carries the ghost of every kid who ever waved
from a boxcar door, every goodbye mumbled
into a cold window, every half-packed bag
left propped by a bedroom door.
For three seconds it fills every crack in the house:
the gap under the front door, the hollow of your throat,
the empty side of the bed,
loud enough to drown out the hum of your fridge,
loud enough to make the dog lift his head from his paws,
loud enough to feel like it’s calling your name,
if you’d just stop long enough to listen.

 Fade to Rail Static
It doesn’t leave all at once.
It thins, first, unravels into rattle of boxcar joints,
clack over the switchyard track half a mile out,
softens to a thrum the crickets can talk over,
until you can’t tell if the hum still in your bones
is the train, or your own blood
remembering how to move.
The dark sews itself back up slow.
The water glass goes still.
The dog drops his head back to his paws.
You lie there, half-asleep,
holding the faint echo like a ticket stub
for some place you don’t have the guts to go,
and the train keeps moving,
carrying all the unspent goodbyes, all the almost trips,
all the sounds the dark is too quiet to hold,
farther, fainter, gone—
until the only thing left
is the quiet,
waiting for the next one.

title: ghazal|moving out of a childhood home
text:
They label the boxes *KITCHEN* in Sharpie, misspelling the chipped mug—
my thumb rubs the old scar where the dryer door bit, age eight.

The basement smells like damp concrete and the trumpet I never learned;
a single retainer glints in the dark, a fossil of someone else's bite.

I find a constellation of pushpin holes above the baseboard,
the map torn down: every city I was going to be by now, gone.

The new tenants will sand the pencil marks off the doorframe,
my height arrested at fourteen, jaw set against being measured.

I leave the spare key under a frog whose paint has flaked to one eye.
The porch light keeps its post. The street does not bother to wave.

On the counter: a rubber band, a dead AAA, the dust doing its slow work.
Whatever I was here, the house has already begun to forget.

title: villanelle|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
Tide Pool Villanelle
The shallow pools hold back the ebbing tide,
where barnacles crust stone with chalky white—
small hermit crabs drag borrowed shells to hide.

They scuttle past the fronds of kelp that glide
when ripples kiss the rim of sun-warmed bright,
the shallow pools hold back the ebbing tide.

One taps a spiral whelk, unsatisfied
with cracks that let the sharp salt air bite—
small hermit crabs drag borrowed shells to hide.

A child leans close, eyes wide, and tries to guide
a skittish one to where the tide pools bite
the shallow pools hold back the ebbing tide.

They know the moon will pull the sea outside,
will leave them cupped in stone till next twilight:
small hermit crabs drag borrowed shells to hide.

What home do we all haul, unsatisfied,
what small bright pocket keeps the world at bay,
while shallow pools hold back the ebbing tide,
small hermit crabs drag borrowed shells to hide?

title: ballad in quatrains|a mother's hands
text:
My mother’s hands smelled of lemon Pledge
and the cigarette she hid behind the mixer,
one thumbnail permanently bruised black
from the Honda’s door, November of ’84.

They shook when she poured the coffee,
those hands, the right one especially—
a tremor the doctor called benign,
as if tremors had manners.

I watched them button my brother’s corpse
in the blue shirt he hated,
her fingers remembering each button
like a road she had driven blind.

After the funeral she made toast,
cut it diagonals, both of us standing.
Her hands did not shake then.
They did not cry either, though I did.

Last week in the nursing bed
she plucked at the sheet’s edge, plucked, plucked,
trying to fold a fitted sheet
that wasn’t there, and never was.

I held the hand that wasn’t there either—
knuckles, paper, a ring gone loose—
and the hum of the machines kept on
and outside someone was watering asphalt.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|watching a parent grow old
text:
Sonnet to the Fading Light
I watch her fumble with the teacup’s rim—
The bone-china cup she once could lift one-handed,
Her knuckles ridged now, gnarled where soft skin landed
When she would tuck my hair back, stray and dim.
She pauses mid-sentence, lost where old words swim,
The lilt of her old stories half-stranded,
Her eyes fixed on the oak where we once planted
A sapling, now broad-boughed, while her steps grow slim.
I do not rage against the slow unspooling,
Nor beg the years to give back what they take;
I only mark how light leans, soft and cruel,
Gilding the silver at her temple, pooling
In the thin lines where her old smiles used to break—
Love is to hold the cup when her hands fail.

---
*Form note: Strict Petrarchan structure: ABBA ABBA octave (concrete, sensory scenes of small, unspoken change) turning at the volta (line 9) to the sestet (CDE CDE, quiet, unflinching devotion rather than cliché grief, anchored to the opening teacup motif for narrative and emotional cohesion).*

title: sequence of haiku|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
Dawn Launch
Cold breath on the lake
Paddle dips without a word
Mist hugs both our coats

 The Wait
Lines hum soft and low
He points where the shadows drift
Silence learns to bite

 Shore Return
Twilight strings our catch
His calloused hand taps mine once
Boat bumps sandy shore

title: dramatic monologue|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
The Library on Sunday Afternoon
The rain presses its cold palm to the leaded pane
like a penitent begging entry, but the doors are latched
to the world that honks and brawls out on the main—
here, only the hush breathes, slow and unmatched.

I run my thumb along the cracked spine of a verse
some child marked with crayon back in ‘52:
a purple rabbit scrawled across the universe
of lines that once made someone’s chest feel new.
The carpet holds the ghost of every step:
the girl who snuck a romance in her bag,
the widower who came to read the kept
obituaries clipped from the evening rag,
the boy who hid from bullies in the stacks,
the student cramming theorems till his eyes burned black.

The dust motes dance in slants of honeyed light
that slants through smudged glass thin as altar veil,
each fleck a word unspoken, held too tight,
loosed when a page turns with a soft, frail wail.
A biography of Mary Shelley leans
as if it might whisper how the cold
seeped through that villa when the ghost scenes
unspooled from the dark, before the tale was told.
A cookbook sags with clippings, smudged with lard,
its margins scribbled with a grandmother’s note:
*add extra nutmeg—life is always hard*—
the ink faded where a teacup smote
the page, back when she brought her pie to feed
the librarians, who let her stay and read.

The heat hums low, a drowsy, constant hymn.
Someone’s bookmark is a 1973
ticket stub to *Paper Moon*, its edge worn thin,
tucked where a story about grief used to be.
The microfilm reels hold every old regret:
the wedding notice printed wrong, the game
the home team lost, the fight no one forgets,
the baby born without a listed name.
I pull a book of sonnets from the shelf—
and there, pressed flat between page eighty-four,
a four-leaf clover, browned and dry itself,
left by someone who hoped to keep a door
propped open to luck, to a day when the sun
shone warm enough they didn’t need to run.

The clock ticks soft, no rush to ring the close.
We don’t check out just words here, not today:
we borrow the quiet to stitch up our throats
from all the things we didn’t know how to say
in the loud week ahead, the noise, the fray,
the parts of us the world will scrape and fray.
The shelves hold more than paper, more than ink:
they hold the parts of us that don’t know how to shrink.
When the bell rings at last, when we step back to the street,
the rain will still be falling, the world still sharp and fleet—
but we will carry a little of the hush in our bones,
a line, a clover, a ghost that won’t be gone.

title: poem in tercets|an abandoned railway station
text:
Abandoned Railway Station

The platform breathes beneath thick dust and rust,
No ticket voice disturbs the hush, the crust
Of years where hurried feet were once thrust.

A cracked clock hangs, its hands too tired to chase
The hours that once quickened every pace;
Now shadows keep the only time in place.

Weeds split the tracks where iron engines rolled,
Their whistle lost in rain and wind grown cold,
While moss unfolds a story green and old.

A single bench still faces empty skies,
As if it waits through muted lullabies
For smoke and light that nevermore arise.

title: elegy|a mother's hands
text:
Hands

The knuckle on her left index
swelled thick as a cherry pit
after the canning pot slipped, 1998,
she held it under cold tap water
laughing so she wouldn’t cry,
burn blister shiny as a jar lid.

I found her once in the dark pantry
plucking splinters of glass from her palm
with a sewing needle, no light on,
said she didn’t want to wake anyone—
the peach preserves had exploded
when she lifted them out of the boil.
There’s still a faint scar there,
pale as a thread, where one shard
dug too deep to dig out.

Those hands could snap a chicken’s neck
quicker than I could blink,
could yank a splinter out of my knee
before I even registered the sting,
could braid my hair so tight my eyes watered
while she hummed old Patsy Cline off-key,
could peel a potato in one unbroken curl
that looked like a rose if you held it right.

They shook, the last year.
Not the small tremor of age—
the big, unruly shake
that made her spill her coffee
down the front of her house dress,
that made her fumble the pill bottle
so the oxycodone skittered across the linoleum
like tiny white bugs.
She’d get mad then,
swat at the air like the shake was a fly
she could kill if she hit it hard enough.

I held them when she died.
They were cold, colder than the tap water
she ran over that burn,
the swollen knuckle still hard under my thumb,
the glass scar still there,
the nails still chipped from weeding the marigolds
she planted every spring along the porch,
even the year she could barely bend over.

I tried to braid my own hair last week
like she did.
It came loose in ten minutes.
The potato I peeled broke into three pieces.
I keep reaching for her hand
when I cross the street,
still,
like I’m seven again,
like she’s still there
to yank me back before the car comes.

Last night I found a jar of peach preserves
in the back of the pantry,
labeled in her wobbly handwriting,
2019, the year before.
The lid was stuck.
I couldn’t get it open.
I sat on the floor and cried
not because I missed her,
not really—
because my hands aren’t strong enough.

title: ghazal|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
First Snow in a Hospital Parking Lot

The sodium lamps bleed amber through the dark
where snow descends, unhurried, on the parking dark.

Each flake dissolves against the windshield glass—
a brief white breath, a question in the dark.

I watch it gather on the ambulance roof,
soften the stretcher rails, the iron dark.

Inside, a monitor keeps counting time;
outside, the world goes quiet in the dark.

A nurse steps out, untucks her cigarette,
and for one moment snowlight fills the dark.

The plow has not yet come. The lot is whole,
all tire-strokes buried, healed beneath the dark.

I stand between two doors: one warm, one cold,
holding your name like footprints in the dark.

By morning every flake will turn to slush,
but tonight, snow leans in close and whispers through the dark.

—for you, still inside, still breathing in the dark.

title: poem in tercets|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The Mark on the Doorjamb
We scrape the pencil lines free
where heights were scrawled in smudged lead—
each year a ghost we can’t see.

The paint chips stick to our palms,
dates half-rubbed by the door’s swing:
five, seven, ten, all gone numb.
We don’t say how the wall shrank
once we outgrew its thin marks—
just sweep the dust to the bank
of trash bags propped by the stairs.

---

 The Box of Mismatched Things
We find it under the bed:
a tooth from the first lost molar,
crayon maps of roads we led
through backyard fern and clover,
a sock striped like a bumblebee,
report cards where the teacher
wrote talks too much, draws too free.
We don’t fold the memories neat—
just tuck them tight, clumsily,
tape the lid against the heat
of the hall light’s yellow glow,
afraid if we hold them too sweet
they’ll stick to our palms and not go.

---

 The Lock Turns Twice
We haul the last box to the curb,
the key cold in the lock’s throat—
no sound but the oak’s old curb-
side murmur, the thin remote
hum of a truck down the block.
We don’t look back at the coat
hook where our first backpack hung,
don’t call out the names we used
to yell up the stairs, when young
we thought the walls would keep our bruise
and our joy, keep the small us
tucked tight in the floorboards’ crews.
The lock clicks twice. The world is wide.
The house breathes out, and we glide.

title: prose poem|a small-town Friday football game
text:
The Last Huddle of Autumn
The bleachers groan with the weight of the whole town—grandmas in wool shawls, boys with scuffed boots dangling over the edge, the mayor balancing a thermos and a scorebook he never writes in. The air smells like burnt hot dogs, cinnamon gum, and the sharp, green breath of the field after a week of rain. The sun bleeds tangerine over the water tower, painting every helmet a soft, burning gold, and the marching band’s brass notes warble a little off-key, held aloft by the crowd’s off-key singing.

The quarterback’s hands shake, not from cold, when he takes the snap—his father’s voice somewhere in the stands, his girlfriend’s pom-pom a flash of scarlet, the whole season coiled tight in this last thirty seconds. A tackle hits like a fallen oak, mud flying in dark arcs that spatter the cheerleaders’ socks, and for a heartbeat no one breathes—then the ball spirals, perfect as a prayer, into the end zone.

The stands erupt. Old men spill their coffee. Kids tumble over the railings, already running for the field. The winning pass floats down into a pile of jackets and laughing, and no one remembers the score by the time the first floodlight buzzes on, bright as a second moon. On the sidelines, the coach claps a player’s shoulder so hard he stumbles, and says nothing at all.

Cars creep down Main Street afterward, horns beeping, flags trailing from windows. The diner flips its neon sign to *OPEN*, and chocolate milkshakes steam in the cool night air. Under the goalposts, a few seniors linger, their cleats caked in mud, knowing this is the last time the lights will ever shine on them quite like this—bright, warm, and endless, while the whole town cheers just for them.

title: free verse poem|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
The geese come low enough
I can count the chipped white bar
on the lead bird’s left wing,
the faint smear of berry juice
on the beak of the one lagging
three feet back, like it stopped
for a last slurp of road-side jam
before the north pulled hard
on its hollow bones.

The lake below holds last month’s
thaw frozen mid-bubble, a school
of minnows suspended like commas
no sentence ever came for,
the half-buried sled some kid
abandoned when their mom yelled
dinner, its red runner glinting
like a shard of stopped sunset.
The geese don’t honor that stasis.
Their shadows skid across the ice
without traction, dark smudges
that never stick, even when one
lets fall a guano splat that hits
a bubble dead-center, cracks
a spiderweb of white into the clear
frost, so the minnow just under
looks like it might finally dart.

No one calls them arrows.
They honk like a crew of road workers
yelling over jackhammer noise,
like my cousin’s truck radio blaring
classic country when he rumbles
