up the driveway for Thanksgiving,
loud, unpretty, sure of where the line is.
One veers sharp, dips so close
its wingtip brushes the frost,
kicks up a puff of ice crystals
that glint for half a second
like a handful of crushed diamond
before settling back. I think
it’s showing off. I think
it knows the ice is a mirror
that won’t hold it, that it could
land if it wanted, tuck its feet
into the slush at the edge,
wait for the thaw like the rest of us.

But the lead bird caws, sharp
as a referee’s whistle, and the flock
veers up, formation gapping for a beat
before locking back in, their calls
thinning to static as they clear the treeline.
The crack in the ice stays. The minnow
hangs, still waiting. Somewhere south
of here, a farmer is turning over soil,
and the geese will find it, will shit
on his new fence posts, will fight
over the last cracked corn in his feedlot,
will not waste a single thought
on the frozen mirror they skated across,
on the shadow of themselves
that lay there for ten seconds,
cold and sharp and almost alive.

title: free verse poem|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
Uncle Ray kept lures in a Band-Aid box,
hooks tangling with old gauze.

We waded the crick where carp rolled
under slick rainbows of gas
from the body shop uphill.
He never said much. Once he showed me
how to thread a worm by feel,
fingers calloused as a boot's tongue,
and turned back to the water
like the fish owed him money.

I caught a bluegill small as a matchbook.
He baited my hook again.
Somewhere a dog barked the exact same bark
for an hour.

His hat had a patch for a company
that went under in '89.
We ate peanut butter crackers
standing in mud, no blanket.
I talked enough for both of us—
Little League, the time I found a turtle,
how Dad's snoring kept the house awake—
and he only nodded,
but the nod was a door
left slightly open.

I never caught a bass.
He never said a word
about being disappointed.
At dusk he strung my three bluegill
through the gills like they mattered,
handed me the stringer,
cold water running down my wrist,
and we drove home in the pickup
with the window stuck halfway down,
radio fuzz,
him chewing the inside of his cheek,
me practicing the kind of silence
that doesn't need filling.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|an abandoned railway station
text:
Sonnet to the Abandoned Station
The iron track bites through where thistles throng,
Its rusted ribs drink slow the summer rain;
No porter’s call cuts through the weeds’ long song,
No ticket punch clicks out hope or refrain.
The platform cracks cradle crushed glass and clover,
The signal arm hangs slack, half-lost in mist;
Once scuffed heels drummed where field mice now scud over,
Last whistle’s wisp dissolved long since, unmissed.
The waiting room’s cracked pane frames no lit face,
No steamed-up glass bears smudged of farewell kisses;
Only the wind threads through its empty space,
To hum half-remembered names the dark dismisses.
   Yet here, where time unspools unmarked, unsped,
   Each rail still hums the lives it carried, led.

title: blank verse meditation|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
I. The Last Hour

The fluorescent hum has entered her bones.
Room by room, the charting thins to dusk.
A patient asks for water, then forgets
he asked. She fills the cup, and sets it where
his hand might find it later, in the dark.

II. Removing the Scrubs

In the staff bathroom, she unties the gown
and lets the antiseptic air sting her arms.
The badge reel clatters on the metal bench.
She watches water run over her wrists
as if it could unlearn the names she held.

III. Parking Lot, 7:01

Cold air. Wet asphalt. Her keys are bright.
The hospital still burns behind her back,
but she is walking toward her ordinary car,
her ordinary life, which waits like breath—
small, steady, and almost enough.

title: short lyric poem|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
2:17 a.m. Route 14
The stop sign bleeds on wet asphalt
where the bus huffs to a lurching halt—
no fare clinks, the card reader blinks
unblinking, bored, as the doors drink
the dark, then seal it out again.

A crumpled transfer skates the floor
chasing the draft from the cracked back door.
The driver hums a country song
he can’t quite place, the words all wrong,
his thermos steaming thin and brown.

The only rider slumps three rows back,
half-asleep, a half-crushed snack
tucked in his coat, his scuffed work boots
propped on the heat vent’s quiet roots,
watch ticking slow against his wrist.

Streetlights bleed gold across the glass,
stretch neon smudges where they pass—
closed bodega, laundromat,
payphone hanging off its mat,
the world all unbuttoned, half-undressed.

No bell rings, no sharp “next stop,”
the bus rolls on where the stoplights drop
from red to green to red again,
carrying the ones the dark didn’t win:
the tired, the lost, the going home.

It rumbles soft past the quiet park,
exhaust curling thin as a secret spark,
a metal shell holding small, warm things
while the whole rest of the city dreams
of all the places it has to be.

title: dramatic monologue|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
Milltown Lullaby Without the Hum

I still set the coffee pot for six though no whistle answers.

The cat learned the silence quicker than I did.

Last Tuesday I found a sparrow nesting in the hard hat
that hung by the door, twigs laced through the crack
where my name faded in safety orange.

The parking lot became a prairie in three summers:
milkweed splitting seams in asphalt,
a deer stepping through the broken gate
like a new shift supervisor.

At the diner, Earl stirs his coffee with a wrench
he says he stole the day they chained the doors.
No one laughs anymore, but no one stops him either.

At night the smokestack points at nothing.
Stars settle in its rusted throat.

My daughter sent a photograph from the city:
lights so thick they hide the sky,
her face glowing in a glass tower.
She says, *Come see.*

I say, When the wind comes right,
I can smell rain in the empty loading docks.

The vending machine in the break room glows still,
no one knows whose quarter keeps it alive—
one can of root beer sweating behind the glass,
label peeling, patient as a heartbeat.

They say the machines were sold to a town
where people bend over them now,
maybe singing their own songs into the metal.

Here, the fence keeps nothing in.
The fence keeps nothing out.

I keep a jar of shop grease on the windowsill.
In certain light it looks almost like honey.
