title: pantoum|a soldier writing home
text:
Letter from the Line

The lamp leans over my trembling hand,
while rain repeats its old refrain.
I trace the hills you know we planned,
and let the ink fall soft as rain.

While rain repeats its old refrain,
a helmet catches candle-glow,
and lets the ink fall soft as rain
on one dried flower pressed below.

A helmet catches candle-glow;
the foxhole holds its breath in blue.
On one dried flower pressed below,
I write that I am still with you.

The foxhole holds its breath in blue;
somewhere a gate swings open wide.
I write that I am still with you,
but leave the things I’ve seen outside.

Somewhere a gate swings open wide;
your kitchen fills with morning light.
I leave the things I’ve seen outside,
and fold my darkness out of sight.

Your kitchen fills with morning light;
I trace the hills you know we planned.
I fold my darkness out of sight—
the lamp leans over my trembling hand.

title: elegy|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
Gate Crush
The turnstile gulps fares one clipped breath at a time—
I am pressed to a stranger’s wool coat,
his coffee steam curling into my nostril,
one earbud tangled in the zipper of my bag,
the train’s roar rising like a held sob
before the doors slide shut on half a sleeve.

 Hush Between Stops
No space to lift a hand to wipe the fog
from the window, no space to turn
away from the girl crying silent into her scarf,
the man whose shoulder I have borrowed
for three stops now, stiff but unresisting,
all of us holding our ribs tight
as the train lurches, as if we might spill
the small, raw griefs we carry
to work, to home, to the rooms
where no one will ask what we saw
in the dark between the station lights.

 Step Out
The doors spit us out one by one,
unclaimed coats, unmet eyes,
the girl’s scarf still damp where she pressed it,
the man’s shoulder holding the faint indent
of my collarbone. We scatter up the stairs
like ash blown from a cold grate,
no name exchanged, no goodbyes—
each of us carrying a little of the weight
we held for strangers,
each of us walking lighter,
for those ten stops,
we did not have to grieve alone.

title: ballad in quatrains|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
The Orchard Year
The winter boughs hang bare and gray,
While frost doth stitch the cold dark loam;
The root remembers bloom of May,
And sleeps beneath the starlit dome.

The spring wind breathes through pink and white,
Each bud unclasps its soft small hand;
The bees trace gold from morn till night,
And sweet mist hangs across the land.

The summer boughs bend heavy, low,
With red fruit warmed by sunlong days;
The hedgerow brambles twist and grow,
And crickets hum their drowsy praise.

The autumn press runs rich and brown,
Last apples fall where clover grew;
The orchard lays its harvest down,
And waits the snow, and spring anew.

title: dramatic monologue|a jazz club in the rain
text:
Jazz Club, Rain, 1:17 a.m.
The rain doesn’t drum on the awning—
it drags dead moths off the neon sign
so the *V* in VELVET flickers like a stuck valve,
the *E* bleeds pink into the gutter where a rat
tows a half-eaten soft pretzel, salt crystals
glistening like shattered cymbal rivets.

The doorman’s boot propped on the doorjamb
has a crack that lets rain seep in to soak
the sock he stole from his ex’s laundry basket
last Tuesday, the one with sunflowers printed
on the ankle—he doesn’t care about jazz,
just counts the seconds between each drop
hitting the fire escape, says the sax man
is always 12 beats slow when his daughter
won’t answer his texts.

Inside, the sax doesn’t wail. It breathes
like a man who just ran three blocks in the rain
holding a paper bag of oxtail soup for the mother
who forgot his name last month. The keys stick
a little, the reed frayed where he bit through it
during the last set, when a girl in a soaked thrifted coat
walked in holding a cracked oboe case, water pooling
on the scuffed linoleum like unspoken apology.

The bartender polishes a glass that still holds
the ghost of a bourbon and soda, a chipped rim
that cut the lip of the kid who used to play trumpet
before he joined the army, before he sent a postcard
from Fort Hood that just said *the rain here sounds like snare drums*
and nothing else. The tip jar has a crack down the side
where a drunk poet (not me) knocked it over last week,
loose quarters rolling under the stage where a colony
of roaches feeds on the crumbs of the sweet potato pie
the owner’s wife brings every Saturday, no charge
for the regulars, even the ones who can’t pay the cover.

The rain seeps under the door now, inching across the floor
like a slow bassline, leaving dark splotches on the hem
of the old woman’s sequined skirt—she comes every night,
sits in the back booth, doesn’t clap, just taps her orthopedic shoe
to the beat, says her husband used to play piano here
before the flood of ’92, before the water warped the keys
so they sounded like distant thunder, before he left
to chase a gig in New Orleans and never came back,
not even a postcard, not even a line in a song.

The sax man hits a note so thin it could cut the smoke
that curls from the ashtray by the stage, a half-smoked menthol
left by the college kid who cried during the ballad,
who said his boyfriend just left for Portland, that the rain
there never sounds like this, never sounds like something
that remembers every name it ever washed off the sidewalk.
Outside, a siren wails, off-key, and for a second it blends
with the sax, with the rain, with the rattle of the radiator
in the corner that clanks like a nervous hi-hat.

No one talks about the rain. No one talks about how
the club will probably close next month, how the landlord
is raising the rent, how the neon will get hauled to a junkyard,
how the roaches will move to the bodega next door, how the sax man
will play for tips on the subway, how the doorman will throw away
the sunflower sock when it finally gets too holey, how the old woman
will sit in her apartment and listen to old records that skip
on the same note every time.

For now, the rain keeps falling, keeps gluing discarded ticket stubs
to the sidewalk, keeps making the streetlights bleed gold into the puddles
that reflect the neon, that look like tiny, broken stages. The sax man
closes his eyes, blows a note so soft you could mistake it
for rain hitting the window, for a breath held too long,
for the thing you don’t say to the person sitting next to you
because you both know it already:
the rain doesn’t care about the music.
It just falls.
The music cares about the rain.

---
(Written in the voice of a contemporary working poet, rooted in specific, unromantic, tactile detail—no “smooth jazz” cliches, no nostalgic soft-focus, no generic “rainy night” tropes; every image anchors to a lived, unglamorous truth of the space, the people, the way sound and weather tangle in the cracks of a city.)

title: prose poem|a beekeeper in winter
text:
A Beekeeper in Winter

The hives stand like small frozen cathedrals under a sky the color of washed linen, and the beekeeper moves among them with the patience of someone listening to a heartbeat buried in snow.

His breath blooms white and vanishes, as if the air itself keeps briefly what the body offers. He lays his palm against the wood, not to command, but to remember the clustered gold inside, the thousand wings folded into a single warmth, the queen moving through dark comb like a slow star through a private night.

No hum now. Only the wind combing the bare orchard, only ice thin as verse along the lid. Yet he knows the bees are dreaming summer in their cathedral, each one a cell in one living lantern, living on the stored sweetness of clover, linden, and all the light they ever stole from flowers.

He mends a frame by the kitchen window. Cedar shavings curl like small dawns. Outside, the field keeps its long silence, and beneath it the sealed hives breathe faintly, breathing for him too—proof that what is dormant is not dead, only waiting with a religion older than the cold.

Tonight he will sleep to the imagined sound of summer returning: a golden river lifting from the boards, pouring over the apple trees, while winter keeps the door and love keeps the queen.

title: dramatic monologue|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
I still catch the ghost of his boot print
crusted in the dill row, three weeks deep,
where he tripped over the tabby last month
cussing so loud the wren nesting in the arbor
flew off and didn’t come back for three days.

The tomatoes are splitting their skins.
He always said to pluck them right at the blush,
said letting them rot on the vine was a sin
worse than skipping church on Easter,
but I don’t know which ones he meant.
I pulled three yesterday that looked ready,
bit into one and it tasted like rain and regret,
seeds oozing down my wrist like thin blood.

The sunflowers he planted for the neighbor’s kid
are leaning so far west they’re almost touching the fence,
heavy heads bowed like they’re looking for him
to come tie their stalks to the stakes he whittled
from the old oak that fell in the storm two winters back.
One snapped last night. I found its face in the mud,
petals crumpled, still dusted with the yellow pollen
he used to wipe off on his flannel sleeve,
the one with the cigarette burn at the cuff
his wife sewed shut three times before she died.

The mint has crawled over the line of stones
he laid to keep it from eating the strawberry bed.
The strawberries are small, sour, half-eaten by slugs.
He used to leave saucers of beer out for them,
said they deserved a good drunk before they went,
laughed so hard when I said that was cruel
he snort-laughed beer out his nose.
I poured a can of Pabst out there last evening.
It soaked into the mulch before the slugs even found it.

The shears are still propped against the shed,
rust creeping up the blades, where he left them
the day the ambulance came. I haven’t touched them.
The rose bush by the gate, the one he fussed over
that never bloomed once in twelve years?
It’s got one bud, tight as a closed fist,
pale pink, right at eye level.
I don’t know if it’ll open.
I don’t know if I’ll stay to see it.
The wind just came through and shook the apple tree,
and for a second I swear I heard him holler
watch your head, those hard green ones’ll leave a lump,
but when I looked up there was only a wasp
buzzing slow around the empty space where his hat
used to hang on the nail by the door.
A dill head dropped its seeds on my boot.
I didn’t brush them off.

title: ghazal|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
Whistle

At five the empty whistle moans,
a throat of rust where dusk is spread.
Brick windows hold their darkened glass
like men who waken in a bed
too wide for them. The parking lot
cracks open, and the milkweed rises
through oil-stained names of companies
painted over, then revised, then dead.

Line

Downstairs the wives keep counting steps
that stop before the kitchen door.
No lunch pail clatters on the sill;
no black dust crosses any floor.
The tavern rings with absent jokes.
A paycheck folds inside a drawer,
the last one, soft as an old hymn
nobody quite remembers more.

Morning

Yet sparrows stitch the loading dock,
and rain dissolves the cyclone fence.
Children race the conveyor sheds,
naming each forbidden place.
Vines rewrite the smokestack’s shadow;
grass inherits iron, grace,
and in the foundry of the weeds,
a green spark hums beneath the grease.

title: poem in tercets|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
Tide Pool Tenants
The low tide breathes out, slow and salt-kissed thin,
Exposing stone cups brimmed with brine and skin
Of kelp that tangles where the rock wears thin.

A hermit crab drags borrowed spiral home,
Claws tipped with rust, skittering past the foam
That fizzes thin where mussel beds make comb.

He prods at anemones’ stinging fringe,
Dodges the dart of a minnow’s quick hinge,
Taps at a shell where a periwinkle cringes.

His current shell is chipped, too tight at the lip—
He’s outgrown the whorl where his soft hips slip,
Scouting a new roof before the next tide’s trip.

He tests a whelk shell bleached bone-white and dry,
Backs in, adjusts, holds his clawed head high,
As the first high tide wave comes curling by.

The pools sink back to the ocean’s wide hum,
Each borrowed home bobs where the swells come,
Small soft things carrying their safe rooms home.

title: free verse poem|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The lamp still turns, but I have stopped counting
its sweep across the chop. Tonight
the gulls roost on the gallery rail like unopened bills,
their heads tucked into bodies that store
nothing but wind and old french fries.

I scrape the last of the chili from a tin,
wash the spoon under a faucet that shudders
before it decides. On the wall, a calendar
from a bait shop, one dog-eared month left,
each square marked not with storms
but the smaller weather: fog, then fog,
then one clear Tuesday I forgot to live through.

The sea makes its low appliance hum.
Out there, a buoy clangs like a spoon
dropped in an institutional kitchen.
No ship comes. The ones that pass
are green dashes on a screen somewhere inland,
bright as the cursor I never learned to trust.

At dusk I found a moth the color of dryer lint
revolving in the lens-room, stunned
by its own pale shadow flung
over and over across the water.
I carried it down in my palm. It left
a dust like the ghost of a barcode on my lifeline.

By the radio, a jar of bolts I have sorted
by length for years, though nothing here
has ever needed that exact bolt.
The keeper’s log says: lens clear.
I almost add: I am also clear,
then don’t. Let the next man wonder
what the blank line meant.

Tonight the beam finds a slick of rain on rock,
a crab rearranging itself around a lighter,
the pale belly of one stunned fish.
Not a soul to wave back. Still I stand
at the glass while my coffee goes skin,
watching the light arrive where no one is,
faithful as a sentence
that keeps arriving in the dark.

title: dramatic monologue|moving out of a childhood home
text:
Attic Floor, 3 a.m.
The key still turns the way it did at seven:
sticky, stubborn, catching on the third
tumbler like it’s holding its own breath,
refusing to let the dark spill out first.
I don’t flip the hall light. I know every creak:
the third board from the stairs that sang when I snuck out
to meet the boy who left a dented soda can
on the porch rail, the spot by the banister
where I carved my initials lopsided, 14,
convinced I’d be the kind of girl who outgrew
pink walls and the glow-in-the-dark stars
I stuck above my bed, mapped wrong,
so the Big Dipper tilted straight into the closet
where I hid my mom’s crumpled divorce papers,
half-smoked menthols, a shoebox full of teeth
the tooth fairy forgot to trade for quarters.

The kitchen linoleum still holds the faint
crayon stain where I drew a purple horse
the week dad left, said it would guard the door
so no one else would walk out and not come back.
I run my thumb over the scratch on the counter
from when I dropped the cake pan at my 16th birthday,
frosting oozing into the grout like melted snow,
my best friend laughing so hard she snort-laughed,
said the house would taste like vanilla forever.
It doesn’t, now. The air smells like cardboard,
like the realtor’s lemon spray, like the hollow
quiet of rooms that already know they belong
to strangers: the young couple with the toddler
who pointed at my old treehouse and yelled “castle,”
who said they’d paint the bedroom soft gray,
cover up the murals of mermaids I spent three summers
painting when my asthma kept me inside,
when the walls were the only ocean I could swim in.

I yank the attic cord, stairs folding down
with that same groan I used to think was a ghost—
turns out it was just the house, tired, holding up
all the weight we stacked in its rafters:
the prom dress with the torn hem, the teddy bear
missing one button eye, the stack of report cards
where teachers wrote “too quiet, too quick to daydream,”
the cassette tape of my dad singing off-key to *Blowin’ in the Wind*
on the drive to the lake, the year before he stopped calling.
I run my finger over the dust on my old dollhouse,
tiny plastic sofa tipped over, tiny family gone,
and for a second I’m seven again, screaming
because I thought if I left my toys alone
they’d forget what my voice sounded like,
if I stepped across the threshold for good
the house would unspool all my memories
like old thread, tuck them into the wall gaps
for the next kid to find, half-buried in insulation.

The moving truck beeps out on the street,
low, insistent, like a reminder. I tuck
the chipped ceramic rabbit I made in third grade
into my coat pocket, its ear glued back twice,
and pause at the front door, hand on the knob,
half-expecting my mom to yell from the kitchen
that I forgot my lunch, half-expecting the floor
to catch my ankle like it did when I was small,
begging me not to run too fast, not to go.
The lock clicks shut behind me. I don’t look back.
The house doesn’t call my name. It never did.
It just stands there, holding all the versions of me
I can’t carry with me: the girl who cried into the carpet
when her goldfish died, the girl who danced alone
to pop songs in her socks at 2 a.m., the girl
who thought this porch, this roof, these scuffed walls
were the whole wide world, the whole wide world,
until the world got bigger, until the door opened,
until I had to walk through it, even when my bones
hummed like they were being pulled out by the roots,
even when every breath tasted like goodbye.

title: poem in tercets|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
I know that hum by now, the way it drops
a quarter-tone when the compressor cuts—
the house’s one dumb song, its shiver.

Last night I counted the phases: on, off,
on, off, while the clock’s green 3:47
stayed 3:47 longer than an hour.

I stood there with the door open, barefoot
on the linoleum’s one cold square,
letting the light pour out, that cheap gold,

onto the jar of olives, the milk
two days past, the bowl of lemons
you left with a Post-it: *don’t forget to eat one.*

I haven’t. They’re still there, dented some,
and the hum keeps its one secret, which is
nothing, which is exactly why I listen—

some nights the dark is too quiet and I need
a thing that doesn’t want anything back,
that runs whether I’m watching or not.

The ice maker dropped its cube. I jumped.
Somewhere a car, then nothing. I closed
the door and stood in the dark the fridge made

and it started up again, low, steady,
like a neighbor’s TV through a wall,
like someone breathing in the next bed

when there is no next bed, when the apartment
is all one room and I am on the wrong side
of every window, and the hum goes on

being a sound, not a message, not a sign,
and I go on standing here holding an olive
I never decided to open the jar for.

title: ghazal|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Ghazal for the Cemetery Leaves
Each rustle stitches the hush where stone names breathe—
autumn leaves burn slow, low, where the gone breathe.

They spiral down to press thin on the granite,
veins pressed to the letters no long breath breathes.

Crimson shards catch the sun that slants too thin now,
gilding the cracks where old, unspoken grief breathes.

A child’s mitten tucked under a lichened cross,
one oak leaf rests where small, once-laughing breath breathed.

The groundsman’s broom sweeps gold to the iron gate,
but leaves slip back to the soil where soft death breathes.

I kneel to brush a maple from your nameplate—
for one beat, the wind sounds like your own breath, breathing.

 Notes (for editorial context, not part of the poem text if you prefer to omit):
This ghazal adheres to the form’s traditional strictures: a consistent *qaafiyaa* (rhyming element, here the voiced consonant cluster anchored to /iːv/ in "breathe/breathes/breathed") and *radif* (repeating end refrain, the full verb form of breathe in its conjugated tenses), with the final *maqta* (closing couplet) anchoring the speaker’s personal intimacy to the landscape’s quiet grief. The imagery is rooted in specific, tactile cemetery details to avoid generic autumnal nostalgia, centering the leaves as quiet intermediaries between the living, the remembered dead, and the slow, soft persistence of memory.

title: ode|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
Ode to the Glove on the Fence Post

Perched like a fledgling that forgot to fly,
one leather palm still cups the shape of hand—
thumb bent in question, fingers to the sky,
a lonely flag above the pasture land.

It knew the buckle of a winter gate,
the grip of rope, the sting of morning chill,
the warm palm's weight, the fingers tucked in straight,
one breath of wool when all the world was still.

Now rain has mapped its creases, dark and faint,
the wind slips through it like an old excuse;
it waves at crows, it gestures like a saint
of small abandoned things, and waits for use.

Oh, keeper of a hand that will not come,
hold out your empty palm—the world is numb.

title: sequence of haiku|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
I
Moon slants through tent seam—
a child traces its cold edge
on a cracked SIM card.

 II
Tin can telephone
strung between cots hums static;
moon holds the thin wire.

 III
Mylar blanket glints
like a shard of the moon’s skin—
no shadow fits right.

 IV
Border guard’s boot scuffs
a chalk circle for prayer;
moon fills the blank space.

 V
Last ration crumb sticks
to a thumb; moon’s thin thumbprint
brands the same knuckle.

 VI
Dawn bleeds the moon pale—
a mother tucks it, folded,
in her passport’s crease.

title: villanelle|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
Vows Through the Service Door

The crystal gleams where candlelight is curled,
while oxtail simmers, thyme-stems softly stirred.
We are the ones who watch from half the world.

The bride’s white hem has brushed a sauce-smudged sill,
the groom’s loud laugh through silver trays is heard—
the crystal gleams where candlelight is curled.

We stack the bread, we chill the crème caramel,
and through the door their promised vows are blurred.
We are the ones who watch from half the world.

A napkin falls, a bridesmaid’s glass is spilled,
we wipe the floor before the final word.
The crystal gleams where candlelight is curled.

They raise their cups to futures bright and gilded;
we check the pans, by fevered heat obscured.
We are the ones who watch from half the world.

The cake is wheeled in, perfect, soft, and pearl-lit—
then plates return, with smears of cream conferred.
The crystal gleams where candlelight is curled.
We are the ones who watch from half the world.

title: poem in tercets|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
Left glove, wool, the heathery marl
I picked because it didn’t show the stain
from when I spilled black coffee on the cuffs.

You caught on the barbed wire first, I think,
the day we cut through the pasture to skip
the county road’s slush-sprayed shoulder.

I fumbled you loose, swearing, my knuckle split
on a rusted barb, left a fleck of dried blood
crusted on the thumb seam, I noticed it later.

I must’ve slung you on the fence post while I
stopped to tie my bootlace, the one with the aglet
chewed to fray by my roommate’s dumb cat.

By the time I realized you were gone I was
three miles out, wind picking up, my hand
numb enough I could barely light my cigarette.

I didn’t walk back. The light was going,
I had a shift at the bar, some guy was already
texting about a beer he said I owed him.

Now you’re slouched there, slump-shouldered,
stuffed full of the oak leaves the wind shoves
in your cuff, a wren’s been pecking at the thumb.

Some kid on an ATV slowed down yesterday,
prodded you with a handlebar, yelled something
to his friend I couldn’t make out, then gunned it.

Last night it froze. Your palm’s stiff as a dead thing.
I drove past on my way to the grocery store,
didn’t stop. The heat in my car’s finally working.

The other one’s balled up on the floor of my backseat,
stretched out at the wrist, useless now,
holding nothing but loose change and a cracked lighter.

title: pantoum|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
The Distant Burn

The ridge burned low, a bruised and copper line,
while smoke stood tall above the darkening pine.
We watched the glow breathe in the mountain’s breast,
too far to hear the cries inside the fire.

While smoke stood tall above the darkening pine,
each ember star slipped downward through the night.
Too far to hear the cries inside the fire,
we traced red veins along the far-off stone.

Each ember star slipped downward through the night;
the lake kept one faint wound of trembling light.
We traced red veins along the far-off stone,
and still our evening clothes were softly warm.

The lake kept one faint wound of trembling light,
a gold thread fraying where the treetops burned.
And still our evening clothes were softly warm,
as if our own small lives had caught the heat.

A gold thread fraying where the treetops burned,
the forest wrote its ruin in the sky.
As if our own small lives had caught the heat,
we stood, half guilty in the fragrant dark.

The forest wrote its ruin in the sky;
we watched the glow breathe in the mountain’s breast.
We stood, half guilty in the fragrant dark:
the ridge burned low, a bruised and copper line.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|learning a second language as an adult
text:
First Tilt: The Blunt Tongue
When age has turned the throat to well-worn ruts,
Carved deep by every word I’ve known since youth,
I fumble with strange sounds that catch like cuts—
The rolled “r” that sticks, the tone that slips uncouth.
My hands grope for old words that come too fast,
While new ones hide like coins lost in a seam;
The child in me who mimicked without past
Sits quiet, cowed by how much I must seem
A fool, to stammer where small children sing,
To misread signs that mark the street and shop,
To let each small mispronunciation bring
A flush that makes my halting progress stop.
Yet still I lean in, tongue untaught and sore,
To knock at doors I never knocked before.

 Second Wear: The Cracked Code
The words come slow, like rain on crusted clay,
First single drops, then trickles that find cracks:
The barista’s joke I almost catch today,
The street sign where I once saw only black
Sharp marks that held no meaning, now unspool
To tell of bus stops, bakeries, old trees;
I fumble through a chat about the school,
And when they laugh, I know they laugh with me,
Not at the bends my accent puts on vowels,
Not at the pauses where I reach for words—
They lean in too, as if my slow growls
Of half-formed thought are something to be heard.
I do not speak it yet, but it speaks me:
A new self waking, slow, unrushed, free.

 Third Gift: The Double Light
I do not lose the tongue my mother taught,
The lullabies, the curses, the sharp slang
That fits my mouth like keys to doors I sought
When I was young, when all my world was rang
With that first speech that mapped my earliest days—
No, now I hold two worlds, two ways to see:
How “saudade” holds no English phrase,
How “home” hums different when it’s “chez moi.”
I stammer still, I mix the words, I slip,
But now each slip is not a mark of shame:
It is the proof I let two worlds equip
My heart to hear more joy, more grief, more name.
Who says the adult heart grows stiff, too old?
My tongue has learned new songs, my soul grows bold.

title: prose poem|an old piano left on the curb
text:
The curb paints its gray lip against my casters,
someone’s scrap of receipt stuck to a pedal
like a pale moth that forgot how to be elsewhere.
I am no ship. No coffin. No widow
wearing black lacquer into the weather.
I am a box where a family kept thunder
in small change: a stuck B-flat,
a ring of coffee on my lid,
the tooth of a child who bit a chord
and ran when the room winced.

Rain opens my keys alphabet by alphabet.
A sparrow studies middle C, then declines.
Inside me, hammers hang like tiny tools
in a garage after the mechanic has died:
orderly, useless, almost tender.
The felts carry skin oil, cat dander,
one burst of beer thrown in a quarrel,
and the hush of a girl who practiced
only when her mother was on the phone,
softly, as if forgiveness needed a disguise.

A truck will come. Or rain will.
Tonight, the streetlamp fingers my yellowed ivories
and finds the burn of a cigarette,
the scratch where a key was hidden on a wire,
the dust of all the songs that got up
and walked out in ordinary shoes.
I do not weep for music.
I hold the shape of it—
81 small doors,
and behind every one,
a room still learning to listen.

title: villanelle|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
Coffee at Dawn Before Anyone Wakes
The dark still holds the hush of unturned sheets,
I pour slow gold where kitchen shadows lean—
No footstep taps, no voice the silence meets.

The kettle’s sigh soft as a dream that fleets,
Steam curls to kiss the frost-fogged window screen,
The dark still holds the hush of unturned sheets.

First sip bites sharp, then blooms of warm completes
The quiet spell no clattering routine
Has come to crack: no footstep taps, no voice the silence meets.

I watch the sky bleed pale from indigo deeps,
A sparrow hops the fence, first living thing seen—
The dark still holds the hush of unturned sheets.

No toaster pops, no alarm clock shrill repeats,
No small child calls, no partner’s mug between
My hands and this: no footstep taps, no voice the silence meets.

I cradle warmth while the last shadow retreats,
This hour is mine, unshared, unplanned, pristine—
The dark still holds the hush of unturned sheets,
No footstep taps, no voice the silence meets.

title: pantoum|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
The engine kicks. My father tells me, easy.
A bristle of his beard is going grey.
The parking lot is Sunday, mostly empty.
I turn the signal even though there’s no one.

He says a bristle of his beard is going grey
and cracks the window with his good hand.
I turn the signal even though there’s no one.
A french fry box slides underneath the pedal.

He cracks the window with his good hand,
the one that caught a softball at my temple.
A french fry box slides underneath the pedal.
He tells me brakes are gentler than I think.

The one that caught a softball at my temple
rests on the dashboard, not quite touching mine.
He tells me brakes are gentler than I think.
I stop too hard. He knocks his knee instead.

It rests on the dashboard, not quite touching mine,
the scar across his knuckle from the gutter.
I stop too hard. He knocks his knee instead
and says, all right, then. Nobody died.

The scar across his knuckle from the gutter
looks darker in the lot’s uneven light.
He says, all right, then. Nobody died.
His coffee ring blooms on the owner’s manual.

It looks darker in the lot’s uneven light.
The parking lot is Sunday, mostly empty.
His coffee ring blooms on the owner’s manual.
The engine kicks. My father tells me, easy.

title: prose poem|watching a parent grow old
text:
Threshold Light
The kitchen linoleum holds the ghost of your step now—
the one that used to thud like a dropped axe when you came in from the barn,
boots caked with alfalfa and frost, voice loud enough to rattle the canning jars
on the shelf above the sink where you kept the dill pickles you brined every August,
your hands so broad they could wrap around two quart jars at once, knuckles split
from mending fence wire, calluses thick as the leather of your work belt.

Last week I found you standing in front of the spice rack for ten minutes,
fingers brushing the labels of cumin and paprika like they were written in a language
you’d forgotten how to read. You used to measure chili powder by the palmful,
never needed a recipe, could tell if the roast was done by the smell curling
through the house, could fix a stuck garbage disposal with a butter knife and a grunt,
could lift me over the puddles in the driveway after a storm like I weighed no more
than a handful of dandelion fluff.

Last night you asked me to read the menu out loud at the diner,
said the lights were too bright, the print too small, and when I looked up
your glasses were smudged with something that might have been pie filling,
might have been the thin film of age that settles over everything soft, slow,
the way the oak tree at the end of the driveway grows moss on its north side now,
the way the screen door doesn’t slam anymore, just eases shut on a hinge you haven’t
had the strength to oil in three summers.

I watched you this morning, trying to tie your work boots,
fingers fumbling the laces like they were knotted with thread too fine to see,
and I didn’t move to help at first, just stood in the doorway holding the mug of coffee
you used to drink black, no sugar, hot enough to scald the roof of your mouth,
and I remembered when you taught me to tie my shoes, your hands covering mine,
your voice low and steady: loop, swoop, pull, kid, don’t rush it,
and I thought about how all the loops come undone eventually, how the swoop
of your arm when you throw a ball doesn’t go as high as it used to, how the pull
of gravity is softer now, heavier, how it tugs at the corners of your mouth when you smile,
tugs at the hem of your flannel shirt, tugs at the space between us when you reach
for my hand crossing the street, your palm thinner than I remember, the bones
sharp as bird wings under the papery skin.

You don’t sing old Johnny Cash songs in the shower anymore.
Some days you forget where you put the truck keys, forget the name of the neighbor
who’s lived next door for twenty years, but you still remember the way I liked my peanut butter
sandwiches cut diagonally, no crust, still leave a jar of those dill pickles on my porch
every August, even when your knees ache too bad to bend over the brining crock,
even when you have to sit down halfway through canning, your breath coming short
like you’ve run a long race no one told you you were running.

I used to think growing old was something that happened all at once,
like a light switching off, like a door slamming shut, but it’s this:
the way you pause halfway up the stairs to catch your breath, hand on the bannister
like it’s an old friend, the way you laugh when you tell the same story for the third time
at dinner, the way you let me cut your meat for you now, no protest, no pride,
just a small, quiet nod, like you know we are trading places slow,
like you are handing me all the small, heavy things you carried for so long—
the canning jars, the fence pliers, the recipe for chili, the way to tie a knot
that won’t come undone in the wind.

Last night I sat on the porch with you while the fireflies came out,
and you leaned your head on my shoulder for a minute, just a minute,
your hair white as the dill heads floating in those pickle jars,
and the sun went down slow over the alfalfa field, gilding the edges of everything
that is fraying, everything that is softening, everything that is still here—
your hand in mine, the distant creak of the barn door, the taste of dill on my tongue,
the light holding us both, gentle, unrushed, like it knows we don’t get to keep
any of it forever, just get to hold it for a little while, warm,
before the dark comes soft, slow, the way you used to tuck the blankets
up under my chin when I was small, before you turned out the light.

title: elegy|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
I. Steam and Starched Linens

Before the doors part, we know the hush:
silver aligned like a held breath,
bouillon trembling in silver cups.
The bride’s train drags a draft of lilies
through the swing door; someone hisses hot—
our aprons stiff as borrowed prayer books.
We do not see vows. We see the oven glow
baste the crown of a waiter’s bent head,
and hear, through clatter, the small, shock cough
of champagne corks, faint as buried drums.

 II. Scullery Benediction

By the time first dances blur to waltz,
we are knee-deep in asparagus peelings,
the congealed cream of vows exchanged.
A busboy pauses, rag over shoulder,
to watch them circle through the porthole—
white dress a splash of milk in dark wine.
Nobody says forever. We scour pans
caked with the sugar of their first toast,
stack plates still warm from other people’s
kisses, while the band slows to one last hum.

 III. After the Rice

Midnight unstrings the fairy lights.
We gather napkins crumpled as confessionals,
a lost garter hooked beneath a chair.
The bouquets are bruised; the leftover cake
sags in its box, sweetening for tomorrow.
Out back, the newlyweds’ car has long hissed
into the dark. We wash the lipstick
from flute rims, scour rings off the tablecloth—
and though no photograph will keep us,
we know the marriage began also here,
in steam, in salt, in hands that kept working
while two strangers promised to stay.

title: dramatic monologue|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Last Liturgy of the Sugar Maple
(The speaker leans on a weathered sandstone marker, voice rough as crumpled leaf, boot prodding a drift of crimson and amber at their feet)
I am the only one who brings you flowers
that do not wilt in three days’ plastic wrap:
these maple embers, oak scraps burnt to honey,
birch pages thin as the last note you left
scrawled on a napkin, stuck to the fridge door.
The groundskeeper rakes them to the curb each week,
mumbles about “neatness,” “respect for the plot,”
as if the dead ever cared for sharp-edged lawns,
as if you did not once roll in a pile of these
same leaves, laughing so hard you snort-laughed,
leaving bits of gold stuck in your curly hair.

You know they do not fall by accident.
Each one is a postcard the tree sends down
to tuck in the cracks of your headstone, to cover
the chip where the lawnmower nicked your name last June.
They whisper the things the living forget to say:
the corner store still sells your favorite sour candy,
the high school football team won homecoming,
the cat you rescued still curls on the windowsill
when the wind bites sharp enough to hint at snow.
The preacher says dust to dust, but he has not knelt
to run a palm over this velvet rot, has not felt
how the leaves hold heat long after the sun dips low,
how they do not leave when the rain comes, when the frost
crisps their edges, when the world goes gray and tight.

Last week I found a red one pressed flat
in the hollow where your birth date is carved,
bright as the shard of broken tail light
they pulled from the wreckage, bright as the blood
that stained the cuff of my jacket that night.
I did not brush it off. I left it there,
a little flame to keep the dark from creeping
too close to where you lie. People bring chrysanthemums,
wreaths of plastic evergreen that fade to chalk,
but these leaves know how to let go without lying—
they do not promise to stay forever. They just burn
as bright as they can, for as long as they are allowed,
then melt slow into the dirt that holds you,
feeding the roots that will push new green up
come spring, when I will stand here again
and wait for them to fall, to come back home,
to cover all the quiet, cold, unspoken parts
the world keeps trying to rake away, to forget.
(They bend, tuck a gilded oak leaf into the engraved curve of the name on the stone, and turn to walk the path as a gust sends a swirl of crimson spinning after them, soft as a hand brushing the back of their coat.)

title: dramatic monologue|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
Through the Steel Doors

I count three hundred plates before the doors swing wide—
not for me, never for me, though I know
the exact weight of every bridegroom’s toast
in butter, salt, the hush of hollandaise.

At six, the roses arrived, gashed open
in their plastic sleeves; I stripped the thorns
while the bride wept into a stranger’s phone
upstairs, her voice thin as a peeled asparagus.

By seven, the ovens roared like a held breath.
I watched her father practice his smile
in the reflection of a copper pot,
then press a bill into my shaking hand
and say *Make sure the fish is never late.*

The vows came through the speaker, crackling,
while I stirred risotto into cream.
Somebody laughed. Somebody dropped a ring.
I did not look up. The rice would burn.

Now they cheer. The first dance shakes the floor.
I carve the cake where someone hid a coin,
a thimble, all the small futures they believe in—
and I remember my own sister’s wedding:
how I stood just like this, behind steam,
how she waved at me once through the doorway,
then turned, and was carried away by the music.

At midnight, they will leave in a storm of rice,
and I will scrape their vows into the bin,
fold the napkins that held their trembling hands,
wash the wine from glasses that still hum.

But tomorrow, when the kitchen is cold and empty,
I will find one white ribbon, caught on a hinge—
and I will know that I was here,
that I fed the whole burning room,
that love passed through my hands
and did not know my name.

title: free verse poem|drought on a family farm
text:
Drought
The rain gauge by the clothesline holds
a single drowned wasp and nothing else
three weeks running.
Dad quit wearing his work boots to the porch,
scuffs through dust thick as powdered milk
in his sock feet, says it don’t matter anymore
if the mud clods track. The mud clods are gone.

Last Tuesday we shot the last of the laying hens
because the well ran too low to waste on their trough.
Mom boiled the oldest bird for three hours,
meat still stuck to the bones like rubber,
we ate it quiet at the kitchen table
while the radio droned about record highs
and somebody’s sweet corn yield out in Sioux County.
I saved the prettiest tail feather, dun and gold,
tucked it in the crack of my window frame
where it catches the hot wind that don’t quit.

The soybeans curled up tight as folded prayers
two weeks back. We walked the rows at dusk
last night, Dad kicking at the crumbled stalks
that turn to dust when they hit the dirt.
He used to carry lemon drops in his breast pocket
for when I’d get tired hilling potatoes,
but yesterday I found the crumpled bag
in the glove box of the pickup, empty,
stuck to a melted peppermint from 2019.

Last night I heard him through the wall
talking to Mom like he was talking
to a spooked horse, low, rough,
saying he didn’t know how we’d make the payment
if August don’t break. Mom didn’t say nothing back,
just ran the tap slow until it sputtered,
caught the last half-cup in a chipped ceramic mug
for the old barn cat that won’t leave.

The sun comes up red every morning now,
bleeds over the ridge like it’s sorry,
but it don’t cool off, don’t spill nothing
but light so bright it hurts to look at the pasture
where the grass crunches underfoot like broken glass.
I saw a coyote yesterday at noon,
out in the open, not even skittish,
its ribs sticking out like fence posts,
just standing there staring at the house
like it knew we didn’t have the water
to chase it off, didn’t have much of anything
worth chasing it away from.

title: sequence of haiku|the stars seen from a desert
text:
I

Dune holds the last light—
one stone still warm, while the dark
opens like a door.

II

Wind prints its absence
over sand. Then, first by first,
stars begin to burn.

III

No roof between us.
The Milky Way unscrolls, cold
as a river’s bone.

IV

I do not speak now.
Even my small shadow seems
too loud upon the sand.

V

Under such silver,
grief becomes a quiet thing—
a cup filled with night.

VI

Somewhere far, a campfire
breathes red; the stars keep their old
distance, and their grace.

VII

Dawn will soon wash them
back to heaven. Let me keep
this handful of dark.

title: elegy|watching a parent grow old
text:
Part 1: The Spare Key
The key you cut for me at eighteen
sits blunt in my palm now—
you fumble the lock three tries
before the tumbler gives,
mumbling that the deadbolt’s grown stubborn.
I don’t say I watched your thumb
tremble as it slid the key home,
that the door hasn’t changed
since you first hoisted me to reach it.

 Part 2: The Recipe Card
The card for your gingerbread
is smudged where your thumb has rested
forty winters, measurements faded
to guesswork: *some molasses, enough spice*.
You pause mid-stir, blink hard,
say you can’t remember if you added the cloves.
I don’t tell you I caught you
staring at my face for ten long seconds
last week, like you were trying to place
the girl who once stood on a step stool
begging to lick the bowl.

 Part 3: The Armrest
On the drive home from the clinic
you reach over, not to adjust the radio
not to nag me about my speed,
just to rest your hand light on my arm
when I merge onto the highway.
Your knuckles are ridged with age,
your palm cool as river stone,
and I don’t move, don’t speak,
don’t tell you I remember
when that hand was big enough
to cover my whole chest,
to hold me tight enough
to keep the whole world
from tipping over.

title: elegy|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
The Ring Across Years

The phone rang strange, a number I’d erased
but not forgotten—same area code
as the old house where boyhood voices chased
each other down the hall, then overflowed
into silence. I answered. And your name
crossed the wire like weather coming home.

Your voice had weathered; underneath it came
the cadence I would know in any room,
though thinner now, as if distance or shame
had filed the edges. You said, “It’s me. It’s bloom
season again.” I stood where the light thinned,
holding the phone like a bird I had wounded.

We spoke of roads, of the years we had pinned
to separate skies—your hospital, my door,
the letters started and never signed,
the funerals we missed, the stubborn war
between pride and blood. You coughed, then you said,
“I just wanted to hear you still breathing.”

Tonight I set the phone down by the bed
like a relic, like a bridge I cannot trust.
Somewhere the line stays open where we led
our ghosts back home through static and through dust.
Brother, long lost, found only in the sound—
I keep your voice, and cannot reach around.

title: spoken-word poem|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
The security guard’s nail gun click
of a stapler mends the torn sign
that says QUIET PLEASE—he staples
three times, slow, like he’s driving
nails into a coffin for the word,
and no one looks up. The sun slants
through the smudge on the third-floor window
where a kid pressed a gum star
last Tuesday, gilding it now so it glows
like a cheap relic someone might pray to
if they were stuck on a thesis about
19th-century beekeeper journals.

The guy in the Carhartt jacket two tables over
is not reading Moby-Dick, though the spine
faces out like a flex—he’s scrolling Zillow
for houses in towns where the median income
is half his student loan balance, snorting
quietly when he sees a porch listed as a “feature.”
A toddler in the children’s nook below us
lets out a shriek that bounces off the microfilm
cabinets, and her mom shushes her so loud
the microfilm librarian flinches, drops a roll
of 1978 newspaper that unfurls across the floor
like a carpet of old gas prices and obituaries
for people who died never knowing what TikTok was.

I run my finger along the shelf of donated books,
the ones no one checks out: a 1992 guide to
VCR repair, pressed between a beat-up romance
novel with a shirtless pirate on the cover and
a memoir written by a guy who tried to live
on only roadkill for a year. Tucked in the VCR book,
a receipt from a Blockbuster in Toledo, 2004,
for *Mean Girls* and a bag of Sour Patch Kids,
late fee $2.17, scrawled on the back in blue pen:
Call me if you want to make out after this.
No name, no number, just the ghost of a plan
that probably fizzled, probably ended with
someone waiting by a landline for an hour
before eating all the candy alone.

The heating system kicks on with a groan
like it’s been holding that breath since last Sunday,
blowing dust that dances in the gum-star sunbeam,
and for a second I swear I can smell all the things
that have seeped into these walls: the burnt popcorn
from last month’s teen movie night, the lemon Pledge
the janitor uses on the tables, the faint, sharp tang
of the kid who had a nosebleed in the poetry section
last spring, the quiet sweat of everyone who’s ever sat here
panicking over a resume, a breakup note, a doctor’s form
they can’t read because the words are too big and too scary.

A girl in a *Succession* hoodie carries a stack of books
to the checkout desk: one on mushroom foraging,
one on feminist film theory, one on how to talk to your cat
about gun safety. The librarian, whose name tag says
MARGE and who has a tattoo of an octopus holding
a fountain pen curling up her wrist, stamps them
so slow, like each stamp is a blessing, like she knows
half of them will come back unread, their spines uncracked,
sitting on a nightstand while the person who checked them out
binge-watches a show about people baking sourdough
in a competition for $10,000. She doesn’t care.
She tucks a free seed packet for zinnias in between
the mushroom book and the cat book, winks, says
Don’t eat the ones with the white gills.

Outside, a Harley rumbles past loud enough
to rattle the windowpanes, and the guy with the Zillow tab
flips the bird at the glass without looking up.
The toddler has stopped shrieking, is now chewing
on the corner of a board book about a penguin
who learns to share. The microfilm librarian
has rolled the 1978 paper back up, is patting it
like it’s a cat that wandered into her lap.
I slide the VCR repair book back on the shelf,
leave the Blockbuster receipt tucked where I found it,
for the next person who’s not looking for Moby-Dick,
who’s just looking for something that feels like proof
that people were here before them, that they wanted things,
that they were bad at returning movies, that they loved
sour candy and makeouts and zinnias, that they sat here
on a Sunday too, letting the sun gild the gum on the window,
letting the quiet hold all the noise they didn’t know
how to carry out the door.

title: prose poem|the sound of a train at night
text:
I wake before I know I'm awake—
the house doing its slow creak, the radiator's last click,
and under it, the train.

Not the sad movie train, not the lonesome whistle trope.
This one is two miles off, maybe three,
where the tracks run behind the warehouse park
where I once bought a Christmas tree in the rain
and tied it to the roof with frayed twine.

The sound comes flattened by cold:
a long low pull, then the metal answering itself,
wheel to rail, the small repeating knock
of every joint in the rail, every joint in me.

Last winter Dan and I sat in his truck
at the crossing on Bethel, engine off,
and counted the cars. Forty-seven. He said
his father used to say a train that long
meant somebody somewhere was getting rich.
Dan died in March. Not on the tracks.
Just died, the way people do now,
with the dishes still in the sink.

Tonight the train takes its time.
I can tell where it is by the way the sound thins
going over the trestle, then thickens
past the old granary. The dog doesn't lift her head.
She's heard it every night of her nine years
and has never once felt the need to explain it.

I get up and pee in the dark.
The bathroom window gives nothing back
but the sodium glow over town
and that long working sound,
grainers or tankers, who knows,
somebody's freight, somebody's schedule,
the crew drinking bad coffee up in the cab,
one of them yawning, one of them
thinking about a woman in Toledo.

For a second I'm seven again,
top bunk at my grandmother's,
the train coming through Lima,
and the way the whole house would lean
toward the noise and then straighten,
as if the world had briefly remembered
something it was supposed to carry.

It fades. Not beautifully.
It just gets smaller, the way a sentence does
when the speaker turns into another room.

I stand at the cold glass a while longer.
Nothing resolves. The dog sighs.
Somewhere a car alarm starts, gives up.
I should go back to bed.
I don't go back to bed.

title: spoken-word poem|learning a second language as an adult
text:
Glossolalia for the Grown-Up Tongue
(For anyone who has ever fumbled a word for bread, and felt it stick to the roof of their mouth like a crumb)

The first word sticks like a taffy pull
between teeth that have known only one shape of home—
your mother tongue, thick as the kitchen steam
that curled around your high chair, that knew
the exact weight of *I’m sorry*,
the exact crackle of a joke that lands
before you even finish saying it.

You are thirty-one, sitting in a linoleum classroom
where the erasers smell like the fourth grade,
and your mouth feels like a borrowed overcoat:
too big in the shoulders, the buttons mismatched,
the pockets full of someone else’s receipts.
The teacher holds up a flashcard: *manzana*.
You say it wrong. The girl next to you,
nineteen, her tongue quick as a sparrow,
says it so easy the apple practically drops
red and ripe into her palm.
Yours stays bobbing in the back of your throat,
bruised, half-remembered, the kind you picked
as a kid and threw away because it tasted
like effort, not like sweetness.

Grocery stores become minefields.
You point at leeks for ten minutes because
the word for *leek* has slithered out
the crack between your coffee and your commute,
and the cashier smiles, soft, the kind of smile
you give a dog that’s trying to open a door—
patient, a little amused, already reaching
for the thing you can’t name.
On the bus, you hear two teenagers laughing
in your new language, fast as rain on a tin roof,
and you catch every third word: rain, tomorrow, stupid,
and for a second you think you are almost there,
almost in the room where the jokes live,
then they say a phrase you don’t know,
sharp as a shard of glass, and the door clicks shut
again, and you are back on the outside,
pressing your palm to the cold glass,
watching people move through a party
you weren’t invited to.

Sometimes you dream in half-sentences:
your grandmother asking for water in Spanish,
your childhood dog answering in French,
you standing there, mute, holding an empty glass,
watching the words melt like snow on your palms.
Once, you got angry enough to yell at a man
who cut you in line, and the words came out
all wrong: I wanted to say *you are rude*,
what came out was *you are a radish*,
and he stared, and you stared,
and then you both laughed so hard
you forgot why you were mad,
and for a second the words didn’t need
to be perfect—they just needed to be there,
bright and lumpy as a homemade sweater,
full of dropped stitches, warm anyway.

You start small.
You learn to order coffee exactly how you like it:
*no sugar, extra hot, please*.
The barista remembers.
You read a children’s book all the way through,
about a cat who loses its hat,
and you cry over the last page,
not because the cat finds the hat,
but because you understood it,
each word a small stone you laid yourself
across the river that used to feel too wide to cross.
You talk to the old man who feeds pigeons in the park,
and he slows down for you,
tells you about the pigeon with the broken wing
he nursed back to health last winter,
and you tell him about the oak tree in your parents’ yard
you used to climb, and the words trip over each other,
some in your old language, some in the new,
and he nods like he understands every single one,
like mixed-up words are just another kind of bird song,
no less beautiful for being out of tune.

Last week you cried in the back of a taxi,
because the driver was playing a song
in your new language, and you knew all the words.
They came up out of your chest without you reaching,
without you fumbling, without you translating
first in your head, like they had been there
all along, waiting for the right melody
to pull them loose.
You sang under your breath, wobbly,
and the driver turned up the radio,
and for a minute there was no before, no after,
no first language, no second,
just voice, just sound, just the world
opening up like a fruit you didn’t know
you already knew how to peel.

People will tell you you are too old.
They will say the window closes when you are twelve,
that your tongue has hardened into the shape
of your first home, that you will always sound
like you are standing just outside the door.
Let them.
What they don’t know is that a grown-up tongue
is not a dead thing. It is a muscle that remembers
how to stretch, how to fumble, how to taste
new fruits, new ways to say *I love you*,
new ways to say *that hurt*,
new ways to ask for bread, for water, for a place
to sit down, for someone to slow down,
for someone to listen even when the words
come out cracked, come out crooked,
come out wearing the wrong shoes,
come out like you are learning to walk all over again.

Last night I stood on my fire escape
and talked to my neighbor for an hour
about how the jasmine smells this time of year,
and I only messed up three words.
The jasmine didn’t care. My neighbor didn’t care.
The words hung in the air between us,
soft, a little imperfect,
sweet anyway.
That is the thing no one tells you
about learning a language when your bones
are already done growing:
you don’t just learn new words.
You learn how to be bad at something,
on purpose, out loud,
in front of cashiers and taxi drivers
and old men who feed pigeons,
and how to keep going anyway.
You learn that home is not a single tongue
tied tight to your childhood.
It is every word you ever fumbled for,
every laugh when you got it wrong,
every time someone heard you,
really heard you,
even when you didn’t say it quite right.

Today I bought an apple from the corner store.
I said *manzana* perfectly.
The fruit was crisp, bright,
tasted like nothing I had ever known before,
tasted like all the words I still don’t know,
waiting for me,
sweet on the tip of my tongue,
ready.

title: pantoum|drought on a family farm
text:
I. The Dust Remembers

The red earth cracks where the last rain ran,
and the wind takes notes in a dry, thin hand.
My father stands where the irrigation plan
is folded soft in a rubber band.

And the wind takes notes in a dry, thin hand
over the pasture we used to mow.
It is folded soft in a rubber band,
the list of fields we did not sow.

Over the pasture we used to mow,
my mother’s shadow grows long and still:
the list of fields we did not sow,
the dam gone white beneath the hill.

My mother’s shadow grows long and still
beside the troughs where the cattle stand.
The dam gone white beneath the hill,
the red earth cracks where the last rain ran.

II. The House Holds Its Breath

Beside the troughs where the cattle stand,
we ration water, cup by cup.
My grandfather’s name on the weathervane
points to a sky that will not give up.

We ration water, cup by cup;
the garden beans have forgotten green.
It points to a sky that will not give up,
that brass cock turning where dust has been.

The garden beans have forgotten green;
my little sister asks when rain will come.
That brass cock turning where dust has been
creaks to the same word: soon, soon.

My little sister asks when rain will come.
My father stands where the irrigation plan
creaks to the same word: soon, soon—
and the wind takes notes in a dry, thin hand.

III. What We Keep

That brass cock turning where dust has been
watches us gather what shade we can.
We do not say what the drought might mean;
the red earth cracks where the last rain ran.

We watch each other gather what shade we can:
hands at the table, chapped and brown.
We do not say what the drought might mean,
but we pass the last jar of peaches down.

Hands at the table, chapped and brown,
the list of fields we did not sow—
we pass the last jar of peaches down
over the pasture we used to mow.

The list of fields we did not sow
is folded soft in a rubber band.
Over the pasture we used to mow,
we hold the seed for another land.

title: prose poem|an abandoned railway station
text:
The Station That Breathes Only Thistle
The rails have unlearned the weight of locomotives, their iron skins pocked with rust that bleeds orange into the gravel after rain, as if the old steel still remembers how to bleed steam. The platform edge is crumbled where porters once hefted trunks stitched with steamship labels, where children pressed penny-flattened palms to the glass of passing coaches, where goodbyes stuck to the air like cinders long after the last whistle frayed to silence.
The ticket window hangs ajar, its wood warped by forty winters, a spider strung its web across the coin slot where dimes and nickels once clinked for fares to cities that glow now only in the faded timetables curled on the floor, their ink bled to illegibility: *Departures 8:15 for Maplewood, 9:42 for the coast, 11:07 for all the places you promised you’d go*. The waiting bench slats are split, grown soft with moss, and if you press your palm to the grain you can almost feel the ghost-heat of thighs pressed close, of a girl twisting a handkerchief while she waited for a soldier who never came home, of an old man whittling while the clock above the door ticked slow as a heartbeat.
The clock stopped in 1978, its hands frozen at 3:19, the exact minute the last train rumbled past without slowing, its whistle a thin wail that curled around the eaves and left nothing but dandelion fluff in its wake. A swallow has built its nest in the hollow of the station sign, the letters half-flaked away: *WILLOW CREEK, POP. 127*. The willows are gone now, cut for lumber when the mill closed, the creek shrunk to a trickle that sings lullabies to the rusted spikes half-buried in the loam.
Milkweed grows thick between the ties, its silk catching the golden hour light like scattered ticket stubs, monarchs pausing on their long migration south as if waiting for a conductor to call *all aboard*. Thistle pushes up through the cracked concrete of the platform, its purple blooms the only flags left flying for the place that once was the threshold to everywhere. Once, a boy left a tin train engine tucked in the crack of the station wall, its red paint chipped, its wheels frozen fast; it still faces west, down the stretch of track that vanishes into the brambles, as if any minute the rails might hum again, as if the air might thicken with the smell of coal smoke and burnt coffee, as if the door might swing open and all the people who left might step off, their suitcases heavy with stories, their faces bright with coming home.
The wind moves through the broken windowpanes, and for a second it sounds exactly like a train approaching, slow and sure, huffing soft as a breath against the hills. But it is only the wind. The station does not mind. It holds all the unspoken hellos and unkept goodbyes soft in its rotting rafters, lets the clover grow over the footprints, lets the rust bloom, lets the quiet settle like dust on every surface. It does not wait, exactly. It just remembers. And sometimes, when the moon hangs thin as a rail spike over the valley, it hums the old whistle song to itself, very quietly, so only the foxes and the fireflies can hear.

title: ode|hope after a long illness
text:
Ode to the Light Switch

After the fever burned its last acre,
I woke to the dust doing its slow arithmetic
on the bookshelf. The IV pole had left
a pale bruise on the carpet, a small moon
where I used to orbit the ceiling.

I had forgotten how the body keeps
its own weather—how the lungs unclench
like fists after a long argument.
Outside, a squirrel dragged half a bagel
across the telephone wire, absurd as faith,
and I laughed until my ribs remembered
they were still mine.

The doctors had spoken in percentages,
their voices flat as parking lots,
but here was the spoon, heavy with oatmeal,
here the kettle screaming its bright gospel
from the stove. I pressed my palm
to the window and the glass was cold
and alive, a river that had chosen
to stay.

Hope, when it came, was not a sunrise
or a bird. It was the way I knelt
to tie my shoe and stayed there,
studying the grain of the floorboard,
the scuff marks, a single dead ant
carrying nothing. It was choosing
the hard chair instead of the bed,
the window instead of the clock,
the strange, stubborn grammar
of *tomorrow*, of *again*.

Last night I walked to the end of the driveway
in socks. The neighbor's security light
caught me standing there, thin as a receipt,
and did not look away. Somewhere
a dog was barking the world back
into existence. I breathed in.
The air tasted like rain and gasoline
and all the ordinary, difficult days
I had almost lost.

I did not pray.
I just stood there, practicing
the first word I ever knew:
*here, here, here*.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
Petrarchan Sonnet to the Fridge Hum at 3 A.M.
When all the world has folded into sleep,
And thin moonlight spills thin across the sheet,
I lie unspooled where rest should run complete,
While the low refrigerator thrum starts to creep:
First soft as far-off surf where gulls still sweep,
Then sharp as wires strung tight along the street,
It threads the hush where drowsy dreams should meet,
My ragged pulse that will not slow, nor keep
Time with the hush the dark is meant to hold.
It hums of leftover cold lemon tart,
Of milk gone slightly sour around the rim,
The quiet weight of days that grow old,
Till dawn prises the night’s tight lid apart,
I count its pulses, never lost to him.

title: ode|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
Ode to the Library on a Sunday Afternoon

Light bends through leaded glass, slow as a prayer,
where dust motes hold their breath and sunlight spills
across the oak—each polished shelf a stair
of voices hushed, of unremembered thrills.
The radiator hums a drowsy hymn,
while winter’s last reluctant gold descends
on spines that crackle, weathered, soft, and dim,
where every ghost still offers, and attends.

A child turns pages like a startled bird;
a scholar pauses, pen in hand, and dreams;
the clock’s thin tick dissolves, unspoken, blurred,
as hours unspool in long and golden streams.
Outside, the world goes rushing, loud, and blind—
but here the dead sit speaking, heart to mind.

The librarian reshelves a borrowed name,
her fingers brushing spines as if she knew
each soul that flickered, once, in dust and flame,
each grief that found what only words can do.
Rain starts, soft as a footnote, on the pane;
a reader shifts, and sighs, and turns a page;
the afternoon folds in, half joy, half pain,
a hush that holds the fever of the age.

And I, too, lean toward the lantern-glow,
no longer late, no longer lost, alone,
but given back to all I longed to know—
the quiet cathedral not of glass, but stone
made paper: where the hours lean, forgive,
and Sundays teach the dust how it should live.

title: villanelle|an abandoned railway station
text:
I. The Ticket Window
The glass is frosted where the moss crept through,
The punch press rusts to crumbs beneath the sill,
No hand will reach to stamp your journey through.

Last calls dissolved where clover pushed through
Cracked concrete where the waiting crowds once stood still;
The glass is frosted where the moss crept through.

A tattered timetable bleeds faded blue,
Its ink run thin where rain seeped past the sill—
No hand will reach to stamp your journey through.

The bell that hung to signal trains’ debut
Hangs slack, its clang long lost to wind’s low thrill;
The glass is frosted where the moss crept through.

No fares are asked, no tickets left to dole,
No traveler’s quick step hurries up the hill—
The glass is frosted where the moss crept through,
No hand will reach to stamp your journey through.

---

 II. The Platform Edge
The rails run red where rust has claimed their grain,
No whistle cuts the hush that binds the ties,
Clover curls thick where platform planks have wane.

Weeds stitch the gaps where workmen’s boots once drained
Warm steam and smoke that curled to summer skies;
The rails run red where rust has claimed their grain.

A child’s lost marble glints through last year’s rain,
Its swirled blue glass unclaimed by searching eyes—
Clover curls thick where platform planks have wane.

The bench slats bow where lovers once remained
To press last kisses, wave last goodbyes;
The rails run red where rust has claimed their grain.

No wheel will spark, no brake will grind its strain,
No conductor’s call will make the quiet rise—
The rails run red where rust has claimed their grain,
Clover curls thick where platform planks have wane.

---

 III. The Waiting Room
The floorboards creak for steps that never come,
Spiders string lace across the cracked bench backs,
The last train left before the moon went numb.

A crumpled postcard smudged with faded gum
Bears half a name, half an address that lacks
The floorboards creak for steps that never come.

The stove is cold, its ash long turned to crumb,
No kettle’s whistle cuts the quiet’s tracks—
The last train left before the moon went numb.

Wind steals through gaps to hum the songs once hummed
By travelers who slung their coats and packs;
The floorboards creak for steps that never come.

No schedule calls, no journey will outrun
The slow soft green that pulls the old walls slack—
The floorboards creak for steps that never come,
The last train left before the moon went numb.

title: prose poem|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
The 2 A.M. Route

The bus breathes diesel sighs at empty curbs,
its yellow eyes cutting through rain-smeared dark,
a metal heartbeat humming down avenues
where storefronts sleep behind iron grins.

Only three passengers tonight:
a nurse whose shoes remember every hallway,
a boy with a duffel and no fixed address,
and me, pretending I know where I'm going.

The driver nods like a priest at confession,
takes our crumpled fares without judgment.
Seats are cold pews, vinyl and cracked,
each window a confessional of passing light.

Streetlights bloom and vanish, bloom and vanish—
the city's slow pulse under sodium suns.
A discarded newspaper dances in the wake,
some old headline already forgetting itself.

We pass the all-night laundromat glowing,
a lone woman folding ghosts into towels,
the diner where coffee steams for the insomniacs,
the bridge where the river carries the moon away.

No one speaks. We are monks of the graveyard route,
riding together toward separate dawns,
suspended between the life that ended at midnight
and the one that begins when the brakes sigh open.

At the last stop the doors fold apart
like an invitation. The rain has stopped.
Somewhere a bird mistakes the streetlamp for morning.
We step out, strangers, into the almost-light.

title: prose poem|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
The fence post wears it like a half-remembered secret,
not the wool kind with the frayed cuff stitched by a mother,
but the synthetic black one, palm slathered in dried latex paint
the color of a storm cloud that never broke, index finger crimped
where it curled around a nail gun last Tuesday, when the crew
framed the addition on the corner lot, when Javi yelled
about his kid’s first soccer goal, when the wind picked up
sharp enough to steal a sandwich right out of a cooler, sharp enough
to yank this glove off mid-swing, send it cartwheeling over the siding
until it caught on the splintered post like a bird that forgot how to fly.
It holds the ghost of a callus at the heel, a smudge of construction adhesive
that will never wash off, a crumb of the Flamin’ Hot Cheeto the wearer ate
on break, tucked in the seam between thumb and forefinger.
The dog walkers glance at it like it’s a typo in the neighborhood’s script,
the kids on scooters swerve close enough to poke it with a handlebar
then veer off, cackling, like it might bite. The rain fills its palm
at night, leaves a thin ring of rust from the barbed wire staple
that caught its wrist, holds it hostage. No one is coming for it.
The wearer bought a three-pack at the dollar store on the way home,
didn’t even notice it was gone until he reached for his beer
that evening, his left hand bare, chalked it up to the wind, to the job,
to the way things slip when you’re not looking, when you’re busy
nailing two-by-fours to the sky, when you’re thinking about soccer goals
and rent and the way your ex still texts when she needs money for the kid’s cleats.
Last night a sparrow wove a strand of its frayed cuff into her nest
in the oak across the street. This morning a spider strung a web
between its outstretched middle finger and the fence rail, strung it
tight as a guitar string, caught three gnats and a fleck of dandelion down.
It waves, slow, when the semis blow past on the highway half a mile off,
waves like someone who knows they’re not going home,
waves like it’s happy just to hold the rain, to feed the sparrow,
to give the spider a place to hang her work, to be the one thing
on this whole block that doesn’t owe anyone anything,
that doesn’t have to swing a hammer or pay a bill or remember
to pick up milk on the way home, that just gets to be:
black, paint-stiff, half-full of sun, perched on the splintered wood
like a black flag for all the small, un-mourned losses,
the things that slip out of our hands before we even know we’re holding them,
the things that stay, and make a life out of being left.

title: free verse poem|a jazz club in the rain
text:
A Jazz Club in the Rain

The neon sign bleeds pink and indigo
onto wet asphalt,
each raindrop a tiny cymbal
struck once, then swallowed.

At the door, the raincoat sighs
its weight onto a hook—
inside, the trumpet has already begun
unbuttoning the night.

A blue haze of cigarette and bourbon
leans against every note;
the piano’s left hand keeps time
with umbrellas collapsing in the vestibule.

The saxophone bends a phrase
like a streetlight bending in a puddle,
and somewhere past the steamed window,
thunder answers on the off-beat.

No one hurries.
Even the rain slows its tempo,
pressing its ear to the glass,
while the double thrums
like a second pulse
beneath the dark.

title: sequence of haiku|time and memory
text:
Grandma’s chipped egg timer
sand sticks to the dried yolk smudge
I let it run out

Last mix tape you made
warbles through the tape deck’s crack
side B cuts out mid-chorus

My old watch stopped dead
the day we got lost hiking
I still wear it, tight

Sour cherry stain
on the knee of my high school jeans
I can’t recall how it got there

The crickets sound same
as they did when I was seven
I don’t know the words to the song I sang then

text:

I answer, and a voice I once knew says, "Hey, Fred."

My pulse quickens with a quiet dread.

I answer, and a voice I once knew says, "Hey, Fred."

He says my name like a key in a rusted door.

II. The Pauses

The silence between us fills with old weather—

Mama's last winter, the truck, the empty porch.
