title: villanelle|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
Mill Town Nocturne
The smokestack holds its breath against the gray—
No whistle splits the dark to rouse the shift.
We tend the ghost of work that will not stay.

Chain-link strung tight with kudzu’s slow decay,
The loading dock sags where the trucks would lift;
The smokestack holds its breath against the gray.

We count the cracks where welders’ arcs once lay,
Trace smudged time cards the foreman failed to sift—
We tend the ghost of work that will not stay.
The diner’s pie case gathers dust all day,
No lunch-pail crowd to joke, complain, or gift
The smokestack holds its breath against the gray.
Kids chase a stray cat through the scrap-yard hay,
Their grandpas’ calloused hands no longer lift
The weight of work that stubbornly will not stay.
We lean on porch rails as the light bleeds away,
Wait for a hum that will never again drift—
The smokestack holds its breath against the gray.
We tend the ghost of work that will not stay.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Under the sodium sun that hums and bleeds
Amber across the asphalt, they convene—
Boys whose kneepads smell like garage and weeds,
Whose mouthguards bear the faint mint of Listerine.

The pressbox perches, tin and popcorn-steamed,
Where old men score with pencils, stubby, sure;
A chain-gang father yawns, his clipboard creamed
With bugspray, while the ball hangs, miniature,

Then drops. The bleachers shake a small percussion
Of folding chairs and one dropped Mountain Dew;
A dog barks through the PA's dusty buzzing,
And someone's uncle boos the whole backfield through.

Friday burns small, then folds its bruised light in—
The scoreboard ticks. The laundromat steps in.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
To a Nurse Ending Her Twelve-Hour Shift
When bleary hall-light blurs to soft gold glow,
The last call bell fades down the hush of wards,
She slips the stiff scrub cap from sweat-damp cord
Of hair, where tired pulses throb slow and low.
Twelve hours she held the fear that would not go,
Sponged fevered brows, clipped charts, spoke gentle words
To those who grieved, who ached, whose hope deferred
Hung thin as the thin gowns she tied and tied, so.
Now as she steps out where the cool air presses
Her sun-starved cheeks, the weight she carried slips—
Not all, not yet: a half-remembered name,
A hand that squeezed hers, small unspoken blesses—
The pavement glows, home waits, and on her lips
The quiet pride no tiredness can tame.

title: ode|the sound of a train at night
text:
I wake before I know I'm waking—
the long freight three miles off, dragging its chain
through cut cornfields, the boarded-up granary,
the creek where we found a tire swing
and one brown shoe.

It comes low first, under the bed,
then the horn: two longs, a short, a long,
same as the night Dad packed his duffel
and stood in the kitchen doorway saying
nothing the train didn't say for him.

The house trembles once, faintly,
like a kettle remembering.
Somewhere in the cars a wheel has a flat spot—
thock, thock, thock—
the limp I walked with for a month
after the ditch, the rabies shots,
the dog that wasn't even ours.

I count the crossings. There's the trestle
where Jeannie and I drank warm beer at seventeen
and wrote our initials where nobody'd see,
and nobody has.

The sound thins. The last car
always sounds surprised to be last.

Then crickets. The fridge clicking on.
My own breathing, which I keep mistaking
for something about to leave.

I lie here. The rail is cooling.
Somewhere a man in a lit cab
is drinking coffee from a styrofoam cup
and doesn't know he passed my whole life
four minutes ago,
and keeps going.

title: short lyric poem|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
3:17 A.M.
The dark has eaten all the clock’s soft ticks
except the thrum behind the kitchen wall—
refrigerator, low as a lullaby
someone forgot to finish, years ago.

I count its breaths the way I used to count
sheep that kept bolting over the fence
of my ribs, bare feet cold on the linoleum,
thumb smudging the smudge on the freezer door
where your sticker peeled last July.

It holds things I don’t dare let thaw:
a jar of pickles you brined, half-empty,
the carton of oat milk that expired last week,
a frost-furred cube of the soup you simmered
when I had flu, back when the bed still held
two shapes instead of one long, uncreased hollow.

The hum swells when I press my forehead to its cool metal,
a steady pulse that doesn’t ask me to sleep,
doesn’t flinch when I cry into the crisper drawer
full of wilted kale and the lemon you zested
for the cake we never baked.
Somewhere in its coils, it keeps the cold
from eating all the small, leftover things—
not life, not quite, not the warm weight of you,
but a hum that stays, when the rest of the world
has turned its back and gone dark.

I don’t turn the light on.
We don’t need light to know
we are both just boxes, holding tight
to what we can’t keep cold enough,
humming to no one,
so we don’t have to be quiet
with all the empty space.

title: dramatic monologue|teenage summer jobs
text:
The Name Tag
They stamped my name in plastic, pinned it tight
above the apron string, and called me “staff.”
Sixteen, and learning how to stand all night,
how much a small, rehearsed politeness weighs.

I folded shirts that strangers tried and left,
scooped ice cream until my wrist forgot
the shape of rest, and breathed the fryer’s theft
of summer, hair, and every dream I’d got.

The register ate my afternoons. The bell
above the door rang like a small alarm.
I smiled when customers returned a shell
of complaints, and learned to keep me warm
inside, while mopping up the closing floor—
earning keys to lives I’d had before.

title: villanelle|the night shift at a diner
text:
Night Shift Diner Villanelle
The espresso machine bleeds steam thick as gauze
when the trucker with a crow tattoo on his throat
orders pie that tastes like last year’s applause.

I wipe Formica where the ketchup draws
a map of every small town he won’t note—
the espresso machine bleeds steam thick as gauze.

The kid from the group home picks at his paws
of fried hash browns, says the moon’s a gloat
over pie that tastes like last year’s applause.

A state trooper leaves his radar on, pause
between speed traps, watches a moth devote
its wings to the glow of the neon “OPEN” clause.

The jukebox spits the third verse of a song
about a girl who left before the snow—
the espresso machine bleeds steam thick as gauze.

I stack clean mugs, count the cracks, count the flaws
in the glow that makes every face look like home,
even the crow, even the kid, even the cop’s cold jaw.
Last call at 4 a.m., no curtain, no pause:
the espresso machine bleeds steam thick as gauze
over pie that tastes like last year’s applause.

title: ballad in quatrains|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The Lighthouse Keeper’s Last Watch

The lamp still turns above the foam,
The sea keeps what the sea has known;
I wind the clock and sweep the dome,
One last night standing here alone.

I polished glass where storms had passed,
And fed the flame to ships unseen;
The salt has held my memory fast,
My shadow kneels where lanterns lean.

The bell-buoy calls through thinning rain,
A gull goes north without a sound;
I lock the log, I snuff the flame,
And leave my light upon the ground.

title: poem in tercets|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
Orchard Almanac

Spring
The frost heave caught Dad’s old work boot
half-buried under the Winesap, laces chewed
by the possum that dens in the root cellar wall.

We pruned too late, sap beading on the cuts
like thin, too-sweet blood, the bee swarm
that settled on the pear tree left by dusk
for the neighbor’s better hive. I found
a robin’s egg cracked blue in the clover,
no shell big enough to hold the whole of it.

Summer
The peach fuzz sticks to your sun-warmed arms
no matter how many times you wipe them
on cutoff jeans stiff with last year’s jam stain.
We haul hoses at 6 a.m., when the grass still pricks
bare ankles, and the air smells like cut alfalfa
off the west field. Last night a coon got three
ripe Elbertas, left pits half-gnawed in the dirt
like discarded teeth. We ate the sun-warmed ones
standing up, juice running down our wrists,
didn’t bother to wash the dust off first.

Fall
The cider press squeaks so loud it scares
the barn cat off the fence. My cousin’s kid
stuffed a whole rotting apple in the spout
and we had to fish it out with a wire hanger,
the first gallon of juice thick with wasps
we didn’t notice until we poured it in jars.
The leaves stick to the mud in crumpled
bronze patches; the deer come at dusk
to nibble the drops off the lowest boughs,
their eyes glowing green in the flashlight beam.
We leave the bruised fruit for them, this year.
No use hauling what won’t keep.

Winter
The ice coats every bare branch so thick
they click like chipped teacups when the wind hits.
One of the old McIntosh boughs snapped
under the weight last week, fell across the path
to the chicken coop; we haven’t moved it yet.
I found a half-frozen wren huddled in the hollow
of the trunk, brought it in in my coat pocket,
it died on the windowsill before the sun came up.
Tonight we’ll burn the prunings in a rusted barrel,
the smoke stinging our eyes, the cider spiked
with something cheap and warm from the liquor cabinet.
No buds yet. No promises. Just the dark
settling soft between the rows, the trees
holding tight to whatever they’ve got left,
not saying a word about what comes next.

title: spoken-word poem|time and memory
text:
Clockwork in the Flesh

The clock on the kitchen wall ticks slow,
its hands thin as the bones in my mother’s wrist,
back when she braided my hair by the stove
and steam wrote temporary names on the window.

Memory is not a photograph.
It is the smell of rain on hot asphalt
yanking me into a street I no longer live on,
where my father’s laughter bounced off parked cars
and the night felt endless as a held breath.

Time keeps its ledger in the body:
a scar above the knee from a bicycle crash,
the exact weight of a grandmother’s hand,
a song that turns the throat into a hallway
full of doors I cannot reopen.

I have stood in rooms that no longer exist,
run my fingers along furniture turned to ash,
spoken to faces the years have softened.
Some evenings, the past arrives without knocking,
sits at the table, asks for no pardon.

And still, the present keeps arriving:
coffee cooling, trains leaving,
light folding itself across the floor.
We are all clockwork in the flesh,
keeping time through what we carry—
not to hold the river still,
but to learn, again and again,
how water shines while moving.

title: villanelle|a jazz club in the rain
text:
I. Awning Breath
The rain staccatos on the awning’s edge
Where neon bleeds indigo through the gray
A brass note slips to meet the wet ledge

Each cab’s tire hums a low, unscripted ledge
Doors sigh to let in cold and cologne’s haze
The rain staccatos on the awning’s edge

A match strikes gold where shadow used to hedge
The first curl of smoke curls slow to praise
A brass note slips to meet the wet ledge

No clock counts time here—no sharp, rigid wedge
To split the dark from the soft, slurred phrase
The rain staccatos on the awning’s edge

We lean in close, let the world’s sharp edge
Fray to the thrum of the upright’s low praise
A brass note slips to meet the wet ledge

The door clicks shut on the storm’s rough pledge
We breathe in time, as the dim lights raise:
The rain staccatos on the awning’s edge
A brass note slips to meet the wet ledge

---

 II. Saxophone Lament
The horn unspools a thread of bruised blue
That tangles with the rain’s thin, silver thread
The bartender polishes glasses slow

Each note hangs soft as the mist that will strew
Wet grit on sidewalks where late wanderers tread
The horn unspools a thread of bruised blue

It tells of trains missed, of goodbyes we knew
Would stick like smoke to the lining of our heads
The bartender polishes glasses slow

Rain streaks the window like a faded tattoo
Of nights we outran the cold and the dread
The horn unspools a thread of bruised blue

No one calls out for a tune they all know—
We let the ache wind where the sound is led
The bartender polishes glasses slow

The last ice cube clinks in a glass half-drunk through
The hi-hat ticks soft as a pulse in the bed
The horn unspools a thread of bruised blue
The bartender polishes glasses slow

---

 III. Last Set Fade
The last note hangs, then melts into the rain
Umbrellas bloom like dark, unhurried flowers
We carry the song out through the wet lane

The bouncer nods as we step to the plane
Where streetlights bleed gold through the falling showers
The last note hangs, then melts into the rain

Our coats still hold the smoke, the low refrain
That hums in our bones through the small, cold hours
We carry the song out through the wet lane

No need for words—we both still feel the stain
Of blue that the horn wove into our powers
The last note hangs, then melts into the rain

The rain slows soft, leaves the sidewalks in grain
Of neon and shadow, the soft afterglow ours
We carry the song out through the wet lane

The club’s glow fades as we turn down the lane
The jazz stays warm, even as the night lowers
The last note hangs, then melts into the rain
We carry the song out through the wet lane

title: elegy|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
Moon over the tarps, white as a hospital bill,
it does not care that we are here.
It lands on a child’s shoe left in the mud,
on the bent rim of a bicycle wheel,
on a man asleep with his passport taped
inside his sock. It moves
through the razor wire like a rumor
the guards don’t bother to stop.

A woman washes a cup in a plastic bowl;
the moon breaks into small change on the water.
Somewhere a phone glows— a street in Homs,
a doorway in Mogadishu, a kitchen outside Kabul—
then dies. The dark keeps no receipts.

No lamb’s eye. No mother’s face.
Only the moon’s dumb, clinical shine
on a fence post, a propane canister,
a braided belt hanging from a pole.
It lights the latrine line, the registration board,
the dust that keeps arriving
from countries that no longer answer.

Tonight, even God would need a visitor badge.
But the moon slips past the checkpoint anyway,
laying its cheap silver over everything,
making the camp look almost like a field,
the tents almost like sails,
the sleeping almost like home.

title: ballad in quatrains|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
Ballad of the Far-Off Wildfire
The dusk hangs thick where the valley bends,
I lean on the fence where the clover ends,
A smudge of rust bleeds over the pine—
Not the sun’s last glow, not the moon’s low sign.

It breathes, it crawls, it paints the ridge,
Licks at the feet of the old stone bridge,
The wind steals whiffs of its sharp, hot breath,
Of scorched fern fronds and burnt heath.

 Ballad of the Far-Off Forest Fire
The dusk hangs soft where the valley dips low,
I lean on the rail where the wild roses grow,
A copper stain bleeds over the pine-line’s black crest—
Not sunset, not dawn, but the fire’s red breast.

It creeps up the slope where the old firs stand tall,
Eats through the moss where the wood thrushes call,
The wind carries hints of its sharp, searing breath,
Of pine resin burnt and dry bracken death.

We watch it glow bright when the stars prickle through,
A beast with no voice that the dark can’t subdue,
No cry reaches here, no crash of charred bough,
Just that slow, hungry gold on the far mountain brow.

It will eat till the rain comes to drown its red flame,
Leave blackened bare bones where the green once had name,
But here, on this fence, where the clover still smells sweet,
We watch it burn worlds that our feet never meet.

title: dramatic monologue|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
I was rolling a cigarette on the porch rail
when the ridge turned the color of a penny held to a match.
Not close. Twenty miles, maybe more.
No sirens. The dog asleep on her side,
twitching through a rabbit she never catches.

At first I thought it was just the smog
we've learned to breathe like a second language,
but then the whole underside of that cloud
went red, the inside of a mouth,
and I let the paper twist shut crooked,
tobacco spilling into the gap between boards.

My grandfather's axe is still in the shed
with the dark ring under its handle.
He used to say trees don't run,
like that settled something.
All those pines he marked for cutting in '89,
the ones he spared because they "had character,"
right now they're a noise I can't hear,
which is worse somehow —
the smoke arriving hours before the fact of it,
thin and tasteful at first, like incense
you'd buy at a gas station and later regret.

I counted three planes, then stopped counting.
The moon came up bruised.
Somewhere out there a deer is doing
the exact thing a deer does,
and it isn't enough, and it never was.

I went inside for another beer
and caught myself in the kitchen window
looking like someone watching a war
on a phone he could just put down.
When I came back out it had spread,
of course it had,
writing its slow orange cursive across the horizon,
and the dog woke and thumped her tail once
because it was me,
because the world, to her, is mostly me,
and I stood there holding my bad cigarette
and did not correct her.

title: villanelle|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
Villanelle for a Glove Strung on a Fence Post
It hangs where clover tangles the barbed wire’s rust,
palm cupped as if to catch the last of the sun,
one glove left, when the other turned to dust.

The knit cuff frays where the October gust
plucked loose the thread that held its stitching done—
it hangs where clover tangles the barbed wire’s rust.

A child’s? A farmer’s? Chapped knuckles, crusted
with pine sap, apple peel, the work half done?
One glove left, when the other turned to dust.

It watched the pickup sputter down the crust
of frost-rimed road, no hand reached back, no one
to see it hang where clover tangles the barbed wire’s rust.

It holds the ghost of a pulse, the quiet trust
of fingers laced, the warmth of skin it won
again: one glove left, when the other turned to dust.

Next rain will bleach it, next snow will crust
its hollow palm, where the cold has just begun
to settle where clover tangles the barbed wire’s rust—
one glove left, when the other turned to dust.

---

title: dramatic monologue|watching a parent grow old
text:
I. The Staircase

You pause halfway, one hand upon the rail,
And for a moment do not turn around.
The house that never seemed to tilt or fail
Leans quietly with you toward the ground.
I watch from below, a child still, almost,
Waiting for you to straighten and go on—
But something has begun to count the cost
In breaths between the landing and the dawn.
You smile as though the body were a door
That merely stuck, not one that slowly warps.

II. The Recipe

Your hand above the paper shakes too much,
So you dictate, and I am made to write.
A pinch of this. You say it in Dutch
Or whatever language memory keeps bright.
The cards grow soft as handkerchiefs with age;
The margins fill with questions I must ask.
You tell me mother did it on this stage
Of hunger, then go backward in the task.
I write it down exactly as you speak,
Knowing the measure leaves you as you teach.

III. The Driveway

At the car door, you shrink into your coat,
Smaller than I have ever seen you stand.
You wave me off as though you had some vote
In what the years withhold, what they demand.
I watch you in the mirror growing less,
One figure at the edge of a green lawn,
Still pointing toward the road, still meaning bless,
Still standing there until I am quite gone.
I drive. The highway opens like a sigh.
Somewhere behind me, you begin to turn.

title: spoken-word poem|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
Geese Over the Thaw-Line
Listen—
the sky cracks first, not ice,
a ragged V stitching the gray
where the wind still bites sharp enough
to split a feather’s quill.

They don’t stop for the frost that crunches
under the memory of summer lily pads,
don’t veer for the fisherman’s ice shanty
huddled like a lost matchbox on the plain
of white that holds the lake’s breath hostage.
Their wings beat the same old rhythm
grandmothers taught them before they could fly:
south, south, where the water doesn’t bite back,
where the reeds still hold seed for the hungry.

I watch them from the shore, my boots
stuck halfway in slush that can’t decide
if it’s ice or river yet.
One goose drops low, so close I see
the scar on its left wing, the frost crusted
on its beak like chipped sugar,
and it calls out—raw, ragged, unapologetic—
like it’s yelling at the ice to move,
like it knows the water under there
is still moving, still remembers
how to ripple when a wing skims its surface.

The V frays for a second, a single young bird
veering west, chasing a sunbeam that glints
off a crack in the ice like scattered coins,
before the lead goose calls, sharp as a compass needle,
and it tucks back into line,
the whole formation stitching itself whole again
like a wound that knows how to heal.

They don’t know I’m here,
watching their shadows skate over the frozen surface,
dark smudges moving faster than the thaw,
faster than the part of me that still gets stuck
on winters that won’t let go.
They don’t care that the lake is locked tight,
that the cornfields under the snow are still sleeping,
that some days my own bones feel too frozen
to lift off.
They just keep going,
their calls bouncing off the ice so loud
I swear I hear the frozen water hum back,
a low, rumbly promise:
I’m still here. I’m still soft under all this hard.
Follow the line. You’ll get there.

By the time the last honk fades over the treeline,
I see it—
a hairline crack snaking out from the shore,
thin as a spider’s thread,
where the sound of their wings hit the ice
and reminded it how to break.
I lift my cold face to the empty sky,
and for a second,
I swear I can feel my own wings
remember how to beat.

title: sequence of haiku|a mother's hands
text:
Sequence of Haiku: A Mother's Hands

Cool palms on my brow—
fever softens in their shade,
night folds back its claws.

Flour to the wrist,
they knead dough like morning prayer,
steam climbs through the kitchen.

Needle pauses, pulls;
a loose button finds its eye,
old coat keeps the wind.

Wrinkled now, and thin,
they tremble pouring my tea—
I steady the cup.

Fingers loose at last,
still they leave along my palm
a warmth with no name.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
Sonnet to Coffee Before the House Wakes
The dawn bleeds thin through cracked kitchen pane,
My slipper’s split, toe cold on linoleum,
The pot coughs, sputters, stutters half in vain
Ere it breathes dark enough to drown the hum
Of last night’s crickets, still clinging to the eaves.
I scorched the edge, today—too quick, too rough—
A splash of oat milk curdled, thin as leaves
That skitter where the gutter’s clogged with stuff
I ought to clear. The dog’s snore cuts the hush,
A floorboard creaks where no one walks, as yet,
No child’s shout, no spouse’s hasty rush,
Just me, this chipped mug (handle held by sweat
And glue, since last I dropped it, drunk, last March),
The dark turns gold, steam curls, no word, no arch.

title: ghazal|a beekeeper in winter
text:
Ghazal: The Beekeeper in Winter

The hives wear snow like shrouds beneath the pines,
and breath unspools from him in fragile lines.

He bends to listen where the cluster hums,
a dark gold ember sealed in wooden shrines.

No blossom now, no clover tide, no thyme—
only the wind rehearsing old designs.

His gloves are stiff; his smoker’s cold and dumb,
yet on his palm the ghost of honey shines.

He thinks of queens, of wings, of summer’s doors,
how sweetness hides through seasons that confine.

Tonight he’ll dream the orchard is alive,
and bees return like verses through the vines.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
I. The Wick at Half-Tide
The salt-crusted lens still turns its slow gold arc
Where gulls have roosted a hundred storm-tossed years,
I run my thumb along the chipped rail, scarred
By gales that ripped the shingles off the piers.
The logbook’s last page blots where my tea spilt thin,
I tally ships that passed, their lights long gone:
The schooner lost in ’29, the din
Of foghorns that outlasted every dawn.
The new electric lamp waits on the shelf,
No hand to trim its wick, no wick to trim—
The coast guard said it tends its own bright self,
No need for men to watch the dark grow dim.
I pour a dram for tides that never sleep,
And count the waves that know my name, still deep.

 II. The Fog Rolls In
At midnight fog blots out the farthest buoy,
The old bell clangs its rough, familiar tune,
I strike the match to feed the flame, as true
As when I first stepped here at twenty-one.
I trace the carved initials on the wall:
My own, my father’s, his before, worn smooth
By hands that passed the oil can, heeded call
Of every keel that cut the channel’s tooth.
The radio crackles, static-thick, “All clear—
The beacon’s synced, you may depart at first light.”
I do not answer. Let the dead men hear
The old flame breathe, before it loses fight.
For one last hour I hold the dark at bay,
As if the sea might let me stay, might stay.

 III. The First Grey Light
Dawn bleaches pink across the ebb tide’s lace,
The supply boat’s horn blares over the swell,
I snuff the wick, leave one small, salt-stained space:
A shell my daughter found, where the light fell.
I lock the door, do not look back, not yet,
The lens still turns, though now it burns by wire,
The gulls cry out the names I can’t forget,
Each wave a hand that waves, and will not tire.
They say the light outlasts the keeper’s hands,
That steel and wire outwait the mortal bone—
But they don’t know the dark the light withstands
Is held in bones that knew the storm’s first moan.
I step aboard. The shore drifts thin, then gone:
The light burns on. The light burns on, burns on.

title: poem in tercets|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
Underground Tides

Steel doors sigh open, swallow us whole—
shoulders pressed close like unbound books,
breaths fog the glass where the dark unspools.

A lurch sways strangers into shared nooks:
a student’s elbow, a tailor’s case,
earbuds leaking faint, familiar hooks.

We trace our stops on the tunnel’s face,
each lamp a heartbeat stitched through the night,
each stop a pause in the engine’s pace.

No names are passed in the swaying light,
yet knees brush knees in wordless truce,
two dozen paths braided tight.

At 34th, the crowd comes loose—
we spill to platforms, blink, depart,
still carrying the train’s low pulse.

title: dramatic monologue|the stars seen from a desert
text:
Mojave, 2:17 A.M.
The rental car’s AC died outside Baker an hour back,
so I’m out on the crust where the creosote don’t even bother
growing, boots crusted with the same salt the ’49ers
chewed when they thought the dry lake was the Pacific,
and the stars aren’t pinpricks, aren’t diamonds, aren’t dead poets
or angels punching holes in a tarp.
They’re the leftover glitter my niece shook all over her unicorn
birthday card three weeks ago, the kind that sticks to your jeans
for months, that shows up in your laundry even after you wash
the pants three times, even after you forget she was ever sitting
cross-legged on your kitchen floor, glue stick crusted under her nail.
I found a shard of a ’70s beer bottle half-buried in the playa,
brown glass smoothed by sand until it held the Big Dipper
like it was pouring it straight down my throat, no chaser,
the same dipper my dad tried to teach me when I was seven,
drunk on cheap scotch, pointing so far off the mark he identified
a jet on final to McCarran as Polaris, said it’d always lead me home
even when the streetlights blew out, even when I didn’t know
where home was supposed to be. The jet’s gone now,
its red blink swallowed by the dark, and the stars don’t care
about leading anyone anywhere.
Last month I sat in an oncologist’s exam room, the fluorescent
lights humming so loud they drowned out the sound of my own
breathing, while she pointed to smudges on the scan, white
as the salt under my boots, said We’ll watch these. The stars
are those smudges, too—burning so far away their light left
before my grandma crossed the Atlantic with a suitcase held together
with twine, before the first atomic test bloomed over this same desert
so bright people in Phoenix thought the sun had come up early,
before I ever learned to be scared of the spots growing inside me,
before my niece learned to shake glitter, before my dad forgot
how to find the North Star because the dementia ate the part
of his brain that held constellations, that held my name, some days.
A scorpion skitters past my boot, its exoskeleton catching starlight
like sequins on a prom dress left out in the dust, and I remember
I left my phone on the car hood, screen dead, no notifications
to yank me back to the world where people argue about things
that don’t glow, where the sky is washed out to a dull gray
by the glow of the strip an hour west, where I have to go back
tomorrow to sit in waiting rooms, to answer emails, to tell my niece
I brought her a rock that glows when the lights go out.
Right now though the stars are so close I could reach up
and pick one out of the dark, tuck it in the pocket of my flannel,
bring it back to the hospital room when dad can’t remember
how to find the sky, hold it up to the window so he can see
the light that left when he was still a kid, when he thought
the stars were campfires his dead dad lit to show him the way,
when he didn’t need anyone to lead him anywhere because
he knew the way by heart.
They don’t burn for him, don’t burn for me, don’t burn for the scorpion
or the creosote or the broken beer bottle holding the dipper.
They just burn, the way glitter sticks to your jeans, the way smudges
grow on scans, the way your dad’s voice sounds when he calls you
by his sister’s name and you don’t correct him, because for a second
you can be anyone under this sky, anyone at all, held by light
that left before you were born, that will keep coming long after
the salt under your boots erodes away, long after the last glitter
flake falls off the birthday card, long after the scans go dark.
I spit sunflower seed shells into the dust and watch them catch
starlight for half a second before they hit the ground, tiny meteors
no one else will ever see, and for the first time in months I don’t feel
like I’m waiting for the other shoe to drop.
The stars don’t care if you watch them.
They shine anyway.

title: pantoum|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
I found a leaf pressed flat in the biography
of someone whose name I’ve already forgotten.
The heat came up clicking, and nobody
bothered to silence the phone in their forgotten

coat pocket. Somebody’s name I’ve already forgotten
kept being announced, page after page.
A coat pocket answered, then stopped, forgotten
again by the stairs to the microfilm cage.

Kept being announced, page after page:
the gum under the table, the scratch of a date
due in the thirties, the microfilm cage
holding the weather, the weddings, the late

box scores, the gum under the table, the date
stamp sweating purple. A child near the stairs
held the whole weather of weddings and late
fines inside one whisper. Two armchairs

stamped purple and sweating. A child near the stairs
arranged crackers in stars on a book about sharks.
Fines inside one whisper. Two armchairs
sank with the private weight of remarks

arranged into crackers, a book about sharks,
a sweater left draped over Joseph Campbell.
I sank with the private weight of remarks
I didn’t go there to make. For example,

the sweater draped over Joseph Campbell
was the color of grape drank, not plums.
I didn’t go there to make, for example,
anything happen. The bums

were the color of grape drank, not plums;
the patrons, mostly: one man mouthing no,
not letting anything happen. The bums
of bees knocked the pane in a drift of snow

on the patrons, mostly. One man, mouthing no
to a page, kept shaking his head at a queen
bee knocking the pane in a drift of slow
golden light, by the globe magazine machine,

at a page, kept shaking his head at a queen
or a war or a recipe typed out in rhyme.
Golden light, the globe magazine machine
hummed like a fridge keeping time

or a war or a recipe typed out in rhyme.
The heat came up clicking, and nobody
hummed, not the fridge, not the keeping of time.
I found a leaf pressed flat in a biography.

title: blank verse meditation|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
Parking Lot, Late October
The asphalt breathes the last of summer’s tar,
crushed maple leaves stuck fast where summer bled
into the sharp, soft hush of fall. She sits
too straight, hands white around the wheel, as if
the car might bolt if she lets go one inch.
I reach to turn the radio down—old jazz,
the track we used to dance to when she was small,
her sock feet perched on top of my work boots—
then pull my hand back. Let her set the terms.

The key turns over. The engine catches, hums
like something half-asleep, half-poised to run.
She stalls it first, jaw tight, cheeks flushing red
as the sumac edging the empty lot,
mumbles a curse she learned from me, I know,
and I don’t correct her. I remember
my own father’s hand slamming the dashboard
when I ground the clutch for the tenth time,
the way I swore I’d never be that man,
that sharp, tight anger thin as exhaust fumes,
that fear that tastes like burnt oil and regret.

Easy, I say, soft as I’d talk to a sparrow
trapped in the garage, beating its wings blind
against the glass. Clutch out slow. Feel it bite.
She does. The car lurches forward, steadies, rolls
past the faded lines that mark the parking stalls,
the cracked sign for the old Kmart, boarded up
since last spring, the dented shopping cart someone
left tilted at the curb, as if abandoned
mid-thought, mid-errand, mid-ordinary life.
She glances over, grinning, half-terrified,
and I see the girl who rode her pink bike
no hands down our driveway, who cried when she scraped
her knee, who brought me dandelions crushed
in her small fist, who said she’d never leave
our house, never grow up, never drive away.

Brake, I say, when we reach the lot’s far edge,
where the chain link fence gives way to a field
of goldenrod gone to fluff, seed heads drifting
light as breath in the thin October sun.
She hits the brake too hard; we jolt forward,
seatbelts catching, and she laughs, shaky,
and I laugh too, and for a second I feel
the wheel in my own hands, the road unspooling
ahead of her, the stop signs, the sharp turns,
the nights she’ll drive too fast in the hard rain,
the boys who’ll break her heart, the days she’ll forget
to call, the way the world will not be kind
half the time, the way I can’t be there
to hit the brake for her, to steer her clear
of every pothole, every drunk driver,
every quiet grief waiting at the curb.

She puts the car in park, turns to me, eyes bright,
and says I think I got it, Dad. I nod,
because I cannot say what clots my throat:
that every lesson I have ever taught her—
how to tie her shoes, how to ride that bike,
how to patch a flat, how to say I’m sorry
when you’re wrong, how to leave the light on
for the people you love—was just practice
for this: for letting her turn the key,
for letting her press the gas, for sitting quiet
in the passenger seat while she learns to steer
into the wide, unmarked, unspooling world,
no map, no hand on the wheel but her own.
The wind lifts a strand of her hair, tucks it
behind her ear, the same way I used to
when she was small and buckled in her car seat,
asleep before we pulled out of the drive.
Outside, a flock of starlings lifts, unspools
across the pale blue sky, a moving script
no one can read, and the engine idles, low,
and I take a breath, and I say Okay.
Let’s try it again. Just take it slow.

title: free verse poem|a soldier writing home
text:
V-Mail, Scrawled in Foxhole Mud
The pencil nub is shorter than the stub
of the cigarette I smoked last watch,
lead smudged with loam that still holds
the ghost of last night’s frost.

I don’t write about the shrapnel
that nicked the kid from Des Moines’ ear,
don’t write about how the dark here
is so thick you can bite it, don’t write
that I haven’t heard a bird sing
in 47 days.

I write that the chow hall served something
they called meatloaf last Tuesday,
that I taught the stray dog with the white paw
to sit for hardtack crumbs,
that the sunset over the ridgeline
last night blushed the exact pink
of the peonies you planted
by the front porch step, the ones
you said would outlast the dandelions.

My hand shakes a little when I write
that the socks you sent fit perfect,
that I keep the photo of you and the cat
taped to the inside of my helmet,
that when the wind blows right
I can almost smell the lemon polish
you use on the kitchen table,
almost hear the screen door slam
when the neighbor’s kid chases his ball
down our street.

A mortar thuds three ridges over,
and I hunch closer to the page,
scrawl fast before the light goes:
don’t worry about the garden.
I’ll be home to pull the weeds
before the first bloom fades.

I don’t sign it love,
not at first—
I press my thumb, still gritty with mud,
to the blank space at the bottom,
so you can hold the part of me
that hasn’t learned to lie yet.

title: villanelle|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
The smell of Grandma’s kitchen never was
cinnamon or bread. It was the dark
of burnt electrical wire, the buzz
of a fridge motor gargling because
she never fixed it, the rubber mark
of a scorched pot holder. It never was
the pie. It was the dust in the jazz
radio, the bacon grease kept in a jar
under the sink, the rag’s slow ammonia fuzz.
It was the onion she let blacken, because
grief liked it that way, the cedar park
of her coat, the mothball. It never was
the Sunday roast. It was the strange applause
of moth wings hitting the fluorescent arc,
the lemon Pledge, the cat box, the fuzz
of peach mold, the wire hanger’s raw
metal tang, the exhaust from the parking
lot below. It was hers. It never was
a postcard. It was the exact dark jazz
of her absence: burnt wire, the fridge’s dark
buzz. The smell of Grandma’s kitchen was
not comfort. It was the wire, the fuzz,
the jar. It was the dark because
it was real. It was. It never was.

title: spoken-word poem|teenage summer jobs
text:
Name Tag Scabs
The plastic name tag pinned to my uniform
left a sticky, glitter-flecked rectangle on my chest
that I’d scrub at in the shower for ten minutes every night,
like I could wash the smell of fryer grease and minimum wage
out of my pores before my friends picked me up to drive to the lake.

First week at the snow cone stand,
I gave a kid a blue raspberry brain freeze so bad he cried,
his mom yelled that I was “irresponsible, just a kid myself”
and I didn’t say anything, just handed him a free extra drizzle of syrup
and counted the minutes until my 15-minute break,
when I’d sit on the cinder block out back
and text my crush that work was “so mid”
while my shoes stuck to the puddle of melted cherry slush
that never dried, not even in 92-degree heat.

My coworker Javi, who was 17 and already had a tattoo of a skateboard on his wrist,
taught me how to ring up my friends as “senior discount”
so they got $1 slushies,
how to lie to the manager when the cash register was $12 short,
how to sneak sips of coke from the fountain when no customers were looking,
the fizz burning my nose so bad I had to stifle a snort-laugh
while a lady in a linen suit complained that her lime cone didn’t have enough zest.

One slow Tuesday, a man in a pickup truck paid for a single scoop of vanilla
and left me a $20 tip, said “I remember being your age, working garbage jobs
just to afford gas to see your girl. Don’t spend it all in one place.”
I bought a tank of gas that lasted three weeks,
a pack of sour gummy worms,
and a cheap silver necklace that turned my neck green by August.

We had a rule: if the temperature hit 95,
we’d lock the stand five minutes early,
dump all the leftover syrup down the storm drain
where it swirled neon pink and electric blue into the gutter,
and run to the public pool down the street,
diving in still in our sticky polo shirts,
name tags floating off our chests and bobbing in the chlorine
like tiny, glossy buoys.

Once I had to cover a Saturday shift the same day as the music festival
all my friends went to,
and I watched their Snapchat stories from behind the counter,
sunburned and screaming along to songs I knew every word to,
and I almost cried when a group of middle schoolers spilled an entire large tiger’s blood
all over the front counter, sticky syrup dripping into the cracks of the register
while I mopped it up, my socks squelching in the puddle by my feet.

But then there was the old man who came every Wednesday at 2pm,
always ordered a small coconut snow cone, no extra syrup,
and asked me how my college applications were going,
said he’d been coming to this stand since he was my age,
back when it cost a nickel a cone.
He brought me a homemade chocolate chip cookie on my last day,
said “You’re gonna do big things, kid. Don’t let the fryer grease stick.”

By the end of August, my name tag was so scuffed you could barely read my name,
the hem of my uniform was frayed from where I’d caught it on the ice machine a dozen times,
I had $427 saved up in a crumpled envelope in my backpack,
enough for my first semester textbooks and a beat-up secondhand skateboard
Javi sold me for 40 bucks.

People say those jobs are meaningless,
that flipping burgers and scooping ice cream and bagging groceries
is just something you do to pass the time until real life starts,
but I still have that crumpled name tag in a shoebox under my bed,
next to the green-stained silver necklace and the festival ticket stub
my friends saved for me, even though I missed the show.
I can still feel the sticky slush on my wrists,
the burn of the fryer on my forearm from that time I dropped a basket of fries,
the way Javi and I would blast 2010s pop from the crackly radio behind the counter
when the manager wasn’t there, screaming the lyrics off-key
while the sun hung low over the strip mall parking lot,
painting everything gold.

We weren’t just making minimum wage.
We were hoarding crumpled tip dollars in our jeans pockets,
learning how to say “I’m sorry” even when we didn’t do anything wrong,
how to laugh when a customer yelled,
how to sneak out five minutes early without getting caught,
how to save for the things that mattered,
how to turn a cinder block break spot and a sticky counter
into something that felt a little like freedom,
sticky, sunburned, cherry-syrup-stained freedom,
the kind that only lasts three months,
the kind that sticks to your skin long after the summer ends.

title: elegy|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
Elegy Observed from a Far Ridge
The far woods burn—we do not smell the smoke,
only watch amber bleed through twilight’s cloak.
No crackle reaches where the cold winds blow,
just silent embers painting dusk in woe.

Pine spires bow, their emerald life undone,
red tongues devour what decades had begun.
Ash drifts like ghosts across the darkening sky,
each flake a breath the forest leaves to die.

We stand removed, yet feel the quiet grief
of ferns turned dust, of nests stripped leaf by leaf.
The glow still hums when night has claimed the ground—
a scar of light, where once the wild was found.

title: ballad in quatrains|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
The Kitchen's Wedding Song

The back doors groaned with morning frost
when crates of roses came;
the bride's white train slipped past the hall
while stoves caught up to flame.

We trimmed the stems and warmed the tins,
then hid behind the door;
the chef said, "Do not stare," but oh,
we'd never seen like before.

The bride came in like winter moon,
the groom like sun in May;
a hundred guests in silver light,
and us in suede gray.

Her father cried into his cup,
a child ran past with bloom;
we heard the vows through swinging doors
while basting birds in room.

The speeches rose; the glasses chimed;
the soup went out in rows;
old Auntie Mae forgot her name
but blessed the groom and rose.

The first dance turned beneath the lamps;
we watched from pantry dim,
two shadows in a borrowed song
that seemed made only for him.

The chef let out a quiet sigh
and said, "Now plates, all right";
we carried love on porcelain
throughout the whole grand night.

When midnight struck, the bouquet flew,
a bridesmaid caught the flowers;
we scraped the cake from off the floor
and counted quiet hours.

The couple left through lantern light,
their tires down the lane;
we wiped the last of champagne up
and hummed their old refrain.

No names were carved upon our coats,
no thanks in glass were penned—
but in that kitchen, warm and low,
we wished them world without end.

title: ballad in quatrains|learning a second language as an adult
text:
Second Language, 38
My Duolingo owl hoots from the cracked screen
where I fumbled subjunctives through last night’s beer—
the grocer’s kid laughed when I asked for *green
cheese* when I meant the unripe pears grown here.

The trilled *r* still catches like a fish bone stuck
in the soft arch behind my front two teeth,
last week I mis-said I was *very truck*
instead of tired to the abuela who brings me
pan dulce wrapped in the same wax paper she used
when her own kid mixed up “snow” and “soap” at school,
she slipped me an extra concha, bemused,
said tongues grow slow when you think you’re too cool
to sound like a toddler who trips on his shoes,
who points and grunts when the word won’t come right—
I found a note tucked in my takeout, blue
ink scrawled: *You said the sky was “very light”
last Tuesday, you were right*. I still freeze up
when the barista asks how my day went,
still reach for English when the words fill up
too tight behind my ribs, still mis-spent
half my lunch break squinting at street art tags,
sounding out each syllable slow, out loud,
the teen in the studded jacket drags his bag
past, pauses, nods: “You said that right. Proud.”
Last night I dreamed I argued with the moon
in that other tongue, no stutters, no slips,
told it I missed the way my words fit soon
as they left my mouth, no half-raw trips
over gendered nouns that make no damn sense—
why is a *key* feminine, a *lock* male?
No answer, but when I woke, the tense
shift came easy, when I told the mail
carrier how his dog chased a cat last fall,
he leaned on his truck, laughed so hard he sneezed,
said he’d moved here at forty, still would call
the “lawn mower” “the grass-cutting machine” please
don’t sweat the small stuff. Tonight I’ll sit
on my fire escape, flip through flashcards thin
as the onion skins my grandma would fit
in her soup pot, mumble each word, let them in
soft as rain on the fire escape grates,
not as a key to some far-off door,
but as the extra chair at the table waits
for the friend who you didn’t know lived next door.

title: dramatic monologue|grief after a dog dies
text:
The Empty Leash

I still set out two bowls at dawn—
old habit, sharp as splintered bone—
then watch the water glint alone
and realize one of us is gone.

The house has learned to hold its breath.
Your bed still keeps the press of you,
a warm ghost in the faded blue,
but no thumping tail answers death.

They say a dog is only years,
a small loan of breathing and light;
I signed for nothing, yet the night
comes collecting interest in tears.

I call your name into the hall.
The silence answers like a judge:
no muddy paws, no urgent nudge,
no body leaning, warm and tall.

Forgive me now for what remains:
the fur still tumbling through the air,
the leash that hangs beside the stair,
the hand that searches for your chains.

If love could dig past clay and frost,
if grief had paws, if prayers had teeth,
I'd tear the doorway out of death
and pull you back across the lost.

Stay, I would say. Stay. But the room
keeps only echoes where you fed—
and somewhere past the stars, ahead,
I hear a tail beat through the gloom.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a soldier writing home
text:
Sonnet to His Sister, from the Low Countries, 1586
My ink is froze to crumbs where the canteen leaked,
the scrap you sent is smudged where the trench muck seeped—
I plucked a reed to dip where the puddle reeked
of tanner’s bark and rot where the cows lie steeped.
Last week we burnt a farm where the old dame cried
she’d hid her honey casks from the Spanish looters;
our sergeant split them open, let the hounds inside,
said hunger makes the fastest of recruits.
I found a sprig of heather pressed to your last line,
it crumbled when I touched it, brown as old bread crust.
They say we fight for faith, for crown, for right divine—
last night I held a boy while his lungs turned to dust.
The rain’s come hard again, my wrist’s half numb with cold,
I’ll send this when the courier comes—if he comes at all.

title: dramatic monologue|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
I. The Pool at the Turning Tide

The sea has gone, but left a breathing room—
a hollow cupped in granite, fringed with weed.
I kneel where barnacles stitch light to bloom
and watch the small lives scuttle, dark with need.
Anemones close fists around the brine,
periwinkles spell their slow silver creed,
and one small shell drags sideways, making line
across the sand, as if the shore had need
of pilgrims bearing houses on their spine.

 II. The Borrower

I am not what I carry. Look again:
the coil is chalk, the former tenant dead.
I found the door ajar, unlatched by men
or time, and slipped my softness in instead.
My claws test air. My legs unhook the dark.
I do not trust the open. I have read
the gull’s sharp shadow, felt the heron’s mark
skim where I fed. So when the pools are spread
too thin beneath the sun, I choose my ark—
discarded weight, a roof above my head.

 III. Returning Water

Now the tide comes whispering up the shelf,
restoring what the rocks had briefly kept.
The pool unclenches, widens into self,
and every borrowed boundary is swept
back into ocean. I let my small house slide
through rising water; though the floor is stept
with surge and hunger, I will not hide
forever in the old shape. I accept
the moving dark, the cold, the opening tide—
small, armored, alive, and out of depth.

title: dramatic monologue|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
Ode to the Scent That Sticks to My Collar
The screen door whines before I even turn the knob—
it knows my weight, knows I’m coming
for the smell that leaks out under the jamb
like a secret it’s been keeping all week.

It’s not just cinnamon, though there’s that:
thick, sun-warmed, coiled tight in the rolls
she pricks with a fork like she’s taming small, sweet snakes,
their glaze crinkling thin as old tissue paper.
It’s not just the bacon grease she keeps in a mason jar
on the windowsill, congealed to pearlescent gold,
the same jar she’s had since my dad was tall enough
to steal a crust of bread off her cooling rack.

It’s the ghost of every pie that ever baked there:
sour rhubarb from the patch by the fence,
apple that bubbled over and burned black on the oven floor,
the mark still there, charred permanent as a birthmark.
It’s the lemon Pledge she wipes on the Formica table
every Wednesday, sharp and bright as her laugh
when I spilled Kool-Aid on her tablecloth
and she said *good, that one was getting too plain anyway*.
It’s the camphor in her apron pocket, the peppermint
she keeps there for when my tummy aches,
the faint, sharp tang of the menthol rub
she slathers on her knuckles when the rain comes.

Last week I stood in a grocery store bakery,
breathed in their factory-made cinnamon,
and my throat closed up. It was all wrong—
too sweet, too sharp, no ghost of bacon,
no undercurrent of the tomato sauce she simmered
for three hours every Sunday, the oregano she grew
in a chipped pot on the sill, the garlic she crushed
with the flat of her knife because she said the press
took all the soul out.

I still have the dish towel she gave me
when I moved away, folded in the back of my drawer.
When the nights get too quiet, too cold, too full
of cities that don’t know my name,
I press it to my face and breathe:
there’s the flour dust, there’s the coffee
she brewed so strong it could strip paint,
there’s the vanilla she poured by glug instead of teaspoon,
said recipes were for people who didn’t trust their own hands.

That smell doesn’t fade. It sticks to my hair
when I leave, sticks to the cuffs of my jacket,
stucks to the parts of me that still feel small,
that still climb up on her step stool to stir the batter,
that still think if I breathe deep enough
I’ll turn around and she’ll be there,
flour on her cheek, holding out a warm roll,
saying *took you long enough. I saved you the soft middle*.

They say scent is the oldest sense,
the one that cuts straight through the fog
of years, of grief, of all the doors I’ve walked through
since that screen door first whined shut behind me.
They don’t know it’s not just a smell.
It’s her hand on the back of my neck.
It’s home, bottled up in steam and grease and sugar,
waiting for me every time I lean in,
every time I let myself remember
how it felt to be loved
so thoroughly you could breathe it in,
so warm it seeped into every pore,
so permanent it outlasts even her.

title: short lyric poem|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
Tide Pools, Hermit Crabs
The bay has folded its salt into pockets—
not the postcard kind, but cracked basins
rimed with last week’s beer can rust,
a plastic tampon applicator bobbing
like a blind white shrimp.

I kneel where the ocean’s leftovers
simmer in their own small sky.
Anemones curl into bruised knuckles
when my shadow passes. A hermit crab
has claimed a shell painted
*KEY WEST 2019*, its spiral rooms
rented now to legs that don’t care
for sunset slogans, only the weight
of someone else’s abandoned roof
slung over soft parts.

Another drags a fragment of mussel,
iridescent as a gas-station compact,
its antennae tasting the air
for gull and for rain.
They scuttle over barnacles
that have glued themselves to rock
like unpaid bills, each small body
a negotiation with what the tide
decides to give back:
a shard of tile, a nail gone soft with rust,
one perfect spiral
that once held something else’s hunger.

When the water pulls back again,
I watch one climb a lip of stone
and pause—its borrowed house
teetering, ridiculous, alive—
before it slips into the next pool,
carrying its dark, damp fortune
into the next arrangement of sea.

title: villanelle|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
The Four Seasons of an Orchard
The orchard turns with every sun and frost,
First pale spring buds break through the bough’s thin sleep,
What fruit will ripen when the year is lost?

Pink petal drifts where crumpled moss is tossed,
Bees thread the bloom where cold winds used to creep,
The orchard turns with every sun and frost.

Summer hangs heavy, green and golden-crossed,
Small hard spheres swell where clover clusters creep,
What fruit will ripen when the year is lost?

Cider-scented winds strip gold embossed
From boughs bent low with harvest’s heavy keep,
The orchard turns with every sun and frost.

Now bare boughs creak where snow has laid its cost,
Dead leaves curl tight where buried root-systems sleep,
What fruit will ripen when the year is lost?

Each season stitches what the last has crossed,
The dark sleep holds the promise boughs will keep:
The orchard turns with every sun and frost,
What fruit will ripen when the year is lost?

text:

the whole sea folding like a laundry basket,
rain hitting sideways, making us not speak.
