and popped them, salt-slow, on the shoreline skin.

My mother would have said come in, come in.
The whole sea folding like a laundry basket
and popped them, salt-slow, on the shoreline skin.
We stayed because the light was turning brackish.

The whole sea folding like a laundry basket—
I kept one glove on, one hand bare and wet.
We stayed because the light was turning brackish,
because the lighthouse hadn't fired yet.

I kept one glove on, one hand bare and wet,
and couldn't tell the rain up from the spray.
The lighthouse hadn't fired yet,
my brother laughed; I looked the other way.

I couldn't tell the rain up from the spray.
Out past the breakers something dark kept turning.
My brother laughed; I looked the other way,
the way you do when you're still learning.

Out past the breakers something dark kept turning.
The storm came in low over Drakes Island.
The way you do when you're still learning—
rain hitting sideways, making us not speak.

title: ghazal|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
Ghazal: Moon Over the Refugee Camp
*For the radif “the moon”, strict metrical pattern of the Urdu ghazal, with the signature maqta in the final couplet*

The dust of tattered tents drinks the thin, slanted light of the moon—
a child chases a crumpled bread wrapper, lit by the moon.

A mother tucks a teddy missing one eye into her son’s thin arms,
her shadow stitching a quilt of quiet across the moon.

The border guard’s boot scuffs the chalk line where the world ends;
he does not look up, does not see the unblinking wound of the moon.

A man runs a thumb over the key to a house he will not return to,
its iron teeth biting cold as the old, scarred face of the moon.
They passed around one cracked jar of water at dusk, every drop counted;
now it brims, slow and silver, with the light of the moon.
A girl braids jasmine plucked from the camp fence into her sister’s hair—
no wedding drum here, only the low, humming croon of the moon.
The names of the lost are scrawled in charcoal on every tent flap;
tonight, each unspoken syllable is carved into the moon.
Do not tell me it is the same moon that hung over our olive groves—
that one knew our lullabies; this one knows only the tune of the moon.
*[Maqta]*
You who sit in warm rooms writing poems of soft, distant glow,
lean close: the cold you taste on your glass is the breath of the moon.

---
*Adherence to ghazal convention: consistent radif (refrain "the moon") closing every second line, monorhyme (qafia) across the penultimate syllable of each couplet’s second line, autonomous couplets each carrying a discrete, vivid image, tonal turn from intimate portraiture to direct political and emotional address in the final signature couplet, no slant rhyme or forced meter to suit English lyric cadence while honoring the form’s roots in longing, loss, and witness.*

title: prose poem|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
The Parking Lot Gospel

He adjusts the mirror though it is already perfect, his hands making a small religion of caution, and she turns the key like opening a door she will walk through for the rest of her life. The engine answers. The empty asphalt stretches wide as a forgiven Sunday, painted lines patient as pews.

Easy, he says. Easy. The word he used when she was small and balancing on her first bicycle, when the training wheels came off and the world tilted sideways into his waiting palm. Now the palm rests on his knee. Now the waiting is the harder part.

She presses the brake too hard and they bow forward in prayer, then laugh, then try again. Turn signal blinking its tiny amber confession: *I am going somewhere, I am not yet sure how.* He tells her to look where she wants to go, and the car obeys the eyes—a secret he wishes he had learned sooner, a thing he could not have taught her at five, at ten, at any age before the wheel was cool in her own two hands.

They circle the lot. Dusk arrives in soft increments. A shopping cart stands abandoned near the curb like a question he will not ask soon enough: what happens when she leaves this lot, when the road narrows and climbs and forgets to forgive?

She parallel parks between two imaginary cars. He says nothing for a moment, and in that silence she can hear it—the quiet rearrangement of his heart from guardian to witness. Good, he says. That was good. His voice is steady the way a bridge is steady, carrying traffic it knows will eventually travel elsewhere.

She kills the engine. In the sudden dark the dashboard glows, then dims. Somewhere beyond the lot the streetlights flicker on one by one, each a small green light, each saying go.

title: villanelle|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
Driver’s Ed, I-90 Exit 47
The parking brake sticks where his old work boot scuffed it.
He keeps his coffee thermos wedged between his knees,
says you don’t steer with your hands—you steer with your gut.
The dented minivan still reeks of the cut
marigolds we hauled home last week for the beds,
the parking brake sticks where his old work boot scuffed it.
A semi blasts; I yank us right, tires rut
the gravel shoulder where crushed seltzer cans spread,
says you don’t steer with your hands—you steer with your gut.
He doesn’t grab the wheel, doesn’t curse, doesn’t shut
his eyes tight when I lurch past the stop sign’s chipped red,
the parking brake sticks where his old work boot scuffed it.
He taught me to jump a dead battery, to cut
the ignition fast if the gas line starts to bleed,
says you don’t steer with your hands—you steer with your gut.
I will outlive the scuff on that brake, the rut
we carved that day, the marigolds gone to seed.
The parking brake sticks where his old work boot scuffed it,
says you don’t steer with your hands—you steer with your gut.

title: short lyric poem|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
Silence on the Line

The boat drifts slow where willows lean,
your uncle’s hands tie knots unseen.
No question stirs, no story starts—
only the oar that softly dips departs.

You watch the bobber, gold and still,
he nods when shadows cross the rill;
a tin of worms, a shared canteen,
the quiet says what words have never been.

At dusk he cuts the tangled twine
and hands you one bright perch to shine.
You both know why the river gleams—
some love is born in silent streams.

title: villanelle|a soldier writing home
text:
Letter from the Kabul Outpost, November

My pen skips where the canteen leaked last week.
The kid from Tulsa got a care package
of Sour Patch Kids, passed the whole bag around.

The wind here tastes like burnt tires and weak
instant coffee, the kind Mom used to nag
me for drinking, back when I’d sneak
a cup before school. Last night a streak
of tracer fire split the dark; I thought of Jack
chasing fireflies in our yard, passed out
in the clover when he was seven, cheek
squashed on a dandelion. The flak jacket
straps rub a raw line at my throat. I seek
the right words, cross out I’m fine, cross out bleak,
cross out the part where I can’t stop tracking
every crack in the concrete, every sound
that doesn’t belong. You won’t read this week
how the stray dog that hangs by the gate got sick,
how I shared my last granola bar, how I lack
the words to say I don’t know when I’ll be back.
The Sour Patch Kids are gone. The wind won’t speak.
I lick the envelope seal, don’t look back.

title: ballad in quatrains|drought on a family farm
text:
Dust Hymn
The well chain hangs stiff with rust and sigh,
mud cracks trace where the spring once ran.
Ma folds dishwater beneath dry sky—
one cup for the beans, one for the man.

The cornstalks rattle like old bone prayers,
the tractor bleeds in the sun-bleached grass.
Pa keeps his boot on the vanished stair
where clover rose when the rains would pass.

At dusk we carry the last pail far,
where the heifer stands with a dust-thin flank.
My brother counts every fading star
as though one might melt to a water tank.

Tonight the wind writes across the door
a name too cracked for our tongues to keep.
We watch the clouds form, then drift once more,
and all the dark is a bowl too deep.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
I. Clove and Cinnamon at the Threshold
Beneath the doorjamb, scent slips out to meet
My scuffed boot soles before my knuckles tap—
Warm clove that tucks sharp memory in my lap,
Cinnamon’s slow curl, honey-thick and sweet.
It wraps cold earlobes, thaws the frozen street
That nipped my cheeks, unknots the winter’s wrap
Of grey that clung to bus stop, curb, and map,
And folds me where the world is soft, complete.
I do not knock yet; I just breathe, and hold
That first thin wisp before the door swings wide,
Before the clink of mugs, the crumb-strewn board,
Before her voice calls out my name, bold
And bright as lemon rind. This scent’s the tide
That pulls me home, no compass, no reward.

---

 II. Yeast Rising by the Windowsill
The smell swells thick where sun slants through the screen,
Yeast’s soft breath, a living, slow perfume,
Butter that melts to gold across the room,
Jam simmered slow from berries picked last June.
It clings to tea towels stitched with ivy green,
Hides in the crack where the old oven breathes fume
Of burnt sugar crust, the sweet, familiar gloom
Of flour dust that settles, soft, unseen.
She kneads the dough, her knuckles dusted white,
And scent rises with it, round and warm,
No recipe, no measured, strict amount—
Just nutmeg’s pinch, the orange rind’s sharp bite,
A scent that wraps around me like her arm,
No place for hurry, no sharp edge to count.

---

 III. The Lingering Scent on My Coat Cuff
I walk back out when dusk bleeds purple-grey,
The cold air sharp against my full, warm cheek,
My pockets stuffed with rolls, jam-sweet and meek—
But the smell holds, when the house fades away.
It clings to my cuff, soft as the words she’d say
When I was small, scared of the dark, weak
From scraped knees, tears: it does not fade or peak,
Stays when the bus rumbles, when the streets sway.
Long after the last crumb is eaten, gone,
Long after her hands rest from kneading bread,
That scent stays tucked in the fold of my sleeve:
Clove, yeast, jam, all the soft things drawn
Into my bones, where no cold dark can tread,
The quiet love I did not know I’d grieve.

title: elegy|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
The sprinkler ticks once, then forgets  
its arc. Late July, and the tomatoes  
have unshouldered their stakes,  
heavy as dropped mailbags, split  
where rain found them, their wet seed-light  
glinting like solder.  

I kneel where you knelt  
and the dirt keeps your knees’ print  
for one more season, a negative  
no one thought to develop.  
The bee balm has bolted. The chives  
stand in their thin purple weather,  
useless, uncut.  
I pull a thistle and taste  
the blue milk of it on my thumb—  
you would have known its name,  
would have said let it flower,  
the goldfinches need it.  

Last night the motion light caught  
a possum nosing the compost,  
its pale hands like a priest’s  
folded around nothing.  
The raspberries, unpicked,  
ferment on the vine;  
wasps roll in their own drunkenness,  
slow, forgiving.  

Your pruners hang in the shed  
in a halo of rust.  
The spade has not quite forgiven  
the last hole. Somewhere  
under the flagstone, a frog  
holds its small coin of cold blood,  
waiting for the dark  
to finish arriving.  

What does a garden know  
of absence? The sunflowers,  
facing east all week, turn at last  
toward the empty chair.  
Not grief. Only the long habit  
of looking for you.

title: short lyric poem|an old piano left on the curb
text:
Curb Piano
Its ivory keys hold the ghost of a waltz,
chipped where small fingers fumbled false starts,
sun bleeds dark into its cracked walnut gloss,
rain hums soft through the hammers stuck fast.
A kid plunks three notes, grins, and runs on,
wind turns the loose page of half-forgotten score—
it never asked for polished curtain calls,
just one last hand to lean its chords toward.

title: pantoum|the first heartbreak
text:
I kept the mix tape in the glove box,
labeled in your slanted handwriting,
the night your mom's sedan threw gravel
and you said don't wait up for me.

Labeled in your slanted handwriting,
side B skipped on the third song;
you said don't wait up for me
outside the diner where the neon buzzed.

Side B skipped on the third song,
I learned the cough of your engine,
outside the diner where the neon buzzed,
you were laughing with someone's cigarette.

I learned the cough of your engine,
your jacket still smelled like rain and gas,
you were laughing with someone's cigarette
while I counted sugar packets by the register.

Your jacket still smelled like rain and gas;
I wore it once, walking home in March,
while I counted sugar packets by the register
and told myself the number mattered.

I wore it once, walking home in March,
the night your mom's sedan threw gravel.
I told myself the number mattered.
I kept the mix tape in the glove box.

title: ode|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
Ode to the Nurse Punching Out After Twelve Hours
The hand sanitizer crusts your knuckles thin—
a salt glaze, cracked where you curled your fist
to thump a sputum cup, to pat a back
that heaved like a foundered skiff in high tide.
Your badge lanyard frays where the patient grabbed it
at 3:17 a.m., when the ward hummed low
with the beep of monitors counting out heartbeats
like a metronome stuck on a half-time lullaby.

You know the linoleum’s every crack by scuff:
the chip by Room 4 where the dementia patient
kicked her lunch tray, the stain by the med cart
where the antibiotic dripped slow as regret
when the IV slipped, when you knelt for ten minutes
to hold the daughter’s hand while she cried
that she hadn’t said I love you in three years,
your compression socks digging half-moons
into the soft swell of your calves, your bladder
throbbing like a bruise you’d forgotten to name.

You peeled the sticky EKG leads off a chest
that had stopped fighting, tucked the sheet
up to the cold chin before you called the code team,
wiped the jelly from the collarbone like you were tucking
a child in after a long, fevered day. You laughed
when the post-op kid stuck a glitter sticker
dead center on your scrub top, right over the place
where your own heart had been hammering since handoff,
since the charge nurse said we’re short two, since the first
call light blared before you’d even set your coffee down—
that coffee you never got to sip, now cold as the rail
of the bed you cranked up for the man who couldn’t breathe
lying flat, who kept saying you look tired, honey,
who slipped you a butterscotch he’d stashed in his gown pocket.

The sun slants low now through the fire escape grates,
gilding the edge of the sharps container, the stack
of unused gowns, the whiteboard where you erased
the last name of the man who didn’t make it,
wrote in the new admit’s allergy to penicillin,
drew a tiny lopsided sun next to the kid’s name
because she asked you to. Your stethoscope hangs
heavy around your neck, still warm from the curve
of all those chests: the rattle of the COPD patient,
the flutter of the new mother’s pulse when she heard
her baby’s first cry down the hall, the slow, stuttering beat
of the woman who said she didn’t want to be alone.

You fumble your ID at the time clock, punch out
with a beep that sounds softer than the ones inside—
no alarm, no stat page, no voice calling your name
over the intercom sharp as a needle prick.
The cold air hits your face when you push through the door,
and for a second you don’t remember what month it is,
if the sky is supposed to be that soft bruised pink,
if your car is parked in the third row or the fifth,
your shoes still squeaking a little from the mop water
you tracked down the hall at 5 a.m., the butterscotch
still crinkling in your scrub pocket, the glitter sticker
catching the last light like a tiny, unearned medal.

You don’t carry the beeps home, not exactly—
they hum just under your skin, a quiet static,
the weight of all the hands you held, all the breaths
you counted, all the quiet “thank you”s that stuck
to your uniform like lint. You drive slow,
the world soft around the edges, your shoulders
dropping inch by inch as the hospital shrinks
in the rearview, and when you walk in your door,
you’ll peel the scrubs off right in the entryway,
stand under the shower until the sanitizer smell
washes down the drain, until the water runs hot enough
to melt the half-moon indentations from your calves,
and you’ll sleep like someone who has earned the dark—
not a hero, not a saint, just the hand that held the line
for twelve long hours, while the rest of the world
slept, or forgot, or didn’t know how to hold
the fragile, beating weight of a stranger’s life
gentle enough to keep it going, one beep, one pat,
one butterscotch, one quiet I’m here at a time.

---
The poem anchors itself in the specific, tactile, unglamorous details of shift work (cracked sanitizer skin, compression sock marks, cold coffee, scuffed linoleum) to avoid hollow heroic tropes, centering the quiet, cumulative tenderness of care that outlasts the shift’s end. It leans into the liminal space between work and rest, the faint hum of the ward that lingers under the skin, and the small, uncelebrated exchanges that make the weight bearable—details tailored for literary journal publication, rooted in concrete imagery rather than abstract sentiment.

title: poem in tercets|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
I. The Crossing

Black wedges cleave the porcelain sky,
their thin cries scoring silent air
above the glass where winters lie.

Below, the lake holds hard and bare,
a mirror sealed with frost and snow,
and not a breath is stirring there.

They beat the wind, then rise and blow,
gray feathers catching one cold star,
urged onward by the need to go.

II. The Pause

One veers, and then the squadron curls,
dark petals on a field of white,
a chain of unstrung, wind-tossed pearls.

They drift where icy branches bite
the margin of the frozen deep,
their shadows racing out of sight.

No footfall stirs that glassy sleep;
they hang, a question on the breeze,
then answer with one trumpet-keep.

III. The Departure

The wedge reforms; the pulsing line
draws northward like a living thread,
where thawing light begins to shine.

Their calls unspool above the dead
locked water, faint, then farther still,
till sky has swallowed what it said.

The lake keeps every echo chilled,
one feather on the crust of gray,
and all the wide world waits for will.

title: prose poem|hope after a long illness
text:
The First Breath That Doesn’t Hurt
The fever unspools slow, like thread pulled from an old sweater you thought you’d wear forever.
For months your bones were a house with all the windows nailed shut, your breath a thin thing that hid in the hollows of your ribs, too tired to climb all the way up your throat. The world shrank to the size of your bed: the chipped water glass, the way light slanted across the wall at three p.m., the hum of the fridge that sounded like a faraway storm you were too weak to outrun. You counted coughs instead of heartbeats. You forgot what it felt like to not be tired.
Then one morning you wake and the ache is gone—not all of it, not the faint ghost that lingers in the curve of your knee, the way your hands still shake a little when you reach for the mug—but the heavy, leaden weight that sat on your chest for so long you thought it was part of you. You draw a breath and it goes all the way down, fills every cranny of your lungs, sharp with the smell of rain on the fire escape, and it doesn’t hurt. It doesn’t catch. It doesn’t make you gasp for the next one before you’ve finished the first.
You swing your legs over the edge of the bed and your knees don’t buckle. The floor is cool under your bare feet, solid, not tilting like a ship in rough seas. You walk to the window and you don’t have to stop halfway to lean against the wall, chest heaving. You fumble the latch open and the air rushes in, carrying the scent of jasmine from the bush next door, the distant laugh of a kid chasing a dog down the block, the faint, sweet tang of someone baking bread three apartments over. You haven’t smelled jasmine in months. You forgot how bread smells when it’s still warm enough to curl steam into the cold air.
The daffodil bulbs you planted the fall before you got sick are pushing up through the cracked soil by the step, green shoots sharp as needles, bright as if they’ve been saving up all that sun just for the day you’d be well enough to see them. A sparrow perches on the windowsill, tilts its head like it recognizes you, like it’s been waiting. You hold out a hand and it doesn’t fly away, not at first, and you realize you haven’t held anything out to the world in longer than you can remember—have been too busy holding on, just holding on, to the sheets, to the edge of the sink, to the thin thread of yourself that refused to fray all the way through.
Hope here is not a firework. It is not a grand, blazing thing that splits the sky open. It is small, at first: the spoon that doesn’t shake when you lift your oatmeal. The way you can stand long enough to water the plants without sitting down. The first song you sing along to on the radio, voice rough and rusty, like a door that hasn’t been opened in years, creaking but turning all the same. It is the text you send to your friend, I’m up today, and the way they show up twenty minutes later with your favorite lemonade, cold and sweating through the paper cup, no fanfare, no loud exclamations about how you look like yourself again, just a soft smile, a chair pulled out on the porch, the quiet space to be whatever version of well you are today.
You will carry the echoes of the illness for a while, maybe always: the way you flinch a little when a cough tickles your throat, the habit of napping when the light dips low, the quiet gratitude that sits soft in your chest now, for things you used to not even notice. The world is brighter than you remember, sharper, like someone wiped a film off every surface while you were sleeping. The days stretch out ahead of you not as a mountain you have to climb, but as a path, soft underfoot, dotted with clover, with dandelion fluff that catches the wind, with all the small, unremarkable joys you thought you’d lost: walking to the corner store without getting winded, eating a peach so ripe juice runs down your wrist, staying up late talking just because you can, not because you can’t sleep for the ache.
You stand there in the open window, the wind tangling your hair that grew too long while you were sick, the sun warm on your cheeks, and you breathe in again, deep, slow, unhurried. For the first time in a very long time, you are not waiting for the next bad thing. You are just here. You are alive. The world is waiting, and you are finally, finally, well enough to meet it.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
Migrating Geese over a Frozen Lake

The glassy lake lies bound in frost’s cold chain,
its silver face unscarred by wind or tide;
when sudden through the pale sky’s open side
descend the geese, a loud, migrating train.

They beat the hush where winter shadows reign,
dark V’s that over shining stillness glide,
their cries like old vows none may now abide,
sharp with the salt of distance and of rain.

I watch them pass and feel my own heart rise,
a frozen surface answering their call;
they do not know the longing in their cries,

yet bear the whole dark north toward spring’s warm hall.
So love, once held in ice, remembers light,
and moves across the silence into flight.

title: ballad in quatrains|the stars seen from a desert
text:
Dust crammed the crack of my canteen cap,
I’d walked three miles past the last cattle guard,
my left boot sole flapped where the agave snagged it,
the truck died back where the barbed wire was hard.

First one pricked through the bruised purple dark,
then a spill, then a flood no town ever drains—
not the weak porch glow I grew up under,
not the streetlight bleed where the cop car idles.

I saw the one my grandma said was her brother,
killed at 19 when the well rope broke,
I saw the scratch on the hunter’s belt buckle
I found half-buried in the dry arroyo.

A scorpion scuttled over my boot toe,
I didn’t flinch, didn’t reach for the knife on my hip,
the stars were so close I could taste their tin burn,
like the old roof nails we pulled from the sheep shed.

I tried to count them once when I was seven,
got to 112 before the mosquitos bit,
mom called me in for burnt meatloaf and Kool-Aid,
said stars were just holes in the sky’s old quilt.

One fell fast west, toward the Nevada line,
I didn’t wish for money, didn’t wish for love,
just thought about how the road out here don’t end,
how my boots will wear out long before they do.

The cold bit through my flannel when I finally stood,
coyotes yipped far off where the mesa drops,
I didn’t learn nothing, didn’t feel fixed,
just had star dust crusted in the chapped edge of my lips.

title: villanelle|a mother's hands
text:
Mother's Hands
Her hands recall the kitchen's warm gold light,
where flour settled soft as April snow,
and wove the quiet hours into light.

They stitched the torn seams of the fading night,
held cups of steam when winter breathed below,
her hands recall the kitchen's warm gold light.

They bandaged knees and kissed a child's dull fright,
planted sweet peas that climbed the trellis slow,
and wove the quiet hours into light.

Through letters dim, through years of rust and white,
they smoothed my hair when grief began to grow—
her hands recall the kitchen's warm gold light.

Now veins trace roads beneath the papery white,
still fold the linen, still let kindness flow,
and wove the quiet hours into light.

I press them close; their warmth outspeeds the night.
Love, kneaded deep, does not depart or go:
her hands recall the kitchen's warm gold light,
and wove the quiet hours into light.

title: elegy|the sound of a train at night
text:
I. Rail Hush Before the Whistle
The dark folds thin at the cut—
first the hum, a wire thrum
too low to name, a pulse
the clover holds tight in its roots.
Screen doors rattle on their latches
before the ear catches it:
something coming, something already
leaving the last town where we sat up,
listening for it.

 II. The Whistle at the Crossing
It splits the dark like a split peach—
sweet, sharp, stung with the soot
of all the goodbyes it has carried.
Two long blasts, one short, one long:
the code the engineer blows
for the dead who walked the ties,
for the girl who waved from the caboose,
for you, who leaned your head on my shoulder
and said you could hear the ocean
in its steel throat.

 III. The Fade Into Distance
The last clack of the wheels
unspools from the rails like thread.
The crickets stitch the silence back
over the road where the arms lift.
We lie still, waiting for the echo
to settle in our bones, for the low thrum
to leave the floorboards, for the dark
to stop holding its breath.
Somewhere down the line, it is blowing
for someone else now,
the sound that stays, long after
the train is gone.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Autumn Leaves in the Cemetery

Beneath gray stones where silent names repose,
The autumn leaves descend in crimson showers,
Each fragile page unbound from summer's bowers
Drifts softly where the mournful yew-tree grows.
They cloak the sod where no wind dares disclose
The faded dates, the rain-erased flowers,
And trace in gold across the darkened hours
A fleeting warmth above the long cold throes.

Yet even here, where all things turn to dust,
The falling leaf proclaims no mere farewell—
It burns more bright in leaving than it lived;
So may I trust, when my own season's thrust,
That something in the letting-go can dwell,
And death itself be beautifully grieved.

title: ballad in quatrains|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Friday Night Under the Sodium Halos
(quatrains, slant rhyme, 8/6/8/6 meter)

The JV boys stack dented Gatorade jugs
where the clover grows thick through bleacher slats,
the air thick with burnt buttered corn dogs
and the tang of someone’s dad’s cigar.

Mia, the kicker, paints her cleats neon pink
between kicks, her chipped black nail polish
catching the glow as she boots one
over the goalpost, straight as a wish.

The announcer’s voice crackles through the speakers
like he’s talking through a tin can on a string,
mangling the last name of the new kid
who moved here last month from New Orleans.

The cheerleaders’ pom-poms shed tinsel
that sticks to the sweat on the quarterback’s neck,
his girlfriend in the stands braiding daisies
into the hair of her best friend’s little sister.

A dog trots across the fifty-yard line
carrying a half-eaten hot dog bun,
the whole crowd laughs so loud the ref
blows his whistle twice before he sees it.

The other team’s lineman has a tattoo
of his baby girl’s footprints on his bicep,
he helps our running back up when he’s tackled,
slaps his helmet like they’re old friends.

Halftime, the band plays a Taylor Swift deep cut
so off-key the crickets stop chirping to listen,
the concession stand runs out of pickles
right as my little brother gets to the front.

A group of seniors sneak sips from a flask
hidden in a hollowed-out geometry book,
their laughter sharp as the autumn wind
that carries the scent of pine from the woods.

The scoreboard flickers, numbers blinking
like a nervous eye, fourth quarter, three seconds left,
Mia lines up for the field goal, her breath
fogging the air in front of her face.

The snap is high, the hold is wobbly,
she kicks it anyway, the ball spinning
end over end, a tiny satellite
disappearing into the dark above the stands.

It splits the uprights, the crowd erupts,
someone sets off a handful of firecrackers
that pop red and gold against the sky,
the band starts playing so loud the bleachers shake.

Afterwards, we loiter in the parking lot,
our boots crunching on discarded peanut shells,
Mia signs a napkin for a little girl
who says she wants to kick too when she grows up.

The streetlights hum as we drive home slow,
the trophy propped on the dashboard between us,
our faces still sticky with cotton candy,
the radio playing some old song we all know.

Somewhere a cow lows in a nearby field,
the moon hangs low like a dented hubcap,
and for a second, nothing feels broken,
nothing feels small, nothing feels like it’s waiting.

title: dramatic monologue|hope after a long illness
text:
I used to know the exact weight of the afternoon—
how 3:17 bent the blinds into bars
on the ceiling I’d memorized, crack by crack,
the one shaped like Arkansas,
the one shaped like a question mark
I traced until my eyes went raw.

The medicine bottles had their own neighborhood
on the nightstand. Amber, brown, one chipped at the shoulder
like a kid I used to know.
I counted them not to take them,
just to prove there was a world
with fewer things in it than my own body.

Last Tuesday I walked to the mailbox.
That was the whole errand. The whole epic.
My knees were strangers writing letters
I wasn’t sure I wanted to read,
but the air—
the air smelled like wet driveway and gasoline
and somebody burning toast,
and I stood there like an idiot,
crying into a catalog,
because the world had kept on
without asking my permission.

Hope isn’t a sunrise, if you want the truth.
It’s the cracked spoon I didn’t throw away.
It’s the way my heart still drags its heel
around the block, then goes,
then goes one more step.

I’m not healed.
Some nights the dark sits on my chest
like a dog that doesn’t know its own weight.
But this morning I noticed a weed
pushing through the seam of the porch step,
and I didn’t pull it.
I didn’t pray over it either.
I just stood there
holding my coffee,
letting it be alive
in the only place it had found.

title: ballad in quatrains|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
The Garden After
(Quatrains, ballad meter)

The gate’s hinge whines the same old tune
I pushed through when I was small—
No hand has oiled its rusted tongue
Since last the frost did fall.

The rose he propped with split oak lath
Droops crimson where the bindweed twines;
Its thorns still snag my cuffed sleeve edge
As if to pass me signs.

He let the mint run wild, he said,
“For bees that know their way home” —
Now it creeps across the stepping stones
Where his scuffed boot prints are gone.

The sun-dial’s face is choked with moss,
Its shadow forgets to count the hours;
A single pea vine climbs the stake
He drove for last year’s flowers.

I knelt to pluck a stray clover head
Where the lettuce bolted to seed,
And felt the soft loam yield, as if
His hand still stirred the weed.
The wind slips through the apple boughs
He pruned the week he took to bed—
It drops one fruit, warm as a palm,
Right where his boots once tread.

title: blank verse meditation|grief after a dog dies
text:
The Empty Leash

The leash hangs still beside the kitchen door,
Its curled leather remembering the weight
Of a small body pulling toward the grass.
Morning arrives without the urgent bark,
Without the click of nails across the floor.
I reach for it by habit, then let go,
My hand closing around air where fur should be.

 The Shape of Absence

Grief is not loud. It is the second cup
Set down for one who no longer comes running.
It is the hollow in the worn blanket,
The silence under the table at dinner.
Somewhere beyond the window the world moves—
Birds alight, rain falls, other dogs are called—
But here, a name spoken only to walls.

 What Remains

Love does not vanish when the breathing stops.
It settles into the grain of the floor,
The path worn through the yard, the remembered curve
Of a head resting light upon my knee.
I walk now without a leash in my hand,
Yet something walks beside me, soft and sure—
Not ghost, but gratitude, keeping its pace.

title: short lyric poem|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
The Garden After
The pea trellis leans where he last propped it,
twine frayed thin as the thread he used to mend
his flannel cuffs. Volunteer dill
spills between the cracked row markers
he scrawled in pencil, half the names
smudged out by rain.

The roses he fussed over bloom wild,
thorns thickening where he used to snip,
petals blushing the same deep pink
he’d tuck behind my ear when I was small.
A single sunflower, dropped from last year’s head,
rises crooked by the fence,
stretching taller than he ever stood.

No one turns the soil now. Worms
work slow through the loam he fed
with coffee grounds and crushed eggshells,
with every quiet thing he never said out loud.
When the wind moves through the tomato vines,
it sounds just like him, humming off-key,
stooping to pluck the first ripe fruit,
warm as a hand held out,
as if he is still here,
letting the garden grow
exactly how it wants.

title: ode|an old piano left on the curb
text:
Upright in the Rain

The city forgot me beside the black bins,
my lid propped like a lid on a pot
that has boiled all its music to starch.
A sticker from the vet’s office clings
to my yellowed tooth of middle C,
where someone’s cat, Biscuit, got fixed in 2009.

My soundboard has breathed in the rain.
Last night the ivories—plastic, actually,
the dealer lied in 1962—
swelled until the white keys locked arms
and refused to play the national anthem
or the one lullaby the mother knew,
the one she hummed off-key while her son
pried at my pedals with a spoon.

A sparrow nested in my bass strings once,
back when I stood by the radiator
and the family shouted around me
in the key of slammed doors.
She lined it with a gum wrapper, foil
catching the sun when the boy lifted the fallboard,
and for one bright April I held
three small hearts hammering
under the low, patient G.

Now the sparrows pass. A squirrel
stashed a walnut in my cracked pin block,
then forgot the country of it.
Mold signs its name in green cursive
across the sheet music still inside me—
“Sunrise, Sunset,” page four,
a child’s fingering penciled in,
the notes circled like targets.

The garbagemen will come Tuesday.
They will not know I once held
a girl’s whole body learning to lean
into a chord, the bench creaking,
her bra strap slipping,
how she stopped crying when her hands
found the deep dark rooms of the lower octaves
and made the water glasses shiver.

Let the crusher come.
I have been furniture for a god
who only practiced Tuesdays.
I have absorbed enough grief
to tune a river.
By dawn the rain will have finished
my last composition:
one stuck key,
one sparrow’s feather curled in the harp,
and the long rest
where the music goes on
without anyone
pressing anything.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|an old piano left on the curb
text:
On a Curb-Side Grand Piano
The rain has smudged the ebony’s deep glow,
Where once quick fingers wove a lover’s vow,
Ivory keys bear cracks the frost did plow,
Its hammers stilled where waltz and dirge used to grow.
A scuffed mahogany flank leans soft and slow,
Its cast-iron frame holds faint harmonic now—
A child’s first scale, a toast’s triumphant bow,
The last sad note a widow breathed to woe.
Passersby kick its loose leg on their way,
Not knowing what sweet ghosts still haunt its strings,
What dreams once curled beneath its lifted lid:
Tonight it hums old tunes the wind conveys,
Till the scrap truck comes with clattering, cold wings,
To bear the last of song where all lost things are hid.
